title: \bf Conjecture
body_md:
Let $f:X\to X$ be a polarized endomorphism and let $Z\subsetneq X$ be a closed subvariety. If
\[Z\cap \mathrm{Preper}(f)\]
is Zariski dense in $Z$, then $Z$ is $f$-special.

label: th-sparsity
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-sparsity}
Let $M$ be either $\mathrm{End}_d^k$ or $\mathrm{Poly}_d^k$. Then, for every $D\geq 1$ and $1 \leq u \leq k-1$, there exists a proper closed subvariety $\mathcal Z_D^u\subsetneq \mathcal X_D^u \times M$ such that, if $Y \in \mathcal X_D^u$ is $f$-special for some $f \in M$, then $(Y,f) \in \mathcal Z_D^u$.

label: th-special-hypersurface
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-special-hypersurface}
Let $M$ and $D\geq1$ as above. There exist a dense Zariski open subset
$\mathcal U_D\subset M$, an integer $B\geq1$, and a morphism
\[
\mathcal H_D:\mathcal U_D\longrightarrow\mathcal X_B^{k-1}
\]
such that, for every $f\in\mathcal U_D$ and every
$1\leq u\leq k-1$, each $f$-special
$Y\in\mathcal X_D^u$ is contained in $\mathcal H_D(f)$.

title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-unif}

\#\bigl((\mathrm{Preper}(f)\cap Y)\setminus\mathcal H_D(f)\bigr)\leq B.

 \#\bigl(Y\cap\mathrm{Preper}(f)\bigr)\leq B.

label: prop-cderiv
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-cderiv}
Let $(p(f))_{f\in M}$ be a family of saddle fixed points satisfying conditions \eqref{eq-bun} and \eqref{eq-res}. There exists a family of $C^2$-linearization maps $(\theta_f)_{f\in M}$, depending continuously on $f$ in the $C^2$ topology, such that for every $y\in W^u_{p(f),loc}\cup W^s_{p(f),loc},$ the differential $D_y\theta_f$ is $\mathbb{C}$-linear and depends holomorphically on both $y$ and $f$.

label: prop-dynaslope
title: \bf Proposition
head: environment

label: eq-valeur
title: Démonstration
body_md:
Let us fix an unstable eigenvalue $\rho_i(f)$ for some $1\leq i\leq u$. We choose homogeneous coordinates on $\mathbb{P}^{k-1},$ depending holomorphically on $f,$ so that
\[e_i^u(f)=[1:0:\cdots:0],\]
while the remaining eigendirections are represented by the other standard coordinate points, indexed according to the ordering of the remaining eigenvalues. It follows that the differential of $f_*$ at the fixed point
\[\hat e_i^u(f):=(p(f),e_i^u(f))\]
is conjugate, after a suitable linear change of coordinates, to the diagonal linear map
\[(x_1,\ldots,x_s,v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})
\mapsto
(\lambda_1(f)x_1,\ldots,\lambda_s(f)x_s,\delta_1(f)v_1,\ldots,\delta_{k-1}(f)v_{k-1}),\]
where the coefficients $\delta_j(f)$ are given by
\begin{equation}\label{eq-valeur}
\delta_j(f)= \begin{cases}
\dfrac{\lambda_j(f)}{\rho_i(f)} & \text{for } 1\leq j\leq s,\\[0.4em]
\dfrac{\rho_{j-s}(f)}{\rho_i(f)} & \text{for } s+1\leq j< s+i,\\[0.4em]
\dfrac{\rho_{j-s+1}(f)}{\rho_i(f)} & \text{for } s+i\leq j\leq k-1.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Hence, $\hat e_i^u(f)$ is a fixed point of index $(2s+i-1,u-i).$ Its local stable manifold $W^s_{\hat e_i^u(f),loc}$ has thus dimension $2s+i-1.$ A resonance among the corresponding multipliers would imply a relation of the form
\[\lambda_1^{m_1}\cdots\lambda_s^{m_s}\,
\delta_1^{m_{s+1}}\cdots\delta_{s+i-1}^{m_{2s+i-1}}
=\lambda_{j_1}^{n_1}\delta_{j_2}^{n_2},\]
where $m=(m_1,\ldots,m_{2s+i-1})$ and $n=(n_1,n_2)$ are tuples of nonnegative integers satisfying $|m|\geq2$ and $|n|=1$.


Observe that, by \eqref{eq-bun} and \eqref{eq-valeur}, each multiplier appearing in this expression has a modulus in $[a^2,b].$ Since $b^{\ell-1}<a^2,$ this implies that if such an equality holds then $|m|\leq\ell-2.$  Hence, \eqref{eq-res} ensures that such relations are not possible.

Therefore, by the Poincar\'e-Dulac theorem, the dynamics on $W^s_{\hat e_i^u(f),loc}$ can be linearized. In particular, there exists an invariant manifold $W_{\hat e_i^u(f),loc},$ corresponding to the eigenvalues $(\lambda_1(f),\ldots,\lambda_s(f))$. This manifold has dimension $s$ and is transverse to all the remaining eigendirections, associated with the multipliers $\delta_1(f),\ldots,\delta_{k-1}(f)$, which generate the tangent space to the fiber $\{p(f)\}\times\mathbb{P}^{k-1}$ at $\hat e_i^u(f)$.

As a consequence, $W_{\hat e_i^u(f),loc}$ is transverse to the fibers in a neighborhood of $\hat e_i^u(f)$, and the natural projection onto $W^s_{p(f),loc}$ restricts to a local biholomorphism. Invariance under the dynamics then ensures that $W_{\hat e_i^u(f),loc}$ defines a holomorphic section over $W^s_{p(f),loc}$. The holomorphic dependence on $f$ follows directly from the fact that the Poincar\'e-Dulac linearization depends holomorphically on the map.

label: prop-bunching
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-bunching}
Under conditions \eqref{eq-bun} and \eqref{eq-res}, assume that $p(f)$
is in standard form on $B_p$. If $\theta_f$ is a $C^\ell$-linearization normalized by
$D_{p(f)}\theta_f=\mathrm{id}$, then its differential is complex diagonal along the local stable and
unstable manifolds, and depends holomorphically on both the base point and $f$.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Since the dependence on $f$ plays no role in the statement, we simplify notation by omitting most references to $f$.

The main step is to show that the bunching condition forces any $C^{\ell-1}$-field of real $2$-planes defined along the stable manifold, invariant under the dynamics and equal to $\mathbb{C}\cdot e_i^u$ at $0$, to coincide with the field associated to $e_i^u,$ induced by $\theta_f$.

To that end, we work in the coordinates defined by $\theta_f$ where the dynamics on the tangent bundle above the local stable manifold, which can be identified to $B^s\times\mathbb{C}^k$ is simply
\[(x_1,\ldots,x_s,v_1^s,\ldots,v_s^s,v_1^u,\ldots,v_u^u)\mapsto(\lambda_1x_1,\ldots,\lambda_sx_s,\lambda_1v_1^s,\ldots,\lambda_sv_s^s,\rho_1v_1^u,\ldots,\rho_uv_u^u).\]
Let $1\leq i\leq u$ and let $(P_x)$ be a $C^{\ell-1}$-field of real $2$-planes defined for all $x$ in a neighborhood of $0$, which is invariant by the dynamics and with $P_0=\mathbb{C}\cdot e_i^u.$ In particular, it is locally transverse to
\begin{equation}\label{eq-decom}
F := E_1^s \oplus \cdots \oplus E_s^s \bigoplus_{j\neq i} E_j^u,
\end{equation}
where $E_j^s := \mathbb{C}\cdot e_j^s$ and $E_j^u := \mathbb{C}\cdot e_j^u$. Since $F\oplus E_i^u=\mathbb{C}^k$, any real $2$-plane transverse to $F$ can be written as the graph of a real linear map
\[L\colon E_i^u\to F.\]
Accordingly, the Grassmannian of such planes can be identified with the space of these linear maps. Using the decomposition~\eqref{eq-decom}, each map $L$ splits as
\[L_j^s\colon E_i^u\to E_j^s
\quad\text{and}\quad
L_j^u\colon E_i^u\to E_j^u.\]
As a consequence, in a neighborhood of $0$, the family $(P_x)$ can be represented by a $C^{\ell-1}$ family of maps $(L_x)$, with $L_0=0$. The invariance under the dynamics of both the family $(P_x)$ and the decomposition~\eqref{eq-decom} implies that
\[L_{j,x}^s(y)=\lambda_j^{-1} L_{j,f(x)}^s(\rho_i y),
\qquad
L_{j,x}^u(y)=\rho_j^{-1} L_{j,f(x)}^u(\rho_i y),\]
where we still denote by $f$ the induced action on the stable manifold. Here, multiplication by a complex number is understood as multiplication by the corresponding $2\times2$ real matrix. Iterating these identities and writing $\rho_i=|\rho_i|\xi$ we have
\[L_{j,x}^s(y)=\lambda_j^{-n}|\rho_i|^nL_{j,f^n(x)}^s(\xi^n y),
\qquad
L_{j,x}^u(y)=\rho_j^{-n}|\rho_i|^nL_{j,f^n(x)}^u(\xi^n y).\]
For $i<j\leq u$, the inequality $|\rho_i|<|\rho_j|$ already implies that $L_{j,x}^u$ vanishes identically. For the remaining factors, we use the bunching condition. Fix $1\leq j\leq s$ and consider $L_{j,x}^s$. The other $u$-components can be treated in the same way.


Since $x\mapsto L_{j,x}^s$ is $C^{\ell-1}$ and real-valued, its Taylor
expansion has the form
\[
L_{j,x}^s(y)=
\sum_{|\alpha|+|\beta|\leq\ell-2}
(A_{\alpha,\beta}y+B_{\alpha,\beta}\bar y)
x^\alpha\bar x^\beta
+O(\|x\|^{\ell-1})\|y\|.
\]
Comparing coefficients in the invariance relation
\[
L_{j,x}^s(y)=\lambda_j^{-1}L_{j,f(x)}^s(\rho_i y),
\]
any nonzero $A_{\alpha,\beta}$ or $B_{\alpha,\beta}$ would give, after
taking moduli,
\[
|\lambda_j|
=
|\rho_i|\prod_{m=1}^s|\lambda_m|^{\alpha_m+\beta_m},
\]
which is excluded by \eqref{eq-res} and hyperbolicity. Hence all Taylor
coefficients of order at most $\ell-2$ vanish, so
\[
\|L_{j,f^n(x)}^s\|=O(b^{(\ell-1)n}).
\]
Therefore, by invariance and \eqref{eq-bun},
\[
\|L_{j,x}^s\|
\leq C(a^{-2}b^{\ell-1})^n\to0.
\]
The same argument applies to $L_{j,x}^u$ for $j<i$, while the case
$j>i$ was already treated above. Thus $L_x=0$ and $(P_x)$ is a constant distribution, as desired.

Returning to the original holomorphic coordinates of $f$, we observe that the images under $\theta_f$ of the dynamical directions along $W^s_{p(f),loc}$ define invariant $C^{\ell-1}$-fields of real $2$-planes. By the previous step, these fields must be constant, hence equal to the standard coordinate axes. Consequently, if $f$ is in standard form, the (real) differential of $\theta_f$ must be block diagonal, with real $2\times2$ blocks corresponding to the restrictions to the dynamical directions.

We first focus on the unstable directions. Since $\theta_f$ conjugates $f$ to its differential, the restriction of $D_x\theta_f$ to $E_i^u$, for $x\in W^s_{0,loc}$, satisfies
\begin{align*}
D_x\theta(v)&=\rho_i^{-n} D_{f^n(x)}\theta\circ D_xf^n(v)=\xi^{-n}D_{f^n(x)}\theta\circ D_xf^n(|\rho_i|^{-n}v)\\
&=\xi^{-n}D_{0}\theta\circ D_xf^n(|\rho_i|^{-n}v)+D_xf^n(|\rho_i|^{-n}v)O(\|f^nx\|)\\
&=\rho_i^{-n}D_xf^n(v)+D_xf^n(|\rho_i|^{-n}v)O(\|f^nx\|),
\end{align*}
where the last equality follows from the fact that $D_0\theta_f=\mathrm{id}$ and $\rho_i=\xi|\rho_i|$.

Since $v$ belongs to the invariant complex line $E_i^u$, the derivative $D_xf(v)$ acts as multiplication by a complex number $\rho_i(x)=\rho_i+O(x).$ Therefore,
\[\rho_i^{-n}D_xf^n=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\rho_i(f^j(x))}{\rho_i}=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1+O(\|f^j(x)\|)),\]
and this product converges to a complex number $\delta_i(f,x)$. This proves that the restriction $D_x\theta_f|_{E_i^u}$ is given by multiplication by $\delta_i(f,x)$. Moreover, the convergence of this infinite product is locally uniform in $f$ and $x$. Hence, $\delta_i$ is holomorphic in both these variables.

The same argument applies to the stable directions, in a simpler form. Indeed, for
$x\in W^s_{0,loc}$ and $v\in E^s_j$, we have
\[
D_x\theta(v)=\lambda_j^{-n}D_{f^n(x)}\theta(\lambda_j^n v)\to v,
\]
since $f^n(x)\to0$ and $D_0\theta=\mathrm{id}$.

This concludes the proof on $W^s_{0,loc}$ and the result on $W^u_{0,loc}$ is obtained by passing to $f^{-1}$.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
First, note that both conditions~\eqref{eq-bun} and~\eqref{eq-res} are symmetric and therefore also hold for $f^{-1}$.
Applying Proposition~\ref{prop-dynaslope} to both $f$ and $f^{-1}$, we obtain dynamical directions along
$W^s_{p(f),loc}\cup W^u_{p(f),loc}$ that depend holomorphically on both the base point and the parameter $f$.
As a consequence, there exist holomorphic coordinates in which $f$ is in standard form, as defined above
Proposition~\ref{prop-bunching}.

Moreover, the bunching condition~\eqref{eq-bun} implies that
\[\frac{\big|\log|\lambda_1|\big|}{\big|\log|\lambda_s|\big|}<\ell\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{\big|\log|\rho_u|\big|}{\big|\log|\rho_1|\big|}<\ell.\]
Setting $Q:=2\ell^2$, it follows from the trivial inequality $\ell^2-\ell\times\ell\geq0$ that the
$Q$-smoothness of $D_{p(f)}f$ in the sense of Sell \cite[Section VII]{sell} is at least $\ell$.
On the other hand, the non-resonance condition~\eqref{eq-res} ensures that $D_{p(f)}f$ satisfies the
strong Sternberg condition of order $Q$.
Therefore, by \cite[Theorems~5 and~9]{sell}, the map $f$ is $C^\ell$-linearizable, with linearization maps
$(\theta_f)_{f\in M}$ depending continuously on $f$ in the $C^\ell$-topology.
Finally, Proposition~\ref{prop-bunching} guarantees that the differential $D\theta_f$ is $\mathbb{C}$-linear
along $W^s_{p(f),loc}\cup W^u_{p(f),loc}$ and holomorphic in the base point and in $f$.

label: prop-holomorphic-jets
title: \bf Proposition
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
For $r=1$, the result and the assumptions are exactly as in Proposition~\ref{prop-bunching}. We may therefore assume that $r\geq2$.

Let
\[
K={\rm diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s,\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_u)
\]
and let $\psi:=\theta^{-1}$. Set
\[
P:=\partial\psi,\qquad Q:=\bar\partial\psi,
\qquad \mu:=P^{-1}Q.
\]
The map $P$ is invertible in a neighborhood of the invariant
manifolds. Since
\[
\psi\circ K=f\circ\psi
\]
and $f$ is holomorphic, the chain rule gives
\[
P_{Kz}K=D_{\psi(z)}f\,P_z,
\qquad
Q_{Kz}\bar K=D_{\psi(z)}f\,Q_z.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-mu-invariance}
        \mu_z=K^{-1}\mu_{Kz}\bar K.
\end{equation}

By Proposition~\ref{prop-bunching}, $D\psi$ is complex linear
along the local stable and unstable manifolds. Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-mu-zero}
        \mu=0
        \quad\text{on}\quad
        W^s_{0,loc}\cup W^u_{0,loc}.
\end{equation}

We treat the stable manifold; the unstable case follows by applying
the same argument to $K^{-1}$. Write
\[
\Lambda:=K|_{E^s}.
\]
For $1\leq q\leq r-1$, set
\[
T_q(x):=D^q\mu_{(x,0)},
\qquad x\in W^s_{0,loc}.
\]
Differentiating \eqref{eq-mu-invariance}, and using that $K$ is
linear, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-Tq-mu}
T_q(x)(v_1,\ldots,v_q)
 =
K^{-1}T_q(\Lambda x)
        (Kv_1,\ldots,Kv_q)\bar K .
\end{equation}

We claim that
\[
D^dT_q(0)=0,
\qquad 0\leq d\leq\ell-2-q.
\]
Indeed, after differentiating \eqref{eq-Tq-mu} $d$ times at $0$
and complexifying the relevant tensor space, each component of
$D^dT_q(0)$ is fixed by multiplication by a quotient of products
of multipliers involving at most
\[
q+d+2\leq\ell
\]
factors. Such a multiplier cannot be equal to $1$ by
\eqref{eq-res} and hyperbolicity. Hence every component vanishes.

Since $T_q$ is of class $C^{\ell-1-q}$, Taylor's formula now gives
\[
\|T_q(\Lambda^n x)\|
 =
O\bigl(\|\Lambda^n x\|^{\ell-1-q}\bigr)
 =
O\bigl(b^{(\ell-1-q)n}\bigr).
\]
On the other hand, iterating \eqref{eq-Tq-mu} in an adapted norm
yields
\[
\|T_q(x)\|
 \leq
C a^{-(q+2)n}\|T_q(\Lambda^n x)\|.
\]
Therefore
\[
\|T_q(x)\|
 \leq
C\left(
a^{-(q+2)}b^{\ell-1-q}
\right)^n.
\]
For $q\leq r-1$, we have
\[
b^{\ell-1-q}\leq b^{\ell-r}
<a^{r+1}\leq a^{q+2},
\]
by \eqref{eq-higher-bunching}. Letting $n$ tend to infinity gives
\[
T_q(x)=0.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq-mu-zero}, this proves
\[
D^q\mu=0
\quad\text{on }W^s_{0,loc},
\qquad 0\leq q\leq r-1.
\]

Since
\[
Q=P\mu,
\]
Leibniz's formula gives
\[
D^qQ=0
\quad\text{on }W^s_{0,loc},
\qquad 0\leq q\leq r-1.
\]
Thus the $r$-jet of $\psi$ is holomorphic along the stable manifold.
Its linear part being invertible, the same holds for the $r$-jet
of its inverse $\theta$.

Applying the argument to $K^{-1}$ proves the assertion along the
unstable manifold.

label: prop-asymptotic-rigidity
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-asymptotic-rigidity}
Under the assumptions and notation of
Proposition~\ref{prop-holomorphic-jets}, write the unstable
multipliers of $p$ as
\[
1<|\rho_1|<\cdots<|\rho_u|
\]
and assume in addition that
\[
|\rho_u|<|\rho_1|^{r+1}.
\]

Let $\Gamma\subset B_p$ be a complex submanifold of dimension $u$
intersecting $W^s_{p,loc}$ transversely at $w_0$, and let
$H\subset\Gamma$ be an analytic subset which is smooth at
$w_0$.

Assume that there exist $n_k\to+\infty$ and $w_k\in H$, with
\[
w_k\to w_0,
\qquad
y_k:=f^{n_k}(w_k)\to y_\infty\in W^u_{p,loc},
\]
such that the orbit segment
\[
w_k,f(w_k),\ldots,f^{n_k}(w_k)
\]
is contained in $B_p$, and all the unstable coordinates of
$\theta(y_\infty)$ are nonzero.

Then
\[
(H,w_0)=(\Gamma,w_0).
\]
In particular, $H$ contains a neighborhood of $w_0$ in $\Gamma$.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop-holomorphic-jets}, the $r$-jet of $\theta$
is holomorphic at $w_0$.

Let
\[
R:={\rm diag}(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_u)
\]
be the unstable part of $D_pf$, and let $\pi_u$ denote the projection
onto the unstable coordinates in the linearizing space. Set
\[
z_k:=\pi_u\theta(w_k),
\qquad
\eta_k:=\pi_u\theta(y_k).
\]
Since the whole orbit segment from $w_k$ to $y_k$ is contained in
$B_p$, the conjugacy relation gives
\[
z_k=R^{-n_k}\eta_k.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\eta_k\to
\eta_\infty:=\pi_u\theta(y_\infty)\in(\mathbb{C}^*)^u.
\]
Since the first coordinate of $\eta_\infty$ is nonzero and
$|\rho_1|<\cdots<|\rho_u|$, there exist constants $c,C>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-asymptotic-size}
c|\rho_1|^{-n_k}
\leq \|z_k\|
\leq C|\rho_1|^{-n_k}
\end{equation}
for all sufficiently large $k$.

Consider
\[
g:=\pi_u\circ\theta|_\Gamma:
(\Gamma,w_0)\to(\mathbb{C}^u,0).
\]
Since $\theta$ sends the local stable manifold onto the stable
linear subspace,
\[
\ker D_{w_0}(\pi_u\circ\theta)
=
T_{w_0}W^s_{p,loc}.
\]
As $\Gamma$ is transverse to $W^s_{p,loc}$ and has dimension $u$,
the differential $D_{w_0}g$ is an isomorphism. Thus $g$ is a local
$C^\ell$-diffeomorphism. By Proposition~\ref{prop-holomorphic-jets},
its $r$-jet is holomorphic, and therefore so is the $r$-jet of its
local inverse.

Let
\[
d:=\dim_{w_0}H
\]
and assume by contradiction that $d<u$. Since $H$ is smooth at
$w_0$, there exists a holomorphic submersion
\[
h:(\Gamma,w_0)\to(\mathbb{C}^{u-d},0)
\]
whose zero set is $(H,w_0)$. Choose a complex linear form $L$ on
$\mathbb{C}^{u-d}$ such that
\[
d(L\circ h\circ g^{-1})_0\neq0,
\]
and set
\[
\varphi:=L\circ h\circ g^{-1}.
\]
The map $\varphi$ is of class $C^\ell$, vanishes on $g(H)$, and has
a holomorphic $r$-jet at $0$. Let $P$ be its Taylor polynomial of
order $r$. Then $P$ is a holomorphic polynomial satisfying
\[
P(0)=0,
\qquad
dP_0\neq0,
\]
and
\[
\varphi(z)=P(z)+O(\|z\|^{r+1}).
\]
Since $z_k=g(w_k)$ and $w_k\in H$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-polynomial-small}
        P(z_k)=O(\|z_k\|^{r+1}).
\end{equation}

Write
\[
P(z)=\sum_{1\leq|\alpha|\leq r}c_\alpha z^\alpha,
\qquad
\rho^\alpha:=\rho_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots\rho_u^{\alpha_u}.
\]
For two distinct multi-indices $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the support
of $P$, the numbers $|\rho^\alpha|$ and $|\rho^\beta|$ are distinct.
Indeed, otherwise
\[
|\rho^{\alpha-\beta}|=1.
\]
This is impossible by hyperbolicity if $|\alpha-\beta|=1$, and by
condition~\eqref{eq-res} otherwise, since
\[
2\leq|\alpha-\beta|
\leq|\alpha|+|\beta|
\leq2r
<2\ell^2+1.
\]

Let $\alpha_0$ be the unique multi-index in the support of $P$ for
which $|\rho^{\alpha_0}|$ is minimal. Using
$z_k=R^{-n_k}\eta_k$, we obtain
\[
P(z_k)
=
(\rho^{-\alpha_0})^{n_k}
\left(
c_{\alpha_0}\eta_k^{\alpha_0}
+
\sum_{\alpha\neq\alpha_0}
c_\alpha
\left(
\frac{\rho^{\alpha_0}}{\rho^\alpha}
\right)^{n_k}
\eta_k^\alpha
\right).
\]
By the choice of $\alpha_0$, every term in the sum tends to zero,
whereas
\[
c_{\alpha_0}\eta_k^{\alpha_0}
\to
c_{\alpha_0}\eta_\infty^{\alpha_0}\neq0.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-polynomial-main-term}
        |P(z_k)|\asymp|\rho^{\alpha_0}|^{-n_k}.
\end{equation}

Finally, since $dP_0\neq0$, the support of $P$ contains a multi-index
of degree one. By the minimality of $|\rho^{\alpha_0}|$,
\[
|\rho^{\alpha_0}|
\leq|\rho_u|
<|\rho_1|^{r+1}.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq-asymptotic-size} and
\eqref{eq-polynomial-main-term}, we obtain
\[
\frac{|P(z_k)|}{\|z_k\|^{r+1}}
\geq
c'
\left(
\frac{|\rho_1|^{r+1}}{|\rho^{\alpha_0}|}
\right)^{n_k}
\to+\infty,
\]
for some $c'>0$, contradicting \eqref{eq-polynomial-small}.

Therefore $d=u$, and since $H$ is smooth at $w_0$, the germ
$(H,w_0)$ is open in $(\Gamma,w_0)$. Hence
\[
(H,w_0)=(\Gamma,w_0).
\]

label: prop-zariski-dense-unstable
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-zariski-dense-unstable}
Under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref{prop-holomorphic-jets}, assume
that $f$ is an endomorphism of $\mathbb{P}^k$. Write
\[
0<|\lambda_1|<\cdots<|\lambda_s|<1
\]
for the stable multipliers of $p$, and assume that
\[
|\lambda_s|^{r+1}<|\lambda_1|.
\]

Assume moreover that there exist $N\geq1$ and
$\tilde q\in W^u_{p,loc}$ such that $D_{\tilde q}f^N$ is
invertible and, setting $q:=f^N(\tilde q)$,
\[
q\in W^s_{p,loc}\setminus\{p\},
\]
the germ $(f^N(W^u_{p,loc}),q)$ is transverse to $W^s_{p,loc}$ at $q$. Assume finally that all the
stable coordinates of $\theta(q)$ are nonzero.

Then $W^u_p$ is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^k$.
head: environment

title: \bf Remark
body_md:
A natural strategy to prove the Zariski density of $W^u_p$ would be to
consider a H\'enon-like map of main dynamical degree $2$, obtained by
 the homoclinic transition through $q$ for a sufficiently large
iterate of $f$. The assumption that $q$ does not lie on any coordinate
axis of $W^s_{p,loc}$ suggests, possibly with additional assumptions, that the main dynamical degree should
strictly dominate all the other dynamical degrees, so that the Zariski density would follow from the results
of Bianchi-Dinh-Rakhimov \cite{BDR-continuity-super-pot}. However, we did not find a simple
proof of this domination.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Let $Y$ be a sufficiently small neighborhood of $q$ in
$W^s_{p,loc}$. In particular, the germ
$f^N(W^u_{p,loc})$ is transverse to $Y$ at $q$. Let $\mathcal P$
be the set of points $x\in Y$ for which there exist $n\geq1$ and
$\tilde x\in W^u_{p,loc}$ such that
\[
x=f^n(\tilde x),\qquad D_{\tilde x}f^n\ \text{is invertible},
\]
and the germ $f^n(W^u_{p,loc})$ is transverse to $Y$ at $x$.

Assume that $\mathcal P$ is contained in a proper analytic subset of
$Y$, and let $H\subsetneq Y$ be an analytic subset of minimal
dimension containing $\mathcal P$. By minimality,
\[
\mathcal P\cap H_{\rm reg}\neq\varnothing,
\]
and let $x\in\mathcal P\cap H_{\rm reg}.$ Choose $n$ and $\tilde x$ as above, and let $\phi$ be the local
inverse of $f^n$ sending $x$ to $\tilde x$. Set
\[
\Gamma:=\phi(Y),\qquad H':=\phi(H),\qquad w_0:=\tilde x.
\]
Then $H'$ is smooth at $w_0$ and $\Gamma$ is transverse to
$W^u_{p,loc}$ there.

We now apply Proposition~\ref{prop-asymptotic-rigidity} to the local
inverse $g:=f^{-1}$. By the inclination lemma, $g^m(\Gamma)$ converges
to $W^s_{p,loc}$. Hence, for $m$ large, it intersects
$f^N(W^u_{p,loc})$ transversely at a point $y_m\to q$. Writing
\[
w_m:=g^{-m}(y_m)\in\Gamma,
\]
we have $w_m\to w_0$, and, by construction,
$\phi^{-1}(w_m)\in\mathcal P$, hence $w_m\in H'$.

The unstable multipliers of $g$ are
\[
|\lambda_s|^{-1}<\cdots<|\lambda_1|^{-1},
\]
and the assumed inequality
\[
|\lambda_s|^{r+1}<|\lambda_1|
\]
is precisely the assumption required in
Proposition~\ref{prop-asymptotic-rigidity}. Moreover, the unstable
coordinates of $q$ for $g$ are the stable coordinates of $q$ for $f$,
which are all nonzero. Proposition~\ref{prop-asymptotic-rigidity}
therefore gives
\[
(H',w_0)=(\Gamma,w_0),
\]
a contradiction. Thus $H=Y$ and  $\mathcal P$ is not contained in any proper analytic subset of
$Y$.

This implies that $W^u_p$ is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^k.$ Indeed, let $F$ be a
homogeneous polynomial vanishing on $W^u_p$. Since
$\mathcal P\subset W^u_p$, the restriction of $F$ to $Y$ vanishes
identically.

Choose local holomorphic coordinates $(x,z)$ near $Y$ such that
$Y=\{z=0\}$, and write
\[
F(x,z)=\sum_{\beta} F_\beta(x)z^\beta.
\]
We claim by induction on $|\beta|$ that all the functions $F_\beta$
vanish identically. This is clear for $|\beta|=0$. Now, for
$q\in\mathcal P$, let $\Gamma_q\subset W^u_p$ be the corresponding
local branch transverse to $Y$. It can be written near $q$ as
\[
x=q+\varphi_q(z).
\]
Since $F$ vanishes on $\Gamma_q$, we have
\[
0=F(q+\varphi_q(z),z)
=\sum_{\beta}F_\beta(q+\varphi_q(z))z^\beta.
\]
Assuming that $F_\beta\equiv0$ for $|\beta|<m$, and using
$\varphi_q(z)=O(\|z\|)$, the homogeneous part of degree $m$ is
\[
\sum_{|\beta|=m}F_\beta(q)z^\beta.
\]
It therefore vanishes identically, so
\[
F_\beta(q)=0
\qquad\text{for all }|\beta|=m.
\]
Since $\mathcal P$ is not
contained in any proper analytic subset of $Y$, we get
$F_\beta\equiv0$ on $Y$.

Thus $F$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $Y$, hence identically.
Therefore no nonzero homogeneous polynomial vanishes on $W^u_p$, so
$W^u_p$ is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^k$.

title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
There exist two holomorphic maps $h\colon N_u\to N_{cs}$ and $g\colon N_{cs}\to N_u$ such that
\[X=\{(h(z),z)\ ;\ z\in N_u\},\ Y=\{(y,g(y))\ ;\ y\in N_{cs}\},\]
with $h(N_u)\Subset N_{cs}$ and $g(N_{cs})\Subset N_u$. In particular, $G:=g\circ h$ is a holomorphic self-map of $N_u$ with $G(N_u)\Subset N_u$. Therefore, it must be contracting, with a unique attracting fixed point $z_0\in N_u$. Since the points in $X\cap Y$ correspond exactly to fixed points of $G$, this intersection is equal to $x_0:=(h(z_0),z_0)$. Moreover, an intersection between the tangent spaces of $X$ and $Y$ corresponds to a fixed point of $D_{z_0}G$. As $z_0$ is attracting for $G$, this intersection is reduced to $\{0\}$.

label: le-dim-relation
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-dim-relation}
Let $(V_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ and $(H_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ be as above and assume there exist compact sets $K_{cu}\subset N_c\times N_u$ and $K_{cs}\subset N_c\times N_s$ such that for all $\lambda\in M$,
\[\pi_{cs}(V_\lambda)\subset K_{cs}, \qquad \pi_{cu}(H_\lambda)\subset K_{cu}.\]
Then
\[M':=\{\lambda\in M\ ;\ V_\lambda\cap H_\lambda\neq\varnothing\}\]
is a closed analytic subset of $M,$ whose irreducible components have dimension $m$ or $m-1$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Since $\pi_{cs}(V_\lambda)\subset K_{cs}$ and $\pi_{cu}(H_\lambda)\subset K_{cu}$, the closure of $V\cap H$ is disjoint from
$\overline{M}\times\partial\mathcal N$. Thus, its projection on $M$ has to be a closed analytic subset of $M$ and it corresponds exactly to $M'.$

Moreover, let $Z$ be an irreducible component of $V\cap H$. Then
\[\dim(Z)\geq \dim(V)+\dim(H)-\dim(M\times\mathcal N)
= (u+m)+(s+m)-(u+s+1+m)=m-1.\]
On the other hand, using again that $\overline{V\cap H}$ is disjoint from
$\overline{M}\times\partial\mathcal N$, we have that $\dim(Z)\leq m$.

label: le-proper
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-proper}
Let $(V_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M},$ $(H_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ and $M'$ be as in Lemma \ref{le-dim-relation} and assume that $M'$ has dimension $m-1.$ Then, if $(\tilde V_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ and $(\tilde H_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ are other holomorphic families of $u$-graphs and $s$-graphs sufficiently close to $(V_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ and  $(H_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ respectively, then their total spaces
\[\tilde V := \{(\lambda,z)\in M\times\mathcal N \; ; \; z\in \tilde V_\lambda\}\ \text{ and }\ \tilde H := \{(\lambda,z)\in M\times\mathcal N \; ; \; z\in \tilde H_\lambda\}\]
satisfy $\dim(\tilde V\cap\tilde H)=m-1$ and this intersection is arbitrarily close to $V\cap H$.

title: Démonstration
body_md: The assumption $\dim(M')=m-1$ exactly says that the intersection $V\cap H$ is proper. Thus, the result is a direct consequence of the stability of proper intersections (see e.g.\cite[\textsection 12.3]{Chirka}).

label: def-hl2
title: \bf Definition
body_md:
\label{def-hl2}
A holomorphic map $f$ defined on a neighborhood of
$\tilde{\mathcal N}$ is called a \emph{degree~$2$ horizontal-like
map of index $(s,u+1)$} from $\tilde{\mathcal N}$ to $\mathcal N'$
if the restrictions $f|_{\mathcal N_+}$ and $f|_{\mathcal N_-}$ are
degree~$1$ horizontal-like maps of index $(s,u+1)$ into $\mathcal N'$.

label: prop-hyp-graphs
title: \bf Proposition
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The first part follows directly from the fact that the graph transform
of an $s$-graph (resp. a $cu$-graph) by $f^{-1}$ (resp. by $f$)
is again an $s$-graph (resp. a $cu$-graph).

For the second point, observe first that, by definition of a
horizontal-like map, there exist compact sets
$K_s \Subset N_s$ and $K_{cu,\pm} \Subset N_{cu,\pm}$ such that
\[\pi_{cu}\big(\tilde{\mathcal N} \cap f^{-1}(\mathcal N')\big)
\subset K_{cu,+} \cup K_{cu,-}
\quad \text{and} \quad
\pi_s\big(\mathcal N' \cap f(\tilde{\mathcal N})\big)
\subset K_s.\]
In particular, for every $x \in \Lambda$, $\pi_{cu}(W^s_{x,loc})\subset K_{cu,+} \cup K_{cu,-},$
so the family of such $s$-graphs is normal. Moreover, by definition of the graph transform, if $x \in \Lambda$ then $f^{-1}(W^s_{f(x),loc}) = W^s_{x,loc},$
and hence $f(W^s_{x,loc}) \subset W^s_{f(x),loc}.$ By the second inclusion above, for each $y \in \Lambda$ we have $\pi_s(f(W^s_{y,loc})) \subset K_s.$
For $n \ge 0$, define
\[g_n := \pi_s \circ f \circ
\big(\pi_{s|W^s_{f^n(x),loc}}\big)^{-1}.\]
Then $g_n(N_s) \subset K_s$, and therefore the family $(g_n)_{n \ge 0}$
uniformly contracts the Kobayashi metric on $N_s$.
It follows that the diameter of the image of $G_n := g_{n-1} \circ \cdots \circ g_0$
converges to $0$.

Since
\[\pi_s\big(f^n(W^s_{x,loc})\big)
\subset G_n(N_s),\]
and since $f^n(W^s_{x,loc}) \subset W^s_{f^n(x),loc}$,
which belong to a normal family of $s$-graphs,
we conclude that for every $z \in W^s_{x,loc}$, $d(f^n(x),f^n(z))$ converges to $0.$
Hence $W^s_{x,loc}$ coincides with the standard local stable
manifold of $x$. The unstable case is proved in the same way.
                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                           
                                                                                      
                                       

If we have a holomorphic family of degree $2$ horizontal-like maps $(f_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ parametrized by $M,$ then by \cite[Theorem~B]{jonsson-motion_hyperbolic} the natural extension $\hat\Lambda(f_\lambda)$ (resp. $\Lambda(f_\lambda)$) can be followed by a holomorphic motion (resp. branched holomorphic motion). The construction above directly implies that if $\hat x(\lambda)\in\hat\Lambda(\lambda)$ (resp. $x(\lambda)\in\Lambda(\lambda)$) then $W^u_{\hat x(\lambda),loc}$ and $W^s_{x(\lambda),loc}$ both depend holomorphically on $\lambda.$

label: prop-renor
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-renor}
Let $(f_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ and $\Gamma_0$ as above. Define by induction, for $n\geq0$
\[\Gamma_{n+1}:=F(\Gamma_n)\cap(\mathcal N\times M).\]
Then, $(\Gamma_n)_{n\geq0}$ is a sequence of closed analytic subsets of $\mathcal N\times M$ converging (possibly with some multiplicity) to
\[W^u_{r(f_\lambda),loc}\times\{\lambda\},\]
for some $\lambda\in M.$
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Observe first that, since for each $\lambda\in M$,
\[f_\lambda(\overline{\mathcal N})\cap\partial\mathcal N
\subset \partial_{u}\mathcal N,\]
each $\Gamma_n$ also satisfies~\eqref{eq-renor}.

On the other hand, again by~\eqref{eq-renor}, the restriction of
the projection
\[\pi\colon\mathcal N\times M\to N_u\]
to $\Gamma_n$ is a ramified covering. Its degree coincides
with the number of intersection points (counted with multiplicity)
between $\Gamma_n$ and
\[H := \{(z,\lambda)\in \mathcal N\times M \; ; \; z\in H_\lambda\},\]
where $(H_\lambda)_{\lambda\in M}$ is a family of $s$-graphs.
Since each $f_\lambda$ has degree~$1$, the sets $H'_\lambda:=f_\lambda^{-1}(H_\lambda)\cap \mathcal N$
also form a family of $s$-graphs, whose total space is denoted by $H'$. Then the number of intersection points (with multiplicity)
of $\Gamma_n\cap H'$ coincides with that of
$\Gamma_{n+1}\cap H$. It follows that the degree of
$\Gamma_n$ is independent of $n$.

Hence $(\Gamma_n)_{n\geq0}$ is a sequence of analytic sets of
dimension $u$ in $\mathcal N\times M$ with uniformly bounded
mass. By Bishop's theorem, it converges (up to extraction) to an
analytic set $\Gamma_\infty$ of dimension $u$. Moreover,
by construction, $\Gamma_n\subset
\bigcap_{i=0}^n F^i(\mathcal N\times M)$, hence
\[\Gamma_\infty\subset \mathcal W^u_{r,loc}.\]

Finally, by assumption, $\Gamma_0$ intersects
$\mathcal W^s_{r,loc}$ at a unique point
$(x_0,\lambda_0)$. If $\lambda\neq\lambda_0$, then
\[\Gamma_0\cap (\mathcal N\times\{\lambda\})=
\Gamma_0(\lambda)\times\{\lambda\},\]
where $\Gamma_0(\lambda)$ is a closed subset of $\mathcal N$ disjoint
from $W^s_{r(\lambda),loc}$. It follows that there exists
$n\geq0$ such that
\[\bigcap_{i=0}^n f_\lambda^{-i}(\mathcal N)\cap\Gamma_0(\lambda)=\varnothing,\]
and therefore
\[\Gamma_\infty\cap (\mathcal N\times\{\lambda\})=\varnothing.\]
Hence,
\[\Gamma_\infty\subset
W^u_{r(\lambda_0),loc}\times\{\lambda_0\}.\]
By dimensional considerations, this inclusion is in fact an equality.
Since the limit does not depend on the subsequence, the sequence
itself converges.

title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:formulafibered}
For any $m\geq\dim \mathcal{Y}$, there is $C(m)\geq1$ depending only on $m$ such that
\[(\pi_{\mathcal{Y},m})_*\left(\hat{T}_{\hat{f}^{[m]}}^{\wedge( um+\dim\mathcal Y)}\wedge[\hat{\mathcal{Y}}^{[m]}]\right)\geq C(m)\cdot\mu_{\mathcal{Y}}\geq T_{\mathcal{Y}}^{\wedge \dim \mathcal{Y}}.\]
Moreover, if $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}$ is a family of hypersurfaces, then $\mu_{\mathcal{Y}}$ and $ T_{\mathcal{Y}}^{\wedge \dim \mathcal{Y}}$ are proportional.

label: prop-empty-interior
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{prop-empty-interior}
Let $\hat{f}:\mathbb{P}^k\times \mathcal{Y}\to \mathbb{P}^k\times \mathcal{Y}$ be a family of regular polynomial endomorphisms of degree $d$ of the affine space parametrized by a quasiprojective variety $\mathcal{Y}$ and let $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}\subset\mathbb{P}^k\times \mathcal{Y}$ be an irreducible closed subvariety,  all defined over a number field. Assume that $p:\hat{\mathcal{Y}}\to \mathcal{Y}$ is surjective and that $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}$ intersects properly $H_\infty\times \mathcal{Y}$.
Assume in addition that
\[\int_{\mathcal{Y}(\mathbb{C})}G_{\mathcal{Y}}\cdot\mu^{\mathrm{pol}}_{\mathcal{Y}}>0.\]
Then there exists $Z\subsetneq \mathcal Y$ Zariski-closed, $\varepsilon>0$ and an integer $N\geq1$ such that for any $t\in (\mathcal{Y}\setminus Z)(\bar{\mathbb{Q}})$, there is a proper subvariety $W_t\subsetneq Y_t$ with $\deg(W_t)\leq N$ such that
\[\{z\in Y_t(\bar{\mathbb{Q}})\, : \ \hat{h}_{f_t}(z)\leq \varepsilon\}\subseteq W_t.\]

label: tm:small-distrib
title: \bf Theorem

label: prop-positivevolume
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-positivevolume}
Under the assumptions \textup{\ref{it:cond1}} and \textup{\ref{it:cond2}} above, we have
\[(z_0,t_0)\in \mathrm{supp}\left(\bigwedge_{j=1}^m p_j^*\left(\hat{T}_{\hat f}^{\wedge(u+1)}\right)\wedge[\hat{\mathcal Y}^{[m]}]\right).\]
In particular, if $m=\dim M$ and if $(f_t)_{t\in M}$ is a family of regular polynomial endomorphisms of $\mathbb{C}^k$, and if $r_j(f_{t_0})\in {\mathbb C}^k$ for all $j$, then we have
\[t_0\in \mathrm{supp}\left(\mu_{\mathcal{Y}}^{\mathrm{pol}}\right).\]
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
For simplicity, we set $F:=\hat f^{[m]}$ and
\[T:=\bigwedge_{j=1}^m p_j^*\left(\hat{T}_{\hat f}^{\wedge(u+1)}\right).\]
Since $\hat{T}_{\hat f}$ has continuous potentials, for any analytic submanifold $M'\subset M$ of dimension $m$ with ${t_0}\in M'$, we have
\[\mathrm{supp}\left(T|_{\pi_{[m]}^{-1}(M')}\wedge [\hat{\mathcal Y}^{[m]}\cap\pi_{[m]}^{-1}(M')]\right)\subset \mathrm{supp}\left(T\wedge [\hat{\mathcal Y}^{[m]}]\right)\]
by e.g.~\cite[Lemma~6.3]{Article1}. Hence, we may replace $M$ by such a submanifold $M'$ of dimension $m$, and $\hat{\mathcal Y}^{[m]}$ by
$\hat{\mathcal Y}^{[m]}\cap\pi_{[m]}^{-1}(M')$, so as to assume that $\mathcal W_{r,loc}^s\cap F^n(U)$ reduces to a single point, provided $U$ is chosen sufficiently small in $\hat{\mathcal Y}^{[m]}.$

On the other hand, recall that $r(f_{t_0}):=(r_1(f_{t_0}),\ldots,r_m(f_{t_0}))$ is a saddle periodic point of index $(sm,(u+1)m)$ for $f_{t_0}^{[m]}.$ Its period is the lcm of the periods of the saddle points $r_j(f_{t_0}).$ As the Green current of $F$ is the same that for its iterates, we can actually assume that this period is $1.$ On the other hand, as the index of $r(f_{t_0})$ is $(m s,m(u+1))$, there exist two polydiscs $N_s\subset\mathbb{C}^{m s}$ and $N_u\subset\mathbb{C}^{m(u+1)}$ and a neighborhood $\mathcal N$ of $r(f_{t_0})$ biholomorphic to $N_s\times N_u$ such that $f_{t_0}^{[m]}$ is a horizontal-like map on $\mathcal N$ of index $(m s,m(u+1))$ and of degree $1$ in these coordinates. As this property is stable under perturbations and that the statement is purely local, possibly by shrinking $M$, we could assume that the map $f^{[m]}_t$ is also horizontal-like on $\mathcal N$ of index $(m s,m(u+1))$ and of degree $1$ for all $t\in M.$

We now restrict the local stable and unstable manifolds of $r(f_t)$ to $\mathcal N$, and adjust the notation
\[\mathcal W_{r,loc}^s:=\left\{(x,t)\in \mathcal N\times M\, : \ x\in W_{r(f_t),loc}^s\right\}\]
and
\[\mathcal W_{r,loc}^u:=\left\{(x,t)\in \mathcal N\times M\, : \ x\in W_{r(f_t),loc}^u\right\}.\]
By the discussion above, after possibly increasing $n_0$ and
shrinking $U$, we may assume that
$\Gamma_0:=F^{n_0}(U)$ intersects
$\mathcal W_{r,loc}^s$ at a unique point. Moreover, since points outside $\mathcal W^s_{r,loc}$ escape from $\mathcal N$ under the dynamics, we may, after possibly
adjusting $n_0$ and $U$ again, assume that $\Gamma_0$ is closed in $\mathcal N\times M$ and
\[\Big(\overline{\partial_s\mathcal N\times M \cup \mathcal N\times\partial M}\Big) \cap\overline{\Gamma_0} = \varnothing.\]
Here, the boundary $\partial_s\mathcal N$ is given as in Section~\ref{sec-hl-renor} via the biholomorphism $\mathcal N\simeq N_s\times N_u.$ From this, by Proposition \ref{prop-renor}, the sequence $(\Gamma_n)_{n\geq0}$ of closed analytic subsets of $\mathcal N\times M$ defined by
\[\Gamma_{n+1}:=F(\Gamma_n)\cap(\mathcal N\times M),\]
converges to $W^u_{r(f_{t_0}),loc}\times\{t_0\},$ with a multiplicity $c,$ corresponding to the intersection number between $\Gamma_0$ and $\mathcal W^s_{r,loc}.$

On the other hand, since $p_j\circ F=\hat f\circ p_j,$ we have $F^*(p_j^*(\hat T_{\hat f}^{\wedge(u+1)}))=d^{u+1}p_j^*(\hat T_{\hat f}^{\wedge(u+1)})$ thus
\[F^*T=F^*\left(\bigwedge_{j=1}^m p_j^*\left(\hat{T}_{\hat f}^{\wedge(u+1)}\right)\right)=\bigwedge_{j=1}^m (p_j\circ F)^*\left(\hat{T}_{\hat f}^{\wedge(u+1)}\right)=d^{m(u+1)}T.\]
Hence,
\begin{align*}
I_n:=\int T\wedge[\Gamma_n]\leq d^{nm(u+1)}\int T\wedge\left[\Gamma_0\right]\leq d^{(n+n_0)m(u+1)}\int T\wedge [\hat{\mathcal Y}^{[m]}].
\end{align*}
Since $[\Gamma_n]$ converges weakly to $c[W^u_{r(f_{t_0}),loc}\times\{t_0\}]$ as $n\to\infty$ and, since the current $T=\bigwedge_{j=1}^m p_j^*\left(\hat{T}_{\hat f}^{\wedge(u+1)}\right)$ is the wedge product of $m(u+1)$ closed positive $(1,1)$-currents with continuous potential, we have
\[T\wedge\left[\Gamma_n\right]\to c\left(T\wedge\left[W^u_{r(f_{t_0}),loc}\times\{t_0\}\right]\right)\]
as $n\to+\infty$. To conclude, it suffices to show that this last measure is non-zero. This is precisely condition~\ref{it:cond1}, since, by the continuity of the potential again, the slice of $T$ by $(\mathbb{P}^k)^{m}\times\{t_0\}$ coincides with $\bigwedge_{j=1}^m \tau_j^*\left({T}_{f_{t_0}}^{\wedge(u+1)}\right)$.

label: le-cond1
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Recall that the saddle periodic point $r(f_{t_0})$ for $f^{[m]}_{t_0}$ is defined by
\[r(f_{t_0})=(r_1(f_{t_0}),\ldots,r_m(f_{t_0})).\]
Its local unstable manifold can be given by
\[W^u_{r(f_{t_0}),loc}:=W^u_{r_1(f_{t_0}),loc}\times\cdots\times W^u_{r_m(f_{t_0}),loc}.\]

Thus, if we denote by $\tau_j:(\mathbb{P}^k)^m\to\mathbb{P}^k$  the projection onto the $j$th coordinate, we have
\[[W^u_{r(f_{t_0}),loc}]=\tau_1^*[W^u_{r_1(f_{t_0}),loc}]\wedge\cdots\wedge\tau_m^*[W^u_{r_m(f_{t_0}),loc}].\]
Hence, each $T_{f_{t_0}}^{\wedge(u+1)}\wedge[W^u_{r_j(f_{t_0}),loc}]$ is non-zero if and only if
\begin{align*}\bigwedge_{j=1}^m \tau_j^*\left({T}_{f_{t_0}}^{\wedge(u+1)}\right)\wedge & [W^u_{r(f_{t_0}),loc}]\\
& =\tau_1^*\left({T}^{\wedge(u+1)}_{f_{t_0}}\wedge [W^u_{r_1(f_{t_0}),loc}]\right)\wedge\cdots\wedge\tau_m^*\left({T}^{\wedge(u+1)}_{f_{t_0}}\wedge[W^u_{r_m(f_{t_0}),loc}]\right)
\end{align*}
is non-zero. More precisely, the mass of this measure is given by
\[\left\|\bigwedge_{j=1}^m \tau_j^*\left({T}_{f_{t_0}}^{\wedge(u+1)}\right)\wedge[W^u_{r(f_{t_0}),loc}]\right\|=\prod_{j=1}^m\left\|T_{f_{t_0}}^{\wedge(u+1)}\wedge[W_{r_j(f_{t_0}),loc}^u]\right\|.\]
On the other hand, we have
\begin{align}
(T_{f^{[m]}_{t_0}})^{\wedge m(u+1)} =
& \left(\tau_1^*\left({T}_{f_{t_0}}\right)+\cdots+\tau_m^*\left({T}_{f_{t_0}}\right)\right)^{\wedge m(u+1)}\nonumber\\
& \geq\tau_1^*\left({T}^{\wedge(u+1)}_{f_{t_0}}\right)\wedge\cdots\wedge\tau_m^*\left({T}^{\wedge(u+1)}_{f_{t_0}}\right).\label{eq-fibered}
\end{align}
This gives
\begin{align*}
(T_{f^{[m]}_{t_0}})^{\wedge m(u+1)}\wedge & [W^u_{r(f_{t_0}),loc}]\\
&\geq\tau_1^*\left({T}^{\wedge(u+1)}_{f_{t_0}}\wedge [W^u_{r_1(f_{t_0}),loc}]\right)\wedge\cdots\wedge\tau_m^*\left({T}^{\wedge(u+1)}_{f_{t_0}}\wedge[W^u_{r_m(f_{t_0}),loc}]\right).
\end{align*}
Hence, condition \ref{it:cond1'} implies \ref{it:cond1''}.

body_md:

title: \bf Definition
body_md:
We say that $\mathcal Y$ is \emph{dynamically full} if
\[
 \Pi\circ\pi_2:\mathcal Y\to\mathscr M
\]
is dominant. We say that $\mathcal Y$ is \emph{maximally varying} if the restriction to $G\times\mathcal Y$ of the conjugacy map
\begin{align*}
 \mathrm{Conj}\colon G\times\mathcal X_D^u\times\mathcal E
 &\to \mathcal X_D^u\times\mathcal E,\\
 (\varphi,(Y,f))&\mapsto
 \bigl(\varphi^{-1}(Y),\varphi^{-1}\circ f\circ\varphi\bigr)
\end{align*}
is generically finite onto its image.

label: prop:local-normalization
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:local-normalization}
Assume that $\mathcal Y$ is dynamically full and maximally varying.
Then there exists a dense Zariski open subset
$\mathcal Y^\circ\subset\mathcal Y$ such that the following holds.

For every $(Y_0,f_0)\in\mathcal Y^\circ$ and every local slice
$\tilde\Omega$ through $f_0$, after possibly shrinking
$\tilde\Omega$ around $f_0$, there exist a complex submanifold containing $(Y_0,f_0)$
\[ \tilde{\mathcal Y}
 \subset
 \mathcal X_D^u\times\tilde\Omega
\]
and a holomorphic map
\[
 \Psi\colon\tilde{\mathcal Y}\to G,\text{ with }
 \Psi(Y_0,f_0)=\mathrm{id},
\]
such that the projection $ \pi_{\tilde\Omega}\colon \tilde{\mathcal Y}\to\tilde\Omega$
is a surjective submersion and the map
\[
 \tilde{\mathcal Y}\to
 \mathcal X_D^u\times\mathcal E,
\]
\[
 z=(Z,g)\mapsto
 \bigl(\psi_z^{-1}(Z),
       \psi_z^{-1}\circ g\circ\psi_z\bigr),
 \qquad
 \psi_z:=\Psi(z),
\]
is a biholomorphism from $\tilde{\mathcal Y}$ onto a neighborhood
of $(Y_0,f_0)$ in $\mathcal Y$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Since $\mathcal Y$ is
dynamically full, the map
\[
 p:=\Pi\circ\pi_2|_{\mathcal Y}
 \colon\mathcal Y\to\mathscr M
\]
is dominant. Hence, there exists a dense Zariski open subset
\[
 \mathcal Y_{\mathrm{full}}
 \subset\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{reg}}
\]
on which $p$ is a submersion. In particular, if
$y=(Y,f)\in\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{full}}$, then $f\notin V$, since
$\Pi$ does not have maximal rank on $V$.

On the other hand, maximal variation means that the conjugacy map
\[
 \mathrm{Conj}\colon
 G\times\mathcal Y
 \to
 \mathcal X_D^u\times\mathcal E
\]
is generically finite onto its image, and hence generically immersive.
Therefore, by equivariance of this map, there exists a dense Zariski
open subset
\[
 \mathcal Y_{\mathrm{mv}}
 \subset\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{reg}}
\]
such that $\mathrm{Conj}$ is immersive at $(\mathrm{id},y)$ for every
$y\in\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{mv}}$. We then define
\[
 \mathcal Y^\circ
 :=
 \mathcal Y_{\mathrm{full}}
 \cap
 \mathcal Y_{\mathrm{mv}}.
\]

Let now $(Y_0,f_0)\in\mathcal Y^\circ$, and let
$\tilde\Omega$ be a local slice at $f_0$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:local-slice}, there exist neighborhoods
$\tilde G$ of $\mathrm{id}$ in $G$ and $\Omega$ of $f_0$ in
$\mathcal E$ such that
\[
 (\varphi,f)\mapsto\varphi^{-1}\circ f\circ\varphi
\]
is a biholomorphism from $\tilde G\times\tilde\Omega$ onto
$\Omega$. Therefore,
\begin{align*}
 F\colon
 \mathcal X_D^u\times\tilde G\times\tilde\Omega
 &\to
 \mathcal X_D^u\times\Omega,\\
 (Y,\varphi,f)
 &\mapsto
 \bigl(\varphi^{-1}(Y),
       \varphi^{-1}\circ f\circ\varphi\bigr)
\end{align*}
is a biholomorphism.

After shrinking around $(Y_0,\mathrm{id},f_0)$, set
\[
 \check{\mathcal Y}
 :=
 F^{-1}\bigl(
 \mathcal Y\cap(\mathcal X_D^u\times\Omega)
 \bigr),
\]
and let
\[
 \pi\colon
 \mathcal X_D^u\times\tilde G\times\tilde\Omega
 \to
 \mathcal X_D^u\times\tilde\Omega
\]
be the natural projection. In the coordinates given by $F$, the
conjugacy map acts only on the $G$-coordinate:
\[
 F^{-1}\bigl(
 \mathrm{Conj}(\eta,F(Y,\varphi,f))
 \bigr)
 =
 (Y,\varphi\eta,f).
\]
Consequently, the immersivity of $\mathrm{Conj}$ at
$(\mathrm{id},(Y_0,f_0))$ exactly implies that
$\pi|_{\check{\mathcal Y}}$ is immersive at
$(Y_0,\mathrm{id},f_0)$. Hence, after shrinking the neighborhoods,
$\pi|_{\check{\mathcal Y}}$ is a biholomorphism onto the complex
submanifold
\[
 \tilde{\mathcal Y}
 :=
 \pi(\check{\mathcal Y})
 \subset
 \mathcal X_D^u\times\tilde\Omega.
\]

We may thus write
\[
 \bigl(\pi|_{\check{\mathcal Y}}\bigr)^{-1}(Y,f)
 =
 \bigl(Y,\Psi(Y,f),f\bigr),
\]
where
\[
 \Psi\colon\tilde{\mathcal Y}\to G
\]
is holomorphic and satisfies $\Psi(Y_0,f_0)=\mathrm{id}$. Setting
$\psi_y:=\Psi(y)$, the map
\[
 \tilde{\mathcal Y}\to\mathcal Y,
 \qquad
 y=(Y,f)\mapsto
 \bigl(\psi_y^{-1}(Y),
       \psi_y^{-1}\circ f\circ\psi_y\bigr)
\]
is a biholomorphism onto a neighborhood of $(Y_0,f_0)$ in
$\mathcal Y$.

Finally, under this biholomorphism, one has
\[
 p
 =
 \bigl(\Pi|_{\tilde\Omega}\bigr)
 \circ
 \pi_{\tilde\Omega},
\]
where $\pi_{\tilde\Omega}\colon \tilde{\mathcal Y} \to \tilde\Omega$
 is the projection. Since $p$ is a submersion and
$\Pi|_{\tilde\Omega}$ is a local biholomorphism, the projection $\pi_{\tilde\Omega}$ is a submersion. After shrinking $\tilde\Omega$ if necessary, it
is surjective.

title: \bf Remark

label: eq-inter-non-vide
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal Y$ satisfy the assumptions of the theorem. Since \eqref{eq-pitch}, the condition $f\in\Omega_u$, and the condition that $Y$ is reduced and irreducible are stable under perturbation, we fix a small open subset $\mathcal Y_0\subset\mathcal Y$ on which all three hold.
Our goal is to prove
that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-inter-non-vide}
\textup{supp}(\mu_{\mathcal Y})\cap\mathcal Y_0\neq\varnothing.
\end{equation}

By Proposition~\ref{prop:local-normalization}, we may choose
\[
(Y_0,f_0)\in\mathcal Y_0\cap\mathcal Y^\circ
\]
and a local slice
\[
f_0\in\tilde\Omega\subset\Omega_u
\]
such that, after a local simultaneous conjugacy and possibly shrinking
$\mathcal Y_0$, a neighborhood of $(Y_0,f_0)$ in $\mathcal Y$ is
identified with a submanifold
\[
\tilde{\mathcal Y}\subset\mathcal X^u_d\times\tilde\Omega,
\]
whose projection on $\tilde\Omega$ is surjective. In particular, by dynamical fullness, Assumptions~\ref{free}
and~\ref{init} remain valid on $\tilde\Omega$. Observe also that we will
freely shrink $\mathcal Y_0$ and $\tilde\Omega$ in what follows.

We now let $m\geq0$ be maximal among the integers for which there exist
periodic points
\[
x_1(f_0),\ldots,x_m(f_0)\in\Lambda(f_0),
\]
in the hyperbolic set given by Assumption~\ref{hyperbolic}, satisfying
the two properties below. For any such choice of periodic points,
condition~\ref{it:cond1} of Proposition~\ref{prop-positivevolume}
follows directly from Lemma~\ref{le-cond1} and Assumption~\ref{misu}.
It remains to establish condition~\ref{it:cond2}.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{(2.\arabic*)}]
\item \label{it:cond21}
For each $1\leq j\leq m$, there are an open subset $U_j$ of
$\hat{\mathcal Y_0}$ and an integer $n_j$ such that
$\hat f^{n_j}(U_j)$ defines a family of $u$-graphs in
$\mathbb{D}_{2R}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}_{3/2}^u$ tangent to $C^{uu}_\eta$.
More precisely, for each $t=(Y_t,f_t)\in\mathcal Y_0$, the fiber
$U_j(t)$ of $U_j$ above $t$ is an open subset of $Y_t$ such that
$f_t^{n_j}(U_j(t))$ is a $u$-graph in
$\mathbb{D}_{2R}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}_{3/2}^u$ tangent to $C^{uu}_\eta$.

\item \label{it:cond22}
If we set
\[
M_j:=
\left\{
t=(Y_t,f_t)\in\mathcal Y_0
\,:\,
f_t^{n_j}(U_j(t))\cap W^s_{x_j(f_t),loc}\neq\varnothing
\right\},
\]
then, possibly after reducing $\mathcal Y_0$,
\[
M^{(m)}:=M_1\cap\cdots\cap M_m
\]
is an irreducible analytic subvariety of $\mathcal Y_0$ of codimension
$m$, containing $(Y_0,f_0)$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{lemma}\label{le-cond2}
Possibly after shrinking $\mathcal Y_0$, conditions
\textup{\ref{it:cond21}} and \textup{\ref{it:cond22}} imply
condition~\textup{\ref{it:cond2}} from Section~\ref{sec-misiu}.
\end{lemma}

Roughly speaking, the set $U$ appearing in~\ref{it:cond2} corresponds
to the fibered product of the sets $U_j$ given by~\ref{it:cond21}.
However, a few technical issues arise: the integers $n_j$ need not
coincide, and $\Lambda(f)$ is only invariant under $f^2$. We therefore
postpone the proof of Lemma~\ref{le-cond2} to Section~\ref{sec-standard}
and continue with the proof strategy.

By condition~\ref{it:cond22}, necessarily
\[
m\leq\dim\mathcal Y,
\]
since $M^{(m)}$ is a non-empty analytic subvariety of $\mathcal Y_0$ of
codimension $m$. It remains to show that
\[
m=\dim\mathcal Y.
\]
Assume that $m<\dim\mathcal Y$. Then $M^{(m)}$ has positive dimension.
By maximality of $m$, no new independent stable/unstable relation
satisfying \ref{it:cond21} and \ref{it:cond22} can be produced along
$M^{(m)}$.

The argument has two main steps.
\begin{itemize}
\item First, we show that the projection of $M^{(m)}$ onto
$\tilde\Omega$ is constant. In other words, the $m$ relations defining
$M^{(m)}$ exhaust all degrees of freedom coming from the dynamics
(see Theorem~\ref{th-point}).

\item Now that the dynamics is fixed along $M^{(m)}$, we show, using
the genericity assumptions~\ref{decalage} and~\ref{grille}, that the
intersection between $f^n(Y)$ and $W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ is rich enough
to also exclude variations of $Y$ (see Theorem~\ref{th-subvar}).
\end{itemize}

Our proof follows in fact a slightly different order, and this variation is
crucial. The first relation we impose is between the local unstable
manifold of the saddle point $p(f)$ defined in Assumption~\ref{saddle},
and a preimage of the local stable manifold of $r_0(f)$ defined in
Assumption~\ref{repelling}. This allows us to fully exploit the
heterodimensional cycle between $p(f)$ and $\Lambda(f)$.

This initial step relies on Assumption~\ref{init}, which also ensures that
the two central multipliers $\chi_{p(f)}$ and $\chi_{r_0(f)}$ generate a
dense subgroup of $\mathbb{C}^*$, a crucial ingredient for the first step above
(see Section~\ref{sec-relation} for details).

\bigskip

\noindent\emph{\textbf{Organisation of this section.}}
In the following subsection, possibly after shrinking $\tilde\Omega$
several times, we derive several consequences of the assumptions in
Section~\ref{sec-ass} and set up the geometric framework needed for the
rest of the proof.

Next, in Section~\ref{sec-control}, we establish two graph transform
control results, respectively near the saddle point $p(f)$ and near
saddle points in $\Lambda(f)$.

At that stage, Section~\ref{sec-relation} establishes the first step
of the proof of Theorem~\ref{th-main-blender} mentioned above, while
Section~\ref{sec-subvar} deals with the second step of the proof.

Finally, Section~\ref{sec-preuve-main} completes the proof of
Theorem~\ref{th-main-blender}.

label: prop-special
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-special}
If $f$ is in $\tilde\Omega$ and if $Y\in\mathcal X_D^u$ satisfies \eqref{eq-pitch} then $Y$ is not $f$-special.
head: environment

label: eq-dense-shifted-orbit
title: Démonstration
body_md:
By~\eqref{eq-pitch}, there exists $n\geq0$ such that $f^n(Y)$
intersects $W^s_{p(f),loc}$ transversely. Fix $m\geq1$. Applying the
inclination lemma to $f^m$, we obtain
\[
W^u_{p(f)}
\subset
\overline{\bigcup_{j\geq0}f^{mj}(Y)}^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}.
\]
On the other hand, Assumption~\ref{homoclinic} and
Proposition~\ref{prop-zariski-dense-unstable} give
\[
\overline{W^u_{p(f)}}^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}=\mathbb{P}^k.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq-dense-shifted-orbit}
\overline{\bigcup_{j\geq0}f^{mj}(Y)}^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}=\mathbb{P}^k.
\end{equation}
In other words, for every $m\geq1$, the $f^m$-orbit of $Y$ is Zariski dense.

In particular, $Y$ is not preperiodic under $f$. Suppose now, by
contradiction, that $Y$ is $f$-special. By the definition of
$f$-specialness, there exist a closed subvariety $Z\subset\mathbb{P}^k$, an
integer $m\geq1$, and a polarized endomorphism $g:Z\to Z$ such that
\[
Y\subset Z,\qquad f^m(Z)=Z,
\]
the maps $f^m$ and $g$ commute on $Z$, and $Y$ is preperiodic under
$g$. Since $Z$ contains the whole $f^m$-orbit of $Y$, the density
proved above implies
\[
Z=\mathbb{P}^k.
\]
Thus $g$ is an endomorphism of $\mathbb{P}^k$ commuting with $f^m$.
By the choice of $\tilde\Omega$ coming from \cite{zhang-iterated-centralizer}, there exists $j\geq1$ such that
\[
g=f^j.
\]
But then the preperiodicity of $Y$ under $g$ implies its
preperiodicity under $f$, a contradiction.

label: le-shadowing
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-shadowing}
Let $f\in\tilde\Omega.$ Let $x,y\in\hat\Lambda(f)$ and $\epsilon>0.$ Then, there exists $n\geq0$ and $z\in\Lambda(f)$ such that
\[z\in W^u_{x,loc}\cap B(x,\epsilon)\ \text{ and }\ f^n(z)\in W^s_{y,loc}\cap B(y,\epsilon).\]
Moreover, if $x$ corresponds to the periodic point $r_0(f)$, then we can assume that $z\notin W^{uu}_{x,loc}.$
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Write $x=(x_j)_{j\leq0}$ and $y=(y_j)_{j\leq0}$.
Since $\Lambda(f)$ is locally maximal, its natural extension $\hat\Lambda(f)$ has local product structure, and therefore the shadowing lemma holds on $\hat\Lambda(f)$ (see, for instance, \cite[Paper I, Theorem~2.4]{jonsson-phd}).
Hence there exists $\eta>0$ such that any $\eta$-pseudo-orbit in $\hat\Lambda(f)$ stays within distance $\epsilon$ of a true orbit in $\hat\Lambda(f)$.

On the other hand, by topological transitivity there exist $\tilde z\in\Lambda(f)\cap B(x,\eta)$ and $n\geq0$ such that
\[f^n(\tilde z)\in B(y,\eta).\]
Applying the shadowing lemma yields a point $z=(z_j)_{j\leq0}\in\hat\Lambda(f)$ such that for all $j\leq0$ and $i\geq0$,
\[d(z_j,x_j)<\epsilon
\quad\text{and}\quad
d\big(f^{n+i}(z_0),f^i(y_0)\big)<\epsilon.\]
Possibly after reducing $\epsilon$, this proves the first part of the statement.

Assume now that $x=r_0(f)$.
By Assumption~\ref{repelling}, the strong unstable manifold $W^{uu}_{x,loc}$ is a $u$-graph tangent to the cone field $C^{uu}_\eta$ inside the blender region $\mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}_{3/2}^u$.
Let $L$ be a leaf of the strong unstable foliation inside $W^u_{x,loc}$ that is close to, but distinct from, $W^{uu}_{x,loc}$.
Then, Assumption~\ref{blender} implies that $L$ intersects $W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ at some point $x'$.
By local maximality of $\Lambda(f)$, we have $x'\in\Lambda(f)$.

Applying the first part of the lemma to $x'$ (viewed as a point of $\hat\Lambda(f)$ whose backward orbit converges to $x$) and choosing $\epsilon<d(L,W^{uu}_{x,loc})$, we obtain $n'\geq0$ and $z'\in\Lambda(f)$ such that
\[z'\in W^u_{x',loc}\cap B(x',\epsilon)
\quad\text{and}\quad
f^{n'}(z')\in W^s_{y,loc}\cap B(y,\epsilon).\]
Since $W^u_{x',loc}\cap B(x',\epsilon)$ is an open subset of $W^u_{x,loc}$ for $\epsilon$ small enough, the conclusion follows by taking preimages of $z'$ inside $W^u_{x,loc}$.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
In this proof, set $\mathcal D:=\mathbb{D}_{2R}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}_{3/2}^u$.

Observe that if $f\in\tilde\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ is a $u$-graph in
$\mathcal U_-$ tangent to $C^{uu}_\eta$, then
$f(\Gamma)\cap\mathcal D$ still has the same properties, since
$f|_{\mathcal U_-}$ is a degree~$1$ horizontal-like map of index
$(s+1,u)$ from $\mathcal U_-$ to $\mathcal D$. This may fail if
$\mathcal U_-$ is replaced by $\mathcal U_+$, since
$f(\Gamma)\cap\mathcal D$ could a priori intersect the central
boundary $(\partial\mathbb{D}_{2R})\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}_{3/2}^u$. However,
this cannot occur if $\Gamma$ intersects $W^s_{x,loc}$ for some
$x\in\Lambda(f)$, since
$\Lambda(f)\subset\mathbb{D}_R\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}_{3/2}^u$ and
$W^s_{x,loc}$ is tangent to $C^{ss}_\eta$.

Therefore, using~\ref{it:cond22} and possibly replacing
$\mathcal Y_0$ by a smaller neighborhood of $(Y_0,f_0)$, we may
replace $n_j$ by $n_j+1$ and $U_j$ by a smaller set $U'_j$ such
that
\[\hat f^{n_j+1}(U'_j)=
\hat f^{n_j+1}(U_j)\cap(\mathcal D\times\mathcal Y_0)\]
defines a family of $u$-graph in $\mathcal D.$

Iterating this procedure, we may replace each $n_j$ by
$n_0:=\max_j n_j$ and assume that all these integers coincide.
We then define $U$ as the fibered product of
$U_1,\ldots,U_m$ over $\mathcal Y_0$.

We claim that $(\hat f^{[m]})^{n_0}(U)$ intersects properly
$\mathcal W^s_{x,loc}$, where
$x(f)=(x_1(f),\ldots,x_m(f))$. Fix a parameter
$t=(Y_t,f_t)\in\mathcal Y_0$. Then each
$f_t^{n_0}(U_j(t))$ is a $u$-graph in $\mathcal D$, hence is
contained in a $cu$-graph. By Lemma~\ref{le-inter}, it
intersects the $s$-graph $W^s_{x_j(f_t),loc}$ in at most one
point. Therefore, the set
\[\left\{(y_j,t)\in\mathbb{P}^k\times\mathcal Y_0 \; ; \;
y_j\in f_t^{n_0}(U_j(t))\cap W^s_{x_j(f_t),loc}\right\}\]
projects biholomorphically onto
\[M_j:=\left\{t=(Y_t,f_t)\in\mathcal Y_0 \, ; \,
f_t^{n_0}(U_j(t))\cap W^s_{x_j(f_t),loc}\neq\varnothing\right\},\]
defined in~\ref{it:cond22}. It follows that
$(\hat f^{[m]})^{n_0}(U)\cap\mathcal W^s_{x,loc}$ is
biholomorphic to
\[M^{(m)}:=M_1\cap\cdots\cap M_m,\]
and therefore has dimension $\tilde m - m$, where
$\tilde m:=\dim(\mathcal Y_0)$.

On the other hand, $(\hat f^{[m]})^{n_0}(U)$ has dimension
$\tilde m+um$, while $\mathcal W^s_{x,loc}$ has dimension
$\tilde m+sm$. Their codimensions in
$(\mathbb{P}^k)^m\times\mathcal Y_0$ add up to
\[(s+1)m+(u+1)m=(k+1)m,\]
which coincides with the codimension
\[\tilde m+km-(\tilde m-m)\]
of $(\hat f^{[m]})^{n_0}(U)\cap\mathcal W^s_{x,loc}$.

label: le-centrer-unstable
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-centrer-unstable}
For each $y\in W^{u}_{p(f),loc}$ let denote by $\mathcal E^c_y$ the dynamical direction associated to the central eigenvalue $\chi_{p(f)}.$ Then, the center-unstable bundle along $W^u_{p(f),loc}$ defined by
\[E^{cu}:=TW^u_{p(f),loc}\oplus\mathcal E^c_y\]
is disjoint from the stable cone field $C^{ss}_\eta.$
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Let $y \in W^{u}_{p(f),loc}$ and let $v \in E^{cu}_y \setminus \{0\}$.
By invariance of the dynamical directions,
\[D_y f^{-n}(v) \in E^{cu}_{f^{-n}(y)} \quad \text{for all } n \ge 0.\]
Since $f^{-n}(y)$ converges to $p(f),$ any limit value $v_\infty$ of
\[v_n := \frac{D_y f^{-n}(v)}{\|D_y f^{-n}(v)\|}\]
belongs to $E^{cu}_{p(f)}$.

By contradiction, if $v \in C^{ss}_\eta$, then, using that this cone field is contracted by $f^{-1}$, we should have $v_\infty \in C^{ss}_\eta$.
This is impossible since,
\[E^{cu}_{p(f)}\cap C^{ss}_\eta=\varnothing,\]
completing the proof.

label: le-control1
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-control1}
Let $(p(f))_{f\in M}$ be in standard form in $B_p$ as in Section~\ref{sec-standard}.
Let $\Delta=(\Delta_f)_{f\in M}$ be a family of $cs$-graphs given by injective holomorphic maps $h_f\colon B^{cs}\to B_p$ preserving the central direction, i.e., such that $D_0h_f(1,0)$ belongs to $E^{cu}$ as defined in Lemma \ref{le-centrer-unstable}.
                                                            
Then, there exists a holomorphic map $\alpha\colon M\to\mathbb{C}^*$ with the following property.

Let $\Gamma=(\Gamma(f))_{f\in M}$ be a family of $u$-graphs in $B_p$ intersecting $W^s_{p(f),loc}$ at $(b^c(f),b^s(f))$, with $b^c(f)\neq0$ on $M.$ Then the graph transform $f^n(\Gamma(f))$ satisfies
\[f^n(\Gamma(f))\cap\Delta_f=\{h_f(a_n(f))\}\text{ where } a_n(f)=\chi_{p(f)}^n\Big[b^c(f)\alpha(f)(1,0)+R_n(f)\Big],\]
 where $R_n\colon M\to\mathbb{C}^{cs}$ are holomorphic maps converging to $0,$ locally uniformly with respect to $f,$ $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$.

label: rk-control1
title: \bf Remark
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Let $\pi\colon \mathbb{C}^{cs}\times \mathbb{C}^u \to \mathbb{C}^{cs}$ denote the natural projection, and define $\tilde\pi$ by 
\[\tilde\pi(y,z) = (y,0), \quad (y,z)\in \mathbb{C}^{cs}\times \mathbb{C}^u.\]
Our goal is to compare,  near the unstable manifold, the map $\tilde\pi$ with the projection
\[G_f = \pi \circ \theta_f^{-1} \circ \tilde\pi \circ \theta_f\]
along the unstable foliation of the $C^2$-linearization. 

A key fact is that, by Proposition \ref{prop-cderiv} the map $G_f$ is $\mathbb{C}$-differentiable on $W_{p(f),loc}^u$. In particular, the map $G_f\circ h_f,$ which is a local diffeomorphism at $0$, is $\mathbb{C}$-differentiable at this point. We denote its inverse by $H_{f}:=(G_f\circ h_f)^{-1}$.

For $n\geq 0$, the graph transform $f^n(\Gamma(f))$ is a $u$-graph                         
   
                                               
    
which intersects $\Delta_f$ in a single point. We consider $(x_n(f))_{f\in M}$ the family of points on $\Gamma(f)$ and $(a_n(f))_{f\in M}$ in $B^{cs}$ such that $f^n(x_n(f))=h_f(a_n(f))$ corresponds to this intersection point. Then
\[G_f(f^n(x_n(f))) 
= \pi\circ\theta_f^{-1}\circ\tilde\pi\circ\theta_f(f^n(x_n(f))) 
= \pi\circ\theta_f^{-1}\circ\tilde\pi\circ K_f^n\circ\theta_f(x_n(f)).\]
Recall that if $(x^c,x^s,x^u)\in\mathbb{C}^{cs}\times\mathbb{C}^u$ then $K_f(x^c,x^s,x^u)=(\chi_{p(f)}x^c,A_fx^s,E_fx^u),$ where $A_f$ is contracting, $E_f$ is expanding, and 
\[\|A_f\|,\ \|E_f^{-1}\|<\tilde\chi^{-2}<\tilde\chi^{-1}<|\chi_{p(f)}|.\] 
Writing $\theta_f(x_n(f))=(x^c_n(f),x^s_n(f),x^u_n(f))$, we obtain
\[K_f^n\circ\theta_f(x_n(f))
= (\chi^n_{p(f)}x^c_n(f),A_f^n x^s_n(f),E_f^n x^u_n(f)).\]
In particular, $x_n^u(f)=o(\tilde\chi^{-2n})$. Since $\Gamma(f)$ intersects $W^s_{p(f),loc}$ at $(b^c(f),b^s(f))$, it follows that
\[x_n^c(f)=b^c(f)+o(\tilde\chi^{-2n}), 
\qquad 
x^s_n(f)=b^s(f)+o(\tilde\chi^{-2n}).\]
Combining this with $\|A_f^n\|=o(\tilde\chi^{-2n})$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq-erreur1}
G_f(f^n(x_n(f)))=\chi_{p(f)}^n b^c(f)(1,0)+o(\tilde\chi^{-2n}).
\end{equation}
On the other hand, since $f^n(x_n(f))=h_f(a_n(f))$, we have
\begin{align*}
a_{n}(f) 
&= H_{f}(G_f(f^n(x_n(f)))) = H_{f}\!\left(\chi_{p(f)}^n b^c(f)(1,0)+o(\tilde\chi^{-2n})\right) \\
&= 0+\chi_{p(f)}^n b^c(f)\, D_0H_{f}(1,0)+o(\chi^n_{p(f)}).
\end{align*}
By assumption, $D_0H_{f}(1,0)$ is equal to $\alpha(f)(1,0)$ for some normalization constant $\alpha(f)\in\mathbb{C}^*.$ This function $f\mapsto\alpha(f)$ is holomorphic, since it is the uniform limit of 
\[f\mapsto \frac{a_{n}(f)}{\chi_{p(f)}^n b^c(f)}.\]
It follows that the remainder
\[R_n(f):=\chi_{p(f)}^{-n}a_n(f)-b^c(f)\alpha(f)(1,0)\]
is holomorphic as well. Moreover, $R_n(f)=o(1)$ as $n\to\infty$. In fact, this remainder splits into two contributions. The first one comes from the error term in~\eqref{eq-erreur1}, which, after factoring out $\chi_{p(f)}^n$, is $o(\tilde\chi^{-n})$ uniformly in $f$ and $\Gamma$. The second one arises from the Taylor expansion of $H_f$, which is uniform in $f$ and $\Delta$, since $\theta_f$ is of class $C^2$ and depends continuously on $f$ in the $C^2$ topology.

label: le-control2
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
We first obtain estimates on the point $\Gamma_l(f)\cap W^{cs}_{r(f),loc}$, which provide control on the integers $n$ for which $f^n(\Gamma_l(f))$ is well defined. In a second step, we obtain control of the graph $f^n(\Gamma_l(f))$, which could in fact be achieved by applying Lemma~\ref{le-control1} to $f^{-1}$.

Actually, as we have seen in Section~\ref{sec-standard}, there exists a unique intersection point
\[z_l(f)=(z_l^c(f),z_l^s(f),z_l^u(f))\]
between $W^{cs}_{r(f),loc}$ and $\Gamma_l(f)$. We use the same notations with $l=\infty,$ with the remark that $z_\infty^c(f)$ and $z_\infty^u(f)$ both vanish by \eqref{eq-gammainfty}.

If $\check{z}_l(f):=\theta_f(z_l(f))=(\check{z}^c_l(f),\check{z}^s_l(f),0),$ then using that $\theta_f$ is the identity on $W^{s}_{r(f),loc}$, we have
\begin{align*}
z_l(f)&=(0,\check{z}^s_l(f),0)+D_{(0,\check{z}^s_l(f),0)}\theta_f^{-1}(\check{z}^c_l(f),0,0)+o(\check{z}^c_l(f))\\
                                                                                                              
&=(0,\check{z}^s_l(f),0)+D_{(0,\check{z}^s_\infty(f),0)}\theta_f^{-1}(\check{z}^c_l(f),0,0)+o(\check{z}^c_l(f)),
\end{align*}
where the second equality follows from the fact that $\check{z}^s_l(f)$ converges to $\check{z}^s_\infty(f)$. On the other hand, since $D\theta_f$ preserves the dynamical directions and is $\mathbb{C}$-linear along $W^s_{r(f),loc}$, we have
\[\check{z}^c_l(f)(\gamma(f),0,0):=D_{(0,\check{z}^s_\infty(f),0)}\theta_f^{-1}(\check{z}^c_l(f),0,0),\]
where $\gamma(f)\neq0$. Here we make two observations. First, the dependence of these objects
(such as $z_l(f)$, $\gamma(f)$, etc.) on $f$ is not a priori holomorphic.
Second, if
$D_{(0,\check{z}^s_\infty(f),0)} \theta_f^{-1}(1,0,0)$
had a nonzero component in the strong unstable direction, then this could
break all the estimates that follow. Thus, Proposition~\ref{prop-cderiv}
plays an essential role here.


To summarize, so far we have
\[z^u_l(f)=o(\check{z}^c_l(f))\ \text{ and } \ z^c_l(f)=\check{z}^c_l(f)(\gamma(f)+o(1)).\]
Thus
\[\check{z}^c_l(f)=z^c_l(f)(\beta(f)+o(1))\ \text{ and }\ z^u_l(f)=o({z}^c_l(f)),\]
where $\beta(f):=\gamma(f)^{-1}.$

The last observation for this part is that, writing $\Gamma_l(f)$ as a $u$-graph
\[\Gamma_l(f)=\left\{(h^c_{l,f}(z^u),h^s_{l,f}(z^u),z^u)\ ; \ z^u\in B^u\right\},\]
gives that
\[z^c_l(f)=h^c_{l,f}(z^u_l(f))=h^c_{l,f}(0)+O(z^u_l(f))=h^c_{l,f}(0)+o(z^c_l(f)).\]
Since by definition $h^c_{l,f}(0)=b^c_l(f)$, we obtain $z^c_l(f)=b^c_l(f)(1+o(1))$ and thus
\[\check{z}^c_l(f)=b^c_l(f)\beta(f)(1+o(1)).\]

As we have $f^n(z_l(f))=\theta_f^{-1}(K^n_f(\check z_l(f)))=\theta_f^{-1}(\chi_{r(f)}^n\check{z}^c_l(f),A^n_f\check{z}^s_l(f),0),$ this point stays in $1/2B_{r}$ as long as
\[|\chi_{r(f)}^n\check{z}^c_l(f)|<1/2\ \text{ and thus if } |\chi_{r(f)}^nb^c_l(f)\beta(f)|<1/4,\]
for $l$ large enough. Thus, using that the strong unstable eigenvalues dominated $\chi_{r(f)}$, for such pair $(n,l),$ the graph transform $f^n(\Gamma_l(f))$ is a well-defined $u$-graph in $B_{r}.$

In this situation, observe that all this discussion above also holds when replacing $z_l(f)$ by any point $x_l(f)\in\Gamma_l(f)$ such that $y_l(f):=f^n(x_l(f))$ stays on the graph transform $f^n(\Gamma_l(f)).$ That is, $\check{x}^c_l(f)=b^c_l(f)\beta(f)(1+o(1)).$ In particular, if we fix $z\in B^u$ and $y_l(f)$ corresponds to the point of intersection of $f^n(\Gamma_l(f))$ with the plane $\{z^u=z\}$ then
\begin{align*}
y_l(f)&=(y_l^c(f),y_l^s(f),z)=\theta^{-1}_f\circ K^n_f\circ\theta_f(x_l(f))\\
&=\theta_f^{-1}\Big(\chi_{r(f)}^n\check{x}^c_l(f),A^n_f\check{x}^s_l(f),E^n_f\check{x}^u_l(f)\Big).
\end{align*}

Thus, using that $\theta_f$ is the identity on $W^u_{r(f),loc}$, we obtain $y_l^s(f)=o(\tilde\chi^{-2n})$ and
\[y_l^c(f)
=\chi_{r(f)}^n\check{x}^c_l(f)+o(\tilde\chi^{-2n})
=\chi_{r(f)}^nb^c_l(f)\beta(f)(1+o(1))+o(\tilde\chi^{-2n}),\]
where $o(1)$ is with respect to $l$ and $o(\tilde\chi^{-2n})$ with respect to $n$. The formulation~\eqref{eq-controle2} then follows from the assumption that $n_l$ is chosen so that
\[\tilde\chi^{-2n_l}=o(b_l^c(f)).\]
It remains to check that $\beta$ and $S_l$ are holomorphic. This follows, using arguments similar to those at the end of the proof of Lemma~\ref{le-control1}, from the fact that, for $n=n_l$, the intersection point $y_l(f)$ between $f^{n_l}(\Gamma_l(f))$ and the plane $\{z^u=z\}$ depends holomorphically on $f$.
