label: th-point
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-point}
If $M$ is as above, then for each $1\leq i\leq N$ the differential $D_{f_0}\chi_{r_i}$ vanishes on $T_{f_0}M$. In particular, by \eqref{star}, $M$ reduces to a point.
head: environment

title: Outline of the proof
body_md:
The proof proceeds by contradiction, assuming that $M$ is not reduced to a point. We can then choose a holomorphic disc in $M$ centered at $f_0$, and, by \eqref{star}, it suffices to show that $D_{f_0}\chi_{r_i}$ vanishes in the tangent direction of this disc. In other words, we may assume that $M$ itself is a disc and prove that $\chi_{r_i}'(f_0)=0$ for all $1\leq i\leq N$. 

The first step is to show that $\frac{\log|\chi_{r_0(f)}|}{\log|\chi_{p(f)}|}$ is independent of $f$. This is equivalent to saying that there exist $\zeta\in\mathbb{S}^1$ and $\omega\in\mathbb{R}$ such that, for all $f\in M$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-relation}
\chi_{r_0(f)}=\zeta\chi_{p(f)}^{-\omega}.
\end{equation}
This is precisely the counterpart of Lemma~3.12 and Proposition~3.13 in \cite{gtv}. The former establishes the normality of a family $(\Xi_{j_n,l_n})_{n\geq0}$, where for $j,l\geq 0$ we denote by $\Xi_{j,l}$ the holomorphic function on $M$ defined by
\[\Xi_{j,l}(f)=\chi_{p(f)}^j \chi_{r_0(f)}^l.\]
We will provide a proof of this result in the present setting (see Lemma~\ref{le-normal}). The key ingredient is the blender property -- forcing intersections between $f^n(\Gamma(f))$ and $W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ -- together with the persistence of these intersections over $M$. The relation~\eqref{eq-relation} then follows exactly as in \cite[Proposition~3.13]{gtv}.


In the second step, the fact that the subgroup $\langle \chi_{p(f_0)}, \chi_{r_0(f_0)} \rangle$ is dense in $\mathbb{C}^*$, is crucial. It implies that, if we fix a preimage $\tilde r_i(f_0)\in\Lambda(f_0)$ sufficiently close to $r_0(f_0)$ of a point on $W^s_{r_i(f_0),loc}$, then we can find arbitrarily large $n$ such that some portion of $f_0^n(\Gamma(f_0))$ passes arbitrarily close to $W^s_{r_i(f_0),loc}$. This in turn implies that a family of maps of the form
\[\Big(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f)\Big)\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n},\]
where $t_i$ is a non-vanishing holomorphic function, is normal. As a consequence, the derivative of $\chi_{r_i(f)}$ must vanish at $f_0$.

\bigskip

\noindent\emph{\textbf{Steps towards Theorem \ref{th-point}.}} As explained above, we assume that $M$ is a disc in $\tilde\Omega$, containing $f_0$ which satisfies $\overline{\langle \chi_{p(f_0)}, \chi_{r_0(f_0)} \rangle}=\mathbb{C}^*$. Moreover, we also assume that there exists an intersection $\tilde r_0(f_0)$ between ${W}^u_{p(f_0),loc}$ and $W^s_{\Lambda(f_0),loc}$ such that $f_0^{m_0}(\tilde r_0(f_0))\in W^s_{r_0(f_0),loc}.$ As all these intersersections persist along $M,$ there is a holomorphic map $\tilde r_0\colon M\to\mathbb{P}^k$ such that $\tilde r_0(f)$ is in $W^u_{p(f),loc}\cap W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ and $f^{m_0}(\tilde r_0(f))\in W^s_{r_0(f),loc}.$ Moreover, since $f$ contracts to cone fields $C^{uu}_\eta$ on $\mathcal U_+\cup\mathcal U_-,$ possibly by increasing $m_0$ and shrinking $M,$ we can assume that $f^{m_0}(W^u_{p(f),loc})$ is arbitrarily close to $W^{uu}_{r_0(f),loc}$ and thus, is a $u$-graph in $B_{r_0}.$

On the other hand, there exist $n_0\geq m_0$ and a $cs$-graph $\Delta_{f_0}$ in $B_p$ such that $f_0^{n_0}(\Delta_{f_0})$ is an open subset of $\mathsf W_{r_0(f_0)}^{cs}$. Possibly after shrinking again $M$, it extends to a family of $cs$-graphs $(\Delta_f)_{f\in M}$. Roughly speaking, using this $n_0$, we have that
\begin{itemize}
\item for $j\geq0$ large enough, the graph transform $f^j(\Gamma(f))$ in $B_p$ is close to $W^u_{p(f),loc}$;
\item thus, some part of $f^{j+n_0}(\Gamma(f))$ is close to a $u$-graph in $B_{r_0}$ intersecting $W^s_{r_0(f),loc}$;
\item applying an appropriated large iterate $f^l$ gives a $u$-graph (in $f^{j+n_0+l}(\Gamma(f))$) close to a leaf of the strong unstable foliation of $W^{u}_{r_0(f),loc},$ whose first coordinates is essentially
\[\Xi_{j,l}(f)=\chi_{p(f)}^j \chi_{r_0(f)}^l.\]
\end{itemize}
The following result makes this final claim more precise, using Lemma \ref{le-control1} and Lemma~\ref{le-control2}.
\begin{lemma}\label{le-doublecontrole}
There exists a holomorphic function $\gamma\colon M\to\mathbb{C}^*$  such that if $(j_n)$ and $(l_n)$ are sequences then for all $f\in M$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-hypdoublecontrole}
\tilde\chi^{-2l_n}=o(\chi_{p(f)}^{j_n})\ \text{ and }\ |\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)\gamma(f)|\leq 1/4,
\end{equation}
the set $f^{j_n+n_0+l_n}(\Gamma(f))$ contains, for all $n$ large enough, a $u$-graph $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)$ in $B_{r_0}$ of the form
\begin{equation}\label{eq-doublecontrole}
\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)=\left\{\left(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)\gamma(f)\Big[(1,0)+S_{n}(f,z)\Big],z\right)\,;\,z\in B^u\right\},
\end{equation}
where the remainders $S_{n}(f,z)$ converges to $0$ locally uniformly.
\end{lemma}
In other words, the $u$-graph $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)$ is arbitrarily close to the vertical space 
\[\{z^c=\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)\gamma(f),z^s=0\}\subset W^u_{r_0(f),loc}.\]

                             
                                                                  
                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                         
             
\begin{proof}
Let $h_f\colon B^{cs}\to B_p$ be the family of injective holomorphic maps defining the $cs$-graphs $(\Delta_f)_{f\in M}$ such that $D_0h_f(1,0)$ belongs to $E^{cu}$ defined along $W^u_{p(f),loc}$.

By Lemma~\ref{le-control1}, there exists a holomorphic function $\alpha\colon M\to\mathbb{C}^*$ such that, for every $j\geq0$, the graph transform $f^j(\Gamma_0(f))$ intersects $\Delta_f$ at the point $h_f(a_j(f))$, where
\[a_j(f)=\chi_{p(f)}^j\Big(b^c(f)\alpha(f)(1,0)+R_j(f)\Big),\]
with $R_j(f)$ converging locally uniformly to zero.

By definition of $\Delta_f$, we have $f^{n_0}(h_f(0))\in W^s_{r_0(f),loc}$. Moreover, since $D_0h_f(1,0)\in E_{h_f(0)}^{cu}$ does not belong to the strong stable cone field, which is expanding, it follows that $D_0(f^{n_0}\circ h_f)(1,0)$ is not tangent to $W^s_{r_0(f),loc}$. In other words, in the coordinates of $B_{r_0}$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq-v}
D_0(f^{n_0}\circ h_f)(1,0)=(v^c(f),v^s(f),0),
\end{equation}
with $v^c(f)\neq 0$.

Hence, $f^{j+n_0}(\Gamma_0(f))$ contains a vertical graph $\Gamma_j(f)$ in $B_{r_0}$ intersecting $\mathsf W_{r_0(f)}^{cs}$ at $(b^c_j(f),b^s_j(f))$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq-control-b}
b^c_j(f)=\chi_{p(f)}^j\big(b^c(f)\alpha(f)v^c(f)+\tilde R_j(f)\big),
\end{equation}
and where $\tilde R_j(f)$ converges locally uniformly to zero.

Therefore, we can apply Lemma~\ref{le-control2}, which in particular provides a function $\beta\colon M\to\mathbb{C}^*$ such that, if $l(j)$ is chosen so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-control3}
\tilde\chi^{-2l(j)}=o(\chi_{p(f)}^{j})\ \text{ and }\ \big|\chi_{r_0(f)}^{l(j)}b^c_j(f)\beta(f)\big|<1/4,
\end{equation}
then the graph transform $f^{l(j)}(\Gamma_j(f))$ in $B_{r_0}$ is a subset of the form
\begin{equation*}
\left\{\left(\chi_{r_0(f)}^{l(j)}b^c_j(f)\Big[\beta(f)(1,0)+S_{l(j)}(f,z)\Big],z\right)\,;\,z\in B^u\right\}.
\end{equation*}
This applies in particular to the two sequences, $(j_n)$ and $(l_n),$ in the statement since \eqref{eq-control3} is satisfied by \eqref{eq-hypdoublecontrole}. Hence, combining \eqref{eq-control-b} and \eqref{eq-control3}, we obtain~\eqref{eq-doublecontrole} by setting
\[\gamma(f):=\alpha(f)\beta(f)v^c(f)b^c(f),\]
and using the fact that
\[\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)\tilde R_{j_n}(f)\]
converges locally uniformly to $0$ as a consequence of~\eqref{eq-control-b}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{le-normal}
Let $(j_n)_{n\geq0}$ and $(l_n)_{n\geq0}$ be two increasing sequences such that $\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)$ converges in $\mathbb{D}^*$. Then the family $\{f\mapsto\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)\}_{n\geq 0}$ is normal in a neighborhood $M_0\subset M$ of $f_0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $\gamma$ be the holomorphic function given by Lemma~\ref{le-doublecontrole}. By multiplying by a suitable power of $\chi_{p(f_0)}$, we may assume that $\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)$ converges to some $\Xi_\infty$ satisfying
\[0<|\Xi_\infty\gamma(f_0)|<1/4.\]
On the other hand, since $\Xi_\infty\neq0$ we have that for all $f\in M,$ $\tilde\chi^{-2l_n}=o(\chi_{p(f)}^{j_n}).$

By Lemma~\ref{le-doublecontrole}, for all sufficiently large $n$, the iterate $f_0^{j_n+n_0+l_n}(\Gamma(f_0))$ contains a $u$-graph $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)$ in $B_{r_0}$ arbitrarily close to the vertical space
\[\{z^c=\Xi_\infty\gamma(f_0),\,z^s=0\}\subset W^u_{r_0(f_0),loc}.\]
Moreover, by the blender property given by Assumption~\ref{blender}, the graph $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)$ intersects $W^s_{x_n(f_0),loc}$ for some point $x_n(f_0)\in\hat\Lambda(f_0)$. We denote by $z_n(f_0)$ this intersection point, and by $y_n(f_0)$ the intersection between $W^u_{r_0(f_0),loc}$ and $W^s_{x_n(f_0),loc}$. Since $\hat\Lambda(f_0)$ is a basic set, the point $y_n(f_0)$ corresponds to a point $\hat y_n(f_0)$ in $\hat\Lambda(f_0)$ which can be followed holomorphically in $\hat\Lambda(f).$ In particular, the same holds for  $y_n(f_0)$ which can be followed in $\Lambda(f)$, and the family $\{f\mapsto y_n(f)\}_{n\geq0}$ is normal.

On the other hand, the distance between $z_n(f_0)$ and $y_n(f_0)$ tends to zero as $n\to\infty$, so the first coordinate of $y_n(f_0)$ converges to $\Xi_\infty\gamma(f_0)$. Hence, on a small neighborhood $M_0$ of $f_0$, the first coordinate of $y_n(f)$ belongs to a fixed compact set $D\Subset\mathbb{D}^*_{1/4}$ for all sufficiently large $n$ and all $f\in M_0$.

We now conclude with three further observations. First, since the intersection between $W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ and $W^u_{p(f)}$ persists along $M$, the point $z_n(f_0)$ can be followed holomorphically as the intersection point $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)\cap W^s_{x_n(f),loc}$, as long as $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)$ is well defined. Moreover, since $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)$ converges to a subset of $W^u_{r_0(f),loc}$, we have $z_n(f)\to y_n(f)$ locally uniformly.

Finally, assume by contradiction that the family $\{f\mapsto\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)\}_{n\geq 0}$ is not normal on $M_0$. Then the same holds for $\{f\mapsto\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)\gamma(f)\}_{n\geq 0}$, which implies that for arbitrarily large $n$ there exists $f_n\in M_0$ such that
\[\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_n)\gamma(f_n)\in\mathbb{D}_{1/4}\setminus D',\]
where $D'\Subset\mathbb{D}_{1/4}$ is an open disc containing $D$ in its interior. This is impossible, since $\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_n)\gamma(f_n)$ is arbitrarily close to the first coordinate of $z_n(f_n)$, whose distance to $y_n(f_n)$ tends to zero.
\end{proof}

It follows, exactly as in \cite[Proposition~3.13]{gtv}, that $\chi_p$ and $\chi_{r_0}$ satisfy a fixed relation throughout $M$.
\begin{proposition}\label{prop-relation}
 There exists $\zeta\in\mathbb{S}^1$ and $\omega\in\mathbb{R}^*_+$ such that for all $f\in M$
\[\chi_{r_0(f)}=\zeta\chi_{p(f)}^{-\omega}.\]
\end{proposition}
At this stage, the strategy in \cite{gtv} was to prove that both $\chi_p$ and $\chi_{r_0}$ are constant on $M$. The argument then concludes through a rather involved step, relying on stability in families in the sense of Berteloot-Bianchi-Dupont and on the equilibrium lamination constructed in \cite{BBD}, to show that all maps $f\in M$ are holomorphically conjugate in a neighborhood of their small Julia sets.

In the present setting, however, we cannot rely on stability in the sense of \cite{BBD} for the family $(f)_{f\in M}$, nor on equilibrium laminations, since the set $\Lambda(f)$ is far from the small Julia set. Fortunately, the results of \cite{t-gorbovickis} considerably simplify the final part of the argument, as it suffices to prove that the derivatives of the multipliers $\chi_{r_i}$ vanish at $f_0$ for all $1\leq i\leq N$.

To this end, we fix $1\leq i\leq N$ and we use Lemma \ref{le-shadowing} with $x=r_0(f_0)$ and $y=r_i(f_0)$ in order to obtain $n_i\geq0$ and $\tilde r_i(f_0)$ in $B_{r_0}\cap W^u_{r_0(f_0),loc},$ but outside $W^{uu}_{r_0(f_0),loc},$ such that $f_0^{n_i}(\tilde r_i(f_0))\in W^s_{r_i,loc}.$ Moreover, possibly after shrinking $M$, we require that for all $f\in M$ the point $\tilde r_i(f)$ is in $B_{r_0},$ and we denote its coordinates in this polydisc by  
\[(R_i^c(f),0,R^u_i(f))\in B_{r_0}.\]
The important data here is its first coordinate $R^c_i(f),$ which is not zero since $\tilde r_i(f)\notin W^{uu}_{r_0(f),loc},$ while the other unstable coordinates $R^u_i(f)$ will not be use.

Since the subgroup $\langle \chi_{p(f_0)}, \chi_{r_0(f_0)} \rangle$ is dense on $\mathbb{C}^*$ there exist two increasing sequence $(j_n)$ and $(l_n)$ such that $\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)$ converges to $t_i(f_0)$ with
$$t_i(f):=\frac{R_i^c(f)}{\gamma(f)},$$
where $\gamma$ is defined in Lemma \ref{le-doublecontrole}.

This has two consequences. The first one is that, if we write, as in Proposition \ref{prop-relation}, $\chi_{r_0(f)}=\zeta\chi_{p(f)}^{-\omega}$ then
\[\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)=\chi_{p(f_0)}^{j_n-\omega l_n}\zeta^{l_n},\]
thus, the convergence of  $\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)$  implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq-omegainfty}
j_n-\omega l_n \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} \omega_\infty := \frac{\log|t_i(f_0)|}{\log|\chi_{p(f_0)}|}\ \text{ and }\ \zeta^{l_n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\frac{t_i(f_0)}{\chi_{p(f_0)}^{\omega_\infty}}.
\end{equation}
Hence, we obtain the convergence on $M$
\begin{equation}\label{eq-Xi}
\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\Xi_\infty(f)
:=\frac{\chi_{p(f)}^{\omega_\infty}}{\chi_{p(f_0)}^{\omega_\infty}}t_i(f_0).
\end{equation}
Since no new relation between $W^u_{p(f)}$ and $W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ arises along $M$, this imposes the following constraint on $t_i(f)$.
\begin{lemma}\label{le-Xi}
For all $f\in M$, we have $t_i(f)=\Xi_\infty(f).$ That is, the point $\tilde r_i(f)$ belongs to 
the vertical space
\[\{z^c=\Xi_\infty(f)\gamma(f),\,z^s=0\}.\]
Moreover, possibly by changing the sequence $(j_n,l_n),$ we can assume that $\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)\neq t_i(f),$ for all $n$ and all $f\in M.$
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By analytic continuation, it is sufficient to prove the result in a neighborhood of $f_0$. A key observation is that, since the assumption~\eqref{eq-hypdoublecontrole} of Lemma~\ref{le-doublecontrole} is satisfied for $(\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f_0))$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and since the family $(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f))$ converges, the same assumption~\eqref{eq-hypdoublecontrole} also holds in a neighborhood of $f_0$ for all large $n$. Hence, Lemma~\ref{le-doublecontrole} implies that, for such $f$, the graphs $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)$ converge to the vertical space
\[\{z^c=\Xi_\infty(f)\gamma(f),\,z^s=0\},\]
which intersects $W^s_{\tilde r_i(f),loc}$, for $f=f_0$, exactly at the point $\tilde r_i(f_0)$. Since these intersections persist along $M$, the first coordinate $R_i^c(f)$ of $\tilde r_i(f)$ in $B_{r_0}$ must equal $\Xi_\infty(f)\gamma(f)$, that is,
\[t_i(f)=\Xi_\infty(f).\]
For the last point in the statement, as $\overline{\langle \chi_{p(f_0)}, \chi_{r_0(f_0)} \rangle}=\mathbb{C}^*,$ we can assume that $(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0))$ converges toward $t_i(f_0)$ while
\[|\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)|\neq |t_i(f_0)|,\ \text{ i.e., }\ j_n-\omega l_n\neq\omega_\infty,\]
by \eqref{eq-omegainfty}. This implies that, for all $f\in M,$ we have
\[|t_i(f)|=|\Xi_\infty(f)|=|\chi_{p(f)}^{\omega_\infty}|\neq|\chi_{p(f)}^{j_n-\omega l_n}|=|\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)|.\]
\end{proof}

This allows us to apply a second time Lemma \ref{le-control2}, from $r_0$ to $r_i.$
\begin{lemma}\label{le-triplecontrole}
There exists a holomorphic function $\delta\colon M\to\mathbb{C}^*$  such that, if $(m_n)$ is a sequence then, for all $f\in M$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-hyptriplecontrole}
\tilde\chi^{-2m_n}=o(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f))\ \text{ and }\ \left|\delta(f)\big(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f)\big)\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n}\right|\leq 1/4,
\end{equation}
the set $f^{j_n+n_0+l_n+n_i+m_n}(\Gamma(f))$ contains a $u$-graph $\tilde\Gamma_{n}(f)$ in $B_{r_i}$ of the form
\begin{equation}\label{eq-triplecontrole}
\tilde\Gamma_{n}(f)=\left\{\left(\delta(f)\big(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f)\big)\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n}\Big[(1,0)+\tilde S_{n}(f,z)\Big],z\right)\,;\,z\in B^u\right\},
\end{equation}
where the remainders $\tilde S_{n}(f,z)$ converges to $0$ locally uniformly.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The proof is very similar to that of Lemma~\ref{le-doublecontrole}. More precisely, we apply Lemma~\ref{le-control2} to the graphs
\[\Gamma_n(f):=f^{n_i}\big(\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)\big).\]
Observe that the sequence $(\Gamma_n(f))$ converges to the image $\Gamma_\infty(f)$, under $f^{n_i}$, of the vertical space $\{z^c=\Xi_\infty(f)\gamma(f),\,z^s=0\}$ in $B_{r_0}$. By Lemma~\ref{le-Xi}, this limit graph satisfies
\[\Gamma_\infty(f)\cap W^s_{r_i(f),loc}\neq\varnothing\]
for all $f\in M.$ Moreover, for each $n$, the graph $\Gamma_n(f)$ intersects $\mathsf W^{cs}_{r_i(f)}$ at $(b_n^c(f),b_n^s(f))$, where
\[b_n^c(f)=\tilde v^c(f)\gamma(f)\big(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f)\big)+o\big(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f)\big).\]
Here, the coefficient $\tilde v^c(f)$ arises from the transfer from $B_{r_0}$ to $B_{r_i}$ by $f^{n_i}$ and plays the same role as $v^c(f)$ in~\eqref{eq-v}. More precisely, the set $f^{-n_i}(\mathsf W^{cs}_{r_i(f)})$ is locally a manifold passing through $\tilde r_i(f)$, which projects injectively onto a neighborhood $V$ in $\mathsf W^{cs}_{r_0(f)}$ of $(R_i^c(f),0)$. The quantity $\tilde v^c(f)$ is then defined as the first coordinate of
\[D_{(R_i^c(f),0)}\phi(1,0),\]
where $\phi\colon V\to\mathsf W^{cs}_{r_i(f)}$ denotes the composition of the inverse of this projection with $f^{n_i}$.

Applying Lemma~\ref{le-control2} now yields the existence of a function $\beta$, and the desired conclusion follows from this lemma,  by setting
\[\delta(f):=\beta(f)\tilde v^c(f)\gamma(f).\]
\end{proof}
We can now conclude the proof of Theorem \ref{th-point}.
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{th-point}]
By~\eqref{star}, there exists $1\leq i\leq N$ such that $\chi_{r_i(f_0)}'\neq 0$. The key ingredient to contradict this fact is to prove that the family
\[\left((\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f))\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n}\right)_{n\geq0},\]
is normal for a suitable sequence $(m_n)$. This argument is very similar to that of Lemma~\ref{le-normal}.

More precisely, the graphs $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)$ converge to the vertical space
\[\{z^c=\Xi_\infty(f)\gamma(f),\,z^s=0\},\]
which intersects $W^s_{\tilde r_i(f),loc}$. Thus, since by Lemma \ref{le-Xi} $\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)\neq t_i(f_0),$ there exists a sequence $(m_n)_{n\geq0}$ tending to $+\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-controletriple}
\left(\delta(f_0)(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)-t_i(f_0))\chi_{r_i(f_0)}^{m_n}\right)_{n\geq0}
\end{equation}
converges in $\mathbb{D}^*_{1/4}$.

Therefore, by Lemma~\ref{le-triplecontrole}, the iterate $f_0^{j_n+n_0+l_n+n_i+m_n}(\Gamma(f_0))$ contains a $u$-graph $\tilde\Gamma_n(f_0)$ in $B_{r_i}$ that is arbitrarily close to a vertical space in $W^u_{r_i(f_0),loc}$, whose first coordinate is exactly given by \eqref{eq-controletriple}. By the blender property in Assumption~\ref{blender}, the graph $\tilde\Gamma_n(f_0)$ must intersect a local stable manifold $W^s_{x_n(f_0),loc}$. Hence, exactly as in Lemma~\ref{le-normal}, the persistence of the intersections between $W^u_{p(f)}$ and $W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ along $M$ forces the family in~\eqref{eq-controletriple} to be normal.

Since $\delta$ does not vanish on $M$, this implies the normality of the family
\[\left((\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f))\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n}\right)_{n\geq0},\]
as desired.

To conclude the proof, we compute the derivative of these functions. Recall that, by Proposition~\ref{prop-relation} and Lemma~\ref{le-Xi},
\[\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)=\chi_{p(f)}^{j_n-\omega l_n}\zeta^{l_n}
\quad\text{and}\quad
t_i(f)=\Xi_\infty(f)
:=\frac{\chi_{p(f)}^{\omega_\infty}}{\chi_{p(f_0)}^{\omega_\infty}}\,t_i(f_0),\]
where $j_n-\omega l_n\to\omega_\infty$ and $\zeta^{l_n}\to t_i(f_0)/\chi_{p(f_0)}^{\omega_\infty}$ (see~\eqref{eq-omegainfty} and~\eqref{eq-Xi}). Dividing by $t_i(f)$, we obtain the normality of the family
\[\left(e^{(j_n-\omega l_n-\omega_\infty)P(f)+i\theta_n}-1\right)\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n},\]
where $P(f):=\mathrm{Log}(\chi_{p(f)})$ and
\[e^{i\theta_n}:=\zeta^{l_n}\chi_{p(f_0)}^{\omega_\infty}/t_i(f_0),\]
which converges to $1$.

Using the Taylor expansion of the exponential function and setting $a_n:=j_n-\omega l_n-\omega_\infty$, there exist constants $0<A<B$ such that, for all $f$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood $V$ of $f_0$ and all $n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-borne}
A<\left|(a_nP(f)+i\theta_n)\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n}\right|<B.
\end{equation}
Since $P(f_0)$ is not purely imaginary, taking first the real part at $f=f_0$ and then the imaginary part yields
\[a_n=O(\chi_{r_i(f_0)}^{-m_n})
\quad\text{and}\quad
\theta_n=O(\chi_{r_i(f_0)}^{-m_n}).\]
On the other hand, if $\chi_{r_i}$ is not constant on $M$, there exists $f_1\in V$ such that
$|\chi_{r_i(f_1)}|<|\chi_{r_i(f_0)}|$, and therefore
\[\left|(a_nP(f_1)+i\theta_n)\chi_{r_i(f_1)}^{m_n}\right|
=O\left(\frac{|\chi_{r_i(f_1)}|^{m_n}}{|\chi_{r_i(f_0)}|^{m_n}}\right)\]
tends to $0$, contradicting the lower bound in~\eqref{eq-borne}. Hence, $\chi_{r_i}$ must be constant on $M$, which contradicts our initial assumption that $\chi_{r_i(f_0)}'\neq0$.
\end{proof}

A key observation is that, since the assumption~\eqref{eq-hypdoublecontrole} of Lemma~\ref{le-doublecontrole} is satisfied for $(\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f_0))$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and since the family $(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f))$ converges, the same assumption~\eqref{eq-hypdoublecontrole} also holds in a neighborhood of $f_0$ for all large $n$. Hence, Lemma~\ref{le-doublecontrole} implies that, for such $f$, the graphs $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)$ converge to the vertical space
\[\{z^c=\Xi_\infty(f)\gamma(f),\,z^s=0\},\]
which intersects $W^s_{\tilde r_i(f),loc}$, for $f=f_0$, exactly at the point $\tilde r_i(f_0)$. Since these intersections persist along $M$, the first coordinate $R_i^c(f)$ of $\tilde r_i(f)$ in $B_{r_0}$ must equal $\Xi_\infty(f)\gamma(f)$, that is,
\[t_i(f)=\Xi_\infty(f).\]
For the last point in the statement, as $\overline{\langle \chi_{p(f_0)}, \chi_{r_0(f_0)} \rangle}=\mathbb{C}^*,$ we can assume that $(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0))$ converges toward $t_i(f_0)$ while
\[|\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)|\neq |t_i(f_0)|,\ \text{ i.e., }\ j_n-\omega l_n\neq\omega_\infty,\]
by \eqref{eq-omegainfty}. This implies that, for all $f\in M,$ we have
\[|t_i(f)|=|\Xi_\infty(f)|=|\chi_{p(f)}^{\omega_\infty}|\neq|\chi_{p(f)}^{j_n-\omega l_n}|=|\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)|.\]

title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The proof is very similar to that of Lemma~\ref{le-doublecontrole}. More precisely, we apply Lemma~\ref{le-control2} to the graphs
\[\Gamma_n(f):=f^{n_i}\big(\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)\big).\]
Observe that the sequence $(\Gamma_n(f))$ converges to the image $\Gamma_\infty(f)$, under $f^{n_i}$, of the vertical space $\{z^c=\Xi_\infty(f)\gamma(f),\,z^s=0\}$ in $B_{r_0}$. By Lemma~\ref{le-Xi}, this limit graph satisfies
\[\Gamma_\infty(f)\cap W^s_{r_i(f),loc}\neq\varnothing\]
for all $f\in M.$ Moreover, for each $n$, the graph $\Gamma_n(f)$ intersects $\mathsf W^{cs}_{r_i(f)}$ at $(b_n^c(f),b_n^s(f))$, where
\[b_n^c(f)=\tilde v^c(f)\gamma(f)\big(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f)\big)+o\big(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f)\big).\]
Here, the coefficient $\tilde v^c(f)$ arises from the transfer from $B_{r_0}$ to $B_{r_i}$ by $f^{n_i}$ and plays the same role as $v^c(f)$ in~\eqref{eq-v}. More precisely, the set $f^{-n_i}(\mathsf W^{cs}_{r_i(f)})$ is locally a manifold passing through $\tilde r_i(f)$, which projects injectively onto a neighborhood $V$ in $\mathsf W^{cs}_{r_0(f)}$ of $(R_i^c(f),0)$. The quantity $\tilde v^c(f)$ is then defined as the first coordinate of
\[D_{(R_i^c(f),0)}\phi(1,0),\]
where $\phi\colon V\to\mathsf W^{cs}_{r_i(f)}$ denotes the composition of the inverse of this projection with $f^{n_i}$.

Applying Lemma~\ref{le-control2} now yields the existence of a function $\beta$, and the desired conclusion follows from this lemma,  by setting
\[\delta(f):=\beta(f)\tilde v^c(f)\gamma(f).\]

title: Démonstration
body_md:
By~\eqref{star}, there exists $1\leq i\leq N$ such that $\chi_{r_i(f_0)}'\neq 0$. The key ingredient to contradict this fact is to prove that the family
\[\left((\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f))\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n}\right)_{n\geq0},\]
is normal for a suitable sequence $(m_n)$. This argument is very similar to that of Lemma~\ref{le-normal}.

More precisely, the graphs $\Gamma_{j_n,l_n}(f)$ converge to the vertical space
\[\{z^c=\Xi_\infty(f)\gamma(f),\,z^s=0\},\]
which intersects $W^s_{\tilde r_i(f),loc}$. Thus, since by Lemma \ref{le-Xi} $\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)\neq t_i(f_0),$ there exists a sequence $(m_n)_{n\geq0}$ tending to $+\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-controletriple}
\left(\delta(f_0)(\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f_0)-t_i(f_0))\chi_{r_i(f_0)}^{m_n}\right)_{n\geq0}
\end{equation}
converges in $\mathbb{D}^*_{1/4}$.

Therefore, by Lemma~\ref{le-triplecontrole}, the iterate $f_0^{j_n+n_0+l_n+n_i+m_n}(\Gamma(f_0))$ contains a $u$-graph $\tilde\Gamma_n(f_0)$ in $B_{r_i}$ that is arbitrarily close to a vertical space in $W^u_{r_i(f_0),loc}$, whose first coordinate is exactly given by \eqref{eq-controletriple}. By the blender property in Assumption~\ref{blender}, the graph $\tilde\Gamma_n(f_0)$ must intersect a local stable manifold $W^s_{x_n(f_0),loc}$. Hence, exactly as in Lemma~\ref{le-normal}, the persistence of the intersections between $W^u_{p(f)}$ and $W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ along $M$ forces the family in~\eqref{eq-controletriple} to be normal.

Since $\delta$ does not vanish on $M$, this implies the normality of the family
\[\left((\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)-t_i(f))\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n}\right)_{n\geq0},\]
as desired.

To conclude the proof, we compute the derivative of these functions. Recall that, by Proposition~\ref{prop-relation} and Lemma~\ref{le-Xi},
\[\Xi_{j_n,l_n}(f)=\chi_{p(f)}^{j_n-\omega l_n}\zeta^{l_n}
\quad\text{and}\quad
t_i(f)=\Xi_\infty(f)
:=\frac{\chi_{p(f)}^{\omega_\infty}}{\chi_{p(f_0)}^{\omega_\infty}}\,t_i(f_0),\]
where $j_n-\omega l_n\to\omega_\infty$ and $\zeta^{l_n}\to t_i(f_0)/\chi_{p(f_0)}^{\omega_\infty}$ (see~\eqref{eq-omegainfty} and~\eqref{eq-Xi}). Dividing by $t_i(f)$, we obtain the normality of the family
\[\left(e^{(j_n-\omega l_n-\omega_\infty)P(f)+i\theta_n}-1\right)\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n},\]
where $P(f):=\mathrm{Log}(\chi_{p(f)})$ and
\[e^{i\theta_n}:=\zeta^{l_n}\chi_{p(f_0)}^{\omega_\infty}/t_i(f_0),\]
which converges to $1$.

Using the Taylor expansion of the exponential function and setting $a_n:=j_n-\omega l_n-\omega_\infty$, there exist constants $0<A<B$ such that, for all $f$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood $V$ of $f_0$ and all $n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-borne}
A<\left|(a_nP(f)+i\theta_n)\chi_{r_i(f)}^{m_n}\right|<B.
\end{equation}
Since $P(f_0)$ is not purely imaginary, taking first the real part at $f=f_0$ and then the imaginary part yields
\[a_n=O(\chi_{r_i(f_0)}^{-m_n})
\quad\text{and}\quad
\theta_n=O(\chi_{r_i(f_0)}^{-m_n}).\]
On the other hand, if $\chi_{r_i}$ is not constant on $M$, there exists $f_1\in V$ such that
$|\chi_{r_i(f_1)}|<|\chi_{r_i(f_0)}|$, and therefore
\[\left|(a_nP(f_1)+i\theta_n)\chi_{r_i(f_1)}^{m_n}\right|
=O\left(\frac{|\chi_{r_i(f_1)}|^{m_n}}{|\chi_{r_i(f_0)}|^{m_n}}\right)\]
tends to $0$, contradicting the lower bound in~\eqref{eq-borne}. Hence, $\chi_{r_i}$ must be constant on $M$, which contradicts our initial assumption that $\chi_{r_i(f_0)}'\neq0$.

title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-subvar}
Assume that $\mathcal Z$ satisfies \eqref{eq-dag}. If $\mathcal Z$ is not reduced to a point, then there exist $n\geq0,$ a local family $(U_Y)_{Y\in\mathcal Z'}$ and $x\in\Lambda$ such that $f^n(U_Y)$ is a $u$-graph tangent to $C^{uu}_\eta$ in $\mathcal U_+$ for all $Y\in\mathcal Z'$ and

is a hypersurface of $\mathcal Z'$.

label: le-zariski
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-zariski}
For all $Y\in\mathcal Z,$ the set of points in $Y$ defined by
\[P:=\left\{w\in Y_{reg}\ ;\ \begin{array}{c}\exists n\geq0,\ f^n(w)\in W^s_{p,loc},\ D_wf^n\ \text{is invertible, and }\\ T_{f^n(w)}W^s_{p,loc}\cap D_wf^n(T_w Y)=\{0\}\end{array}\right\}\]
is Zariski dense in $Y.$
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Fix $Y\in\mathcal Z.$ Let $w_0$ denote a transverse intersection point between $Y$ and $W^s_{p,loc}$ given by~\eqref{eq-dag}. Let $H$ be the Zariski closure of $P$ in $Y$, and assume by contradiction that $H\neq Y$. 

A first observation is that there exists a point $w\in P$ belonging to the regular part of $H$. Therefore, by replacing $(Y,w_0)$ with $(f^n(Y),f^n(w))$ for a suitable $n\geq0$, we may assume that $H$ is smooth at $w_0$.

We now choose coordinates around $p$ such that $p$ is in standard from in $B_p.$ Moreover, by the inclination lemma, for all sufficiently large $n\geq0$, the graph transforms $f^n(Y)$ in $B_p$ are arbitrarily close to $W^u_{p,loc}$. By Assumption~\ref{saddle} and Assumption~\ref{blender}, there exist sequences $(x_n)\subset\Lambda\cap\mathcal U_+$ and $(y_n)\subset B_p$ such that
\[y_n\in f^n(Y)\cap W^s_{x_n,loc},\]
and such that, up to a subsequence, $(y_n)$ converges to a point $y_\infty \in W^u_{p,loc}$ and $(x_n)$ converges to a point $x_\infty \in \Lambda \cap \mathcal U_+$. By continuity of the local stable manifolds, $y_\infty$ also belongs to $W^s_{x_\infty,loc}$. Notice that we do not relabel the subsequence, as this plays no role in what follows.

A key point for what follows is that, by Assumption~\ref{decalage}, none of the coordinates of $y_\infty$ in $W^u_{p,loc}$ vanishes. Finally, Assumption~\ref{homoclinic} combined with the inclination lemma ensures that each $y_n$ is accumulated by points giving transverse intersections between $f^{n+m}(Y)$ and $W^s_{p,loc}.$ In particular, $w_n:=f^{-n}(y_n)$ is in $H.$

In what follows, we consider the image $(\check y_n)$ and $(\check w_n)$ of these sequences under the linearization map $\theta_f$, in order to derive a contradiction.

Observe that the standard form of $p$ allows us, for each $1\leq i\leq u$, to consider the trace of the $i$-th dynamical direction in $T_{w_0}Y$, namely
\[F_i:=T_{w_0}Y\cap\left(T_{w_0}W^s_{p,loc}\oplus\mathcal E^{u,i}_{w_0}\right).\]
Their direct sum $F_1\oplus\cdots\oplus F_u$ equals the full tangent space $T_{w_0}Y$. Therefore, since $H\neq Y$ and since $H$ is smooth at $w_0,$ there exists at least one index $i_0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-trans}
F_{i_0}\cap T_{w_0}H=\{0\}.
\end{equation}
This allows us to obtain precise local information on the image $\check H$ of $H$ under the linearization $\theta_f$ at $p$. More precisely, since $Y$ is transverse to $W^s_{p,loc}$, there exists a $C^2$ germ $g\colon(\mathbb{C}^u,0)\to B^s$ such that locally
\[\check Y:=\theta_f(Y)=\{(g(z^u),z^u)\}.\]
Thus, the transversality condition~\eqref{eq-trans}, together with the fact
that $D_{w_0}\theta_f(\mathcal E_{w_0}^{u,i_0})$ coincides with the
$i_0$-th canonical unstable direction, implies the existence of a
$C^2$ map $h \colon (\mathbb{C}^{u-1},0) \to \mathbb{C}$ such that, locally near $\check w_0:=\theta_f(w_0)$,
\[\check H\subset
\bigl\{(g(z^u),z^u)\ ;\ z^u_{i_0}=h(z^u_{I_0})\bigr\},\]
where $z^u=(z^u_1,\ldots,z^u_u)$ and $z^u_{I_0}=(z^u_1,\ldots,z^u_{i_0-1},z^u_{i_0+1},\ldots,z^u_u).$

Returning to the sequence $(\check y_n)$ defined above, which converges to a point $y_\infty\in W^u_{p,loc}$ whose coordinates in the unstable manifold are all nonvanishing, we can choose constants $0<a<b$ and an integer $N>0$ such that, for all $n\geq N$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-y}
a<|\check y^u_{j,n}|<b,
\end{equation}
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
                                              
                                                                                                                                        

As observed above, the point $\check w_n$, defined by $\check w_n:=\theta_f\bigl(f^{-n}(y_n)\bigr),$ and hence equal to
\[\check w_n=K_f^{-n}(\check y_n),\]
belongs to $\check H$. Consequently, using that $h$ is of class $C^2$ and satisfies $h(0)=0,$ we must have
\[\check w^u_{i_0,n}=h\bigl(\check w^u_{I_0,n}\bigr)=D_0h(\check w^u_{I_0,n})+O(\|\check w^u_{I_0,n}\|^2).\]
Therefore, since $\check w^u_{i,n}=\rho_i^{-n}\check y^u_{i,n},$ where $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_u$ are the unstable multipliers of $p$, this gives
$\rho_{i_0}^{-n}\check y^u_{i_0,n}=\sum_{j\neq i_0}c_j\rho_{j}^{-n}\check y^u_{j,n}+O(\tilde\chi^{-6n}),$ and thus
\[\check y^u_{i_0,n}
=\sum_{j\neq i_0}c_j(\rho_{i_0}\rho_{j}^{-1})^n\check y^u_{j,n}+O(\tilde\chi^{-2n}),\]
by the bunching condition in Assumption \ref{saddle}. On the other hand, by \eqref{star}, the moduli $|\rho_{i_0}\rho_j^{-1}|$ are pairwise distinct and different from $1$. Using~\eqref{eq-y} and the bounds $|\check y^u_{i_0,n}|<b$ and $|\check y^u_{j,n}|>a$, we obtain that $c_j=0$ whenever $|\rho_{i_0}\rho_j^{-1}|>1$. Hence, $\check y^u_{i_0,n}$ tends to $0$, which contradicts the lower bound in~\eqref{eq-y}.

label: prop-subvar
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-subvar}
Fix $Y_0\in\mathcal Z$ and assume that Theorem~\ref{th-subvar} does not hold. That is, $\mathcal Z$ is not reduced to a single point and, for every $n\geq0$, every $x\in\Lambda$, and every local family $(U_Y)_{Y\in\mathcal Z'}$ such that $f^n(U_Y)$ is a $u$-graph in $\mathcal U_+$ tangent to $C^{uu}_\eta$, the set
\[\{\,Y\in\mathcal Z' \; ; \; f^n(U_Y)\cap W^s_{x,loc}\neq\varnothing\,\}\]
is either empty or equal to $\mathcal Z'$.

Then there exist $n_0\geq0$, an open neighborhood $\mathcal Z_0$ of $Y_0$, and a family $(\Gamma_Y)_{Y\in\mathcal Z_0}$ of $u$-graphs in $B_p$ such that $\Gamma_Y\subset f^{n_0}(Y)$ for all $Y\in\mathcal Z_0$, and which intersects $W^s_{p,loc}$ in
\[(b^c,b^s(Y)),\]
where $b^s(Y)$ is not constant on $\mathcal Z_0$.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{le-zariski}, the set of points $P$ associated with $Y_0$ is Zariski dense. Since $\mathcal Z$ is not reduced to $\{Y_0\}$, there exists a point $w_{Y_0}\in P$ whose continuation is not constant as $Y$ varies in $\mathcal Z$. By definition of $P$, there exists $n_0\geq0$ such that $f^{n_0}(w_{Y_0})$ is a transverse intersection point between $f^{n_0}(Y_0)$ and $W^s_{p,loc}$.

This intersection point can therefore be followed holomorphically in a small connected open neighborhood $\mathcal Z_0\subset\mathcal Z$ of $Y_0$, yielding a map
\[y_0\colon \mathcal Z_0 \to W^s_{p,loc}\]
which is not constant. Since $f^{n_0}(Y)$ is transverse to $W^s_{p,loc}$ at $y_0(Y)$, possibly after increasing $n_0$ we may assume that $y_0(Y)$ belongs to a submanifold $\Gamma_Y\subset f^{n_0}(Y)$ arbitrarily close to $W^u_{p,loc}$  for every $Y\in\mathcal Z_0$. In particular, it contains a $u$-graph in $\mathcal U_+$ tangent to the cone field $C^{uu}_\eta$.

Let $(b^c(Y),b^s(Y))$ denote the coordinates of $y_0(Y)$ in $W^s_{p,loc}$. Since $y_0$ is not constant, it remains to show that $b^c(Y)$ is constant on $\mathcal Z_0$.

To this end, by Lemma~\ref{le-control1} and Remark~\ref{rk-control1}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq-controle1surY}
f^n(\Gamma_Y)=\left\{\left(
\chi_p^{n} b^c(Y)\big[\alpha(f)(1,0)+R_n(Y,z)\big],
\, z
\right)\ ;\ z\in B^u\right\},
\end{equation}
where $R_n(Y,z)$ converges locally uniformly to $0$ with respect to both $Y$ and $z$.

On the other hand, by Assumption~\ref{blender}, there exists $x_n\in\Lambda\cap\mathcal U_+$ such that $f^n(\Gamma_{Y_0})$ intersects $W^s_{x_n,loc}$ at a point $q_n(Y_0)$. By the assumption of the proposition, all such intersections persist, and thus define a map $q_n(Y)$ for $Y\in\mathcal Z_0$.

If $b^c(Y)$ were not constant on $\mathcal Z_0$, then~\eqref{eq-controle1surY} would imply the existence of unit tangent vectors in $T_{q_n(Y_0)}W^s_{x_n,loc}$ arbitrarily close to vectors of the form $(v_n^c,0,v_n^u)$ in $B_p$. This is impossible, since $W^s_{x_n,loc}$ is tangent to the strong stable cone field $C_\eta^{ss}$, whereas vectors of the form $(v_n^c,0,v_n^u)$ in $B_p$ do not belong to these cones by Lemma \ref{le-centrer-unstable}.

label: le-grille
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-grille}
Assume that $p$ is in standard form in $B_p$. Let $\Gamma=(\Gamma_t)_{t\in\mathbb{D}}$ be a family of pairwise disjoint $u$-graphs in $B_p$ intersecting $W^s_{p,loc}$ at $(b^c,b^s(t))$, where the map $t\mapsto b^s(t)$ is not constant. Let $V$ denote the total space
\[V:=\bigcup_{t\in\mathbb{D}}\Gamma_t.\]
If $(x_n,v_n)$ is a sequence in the tangent space $TV$ with $x_n\in\Gamma_0$ such that for an increasing sequence $(m_n)$, $(f^{m_n}(x_n),D_{x_n}f^{m_n}(v_n))$ converges in $TB_p$ to a pair $(y,w)$, then there exists $1\leq i\leq s$ such that
$$w\in T_yW^u_{p,loc}\oplus\mathcal E^{s,i}_{y},$$
where $\mathcal E^{s,i}$ is the dynamical direction associated to the $i$-th strong-stable multiplier $\lambda_i.$
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
A first remark is that, since the $\Gamma_t$ are pairwise disjoint, the set $V$ is a (non-closed) submanifold. Second, the argument relies entirely on the fact that the expansion in the unstable direction near $p$ dominates the contraction in the stable direction by Assumption~\ref{saddle}. Therefore, it is independent of the complex setting, and we will work in smooth linearization coordinates.

Let $(x_n,v_n)$ be a sequence with $x_n\in V$ and $v_n\in T_{x_n}V$ as in the statement. We set
\[\check x_n:=(\check x_n^c,\check x_n^s,\check x_n^u):={\theta_f}(x_n)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\check v_n:=(\check v_n^c,\check v_n^s,\check v_n^u):=D_{x_n}{\theta_f}\,v_n,\]
where ${\theta_f}$ denotes the linearization map associated to $p$.

Since $(\Gamma_t)_{t\in\mathbb{D}}$ is a family of $u$-graphs in $B_p$, there exists a family of $C^1$ maps $h_t=(h_t^c,h_t^s)$ such that
\[\check\Gamma_t:={\theta_f}(\Gamma_t)
=\{(h_t^c(z),h_t^s(z),z)\ ;\ z\in B^u\}.\]
We denote by $\check V:={\theta_f}(V)$. In particular, for $\check x\in\check\Gamma_0$, the tangent space of $\check V$ at $\check x$ decomposes as
\[T_{\check x}\check V
= T_{\check x}\check\Gamma_0 \oplus \check E_{\check x},\]
where $\check E_{\check x}$ is generated by the derivatives with respect to $t$ (viewed as two real variables) of the map $(t,z)\mapsto h_t(z)$ at $t=0$.

Accordingly, $\check v_n$ can be written as
\[\check v_n=\alpha_n u_n+\beta_n e_n,\]
where $\alpha_n,\beta_n\in\mathbb{R}$, $u_n\in T_{\check x_n}\check\Gamma_0$, and $e_n\in\check E_{\check x_n}$, with $\|u_n\|=\|e_n\|=1$.

The key point is that, at $z=0$, we have by assumption
\[h_t(0)=(b^c,b^s(t)).\]
Hence, at the point $\check x_0:=(b^c,b^s(0),0)$, the space $\check E$ is generated (over $\mathbb{C}$) by a unit vector $e_0$ in the strong stable direction. As a consequence,
\[e_n=\xi_n e_0+O(\check x_n^u)\]
for some $\xi_n\in\mathbb{S}^1$.

Now let
\[\check y:={\theta_f}(y)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\check w:=(\check w^c,\check w^s,\check w^u):=D_y{\theta_f}\,w.\]
Since $y\in W^u_{p,loc}$ and $D{\theta_f}$ preserves the center direction along this manifold, we have that $\check w^c=0$ if and only if the first coordinate of $w$ vanishes.

To prove that $\check w^c=0$, we consider the image of $\check v_n$ under the linearized dynamics $K^{m_n}=(\chi_p^{m_n},A^{m_n},E^{m_n}),$ and set
\[\check w_n:=(\check w_n^c,\check w_n^s,\check w_n^u):=K^{m_n}\check v_n.\]
By assumption, $\check w_n$ converges to $\check w$ as $n\to\infty$.

Let $\tilde\chi$ be the constant defined in Section~\ref{sec-ass}. Since the sequences $(\check w_n^s)$ and $(\check w_n^u)$ are convergent, we obtain by Assumption~\ref{saddle}
\begin{equation*}\label{eq-s}
\check v_n^s=o(\tilde\chi^{3{m_n}})
\quad\text{and}\quad
\check v_n^u=o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}}).
\end{equation*}
Moreover, since $K^{m_n}(\check x_n)$ converges to $\check y$, we have $\check x_n^u=o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}})$, and therefore
\begin{equation*}\label{eq-e}
e_n=\xi_n e_0+o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}}).
\end{equation*}

Projecting $\check v_n$ onto the unstable direction yields
\[\alpha_n=\beta_n\,o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}})+O(\|\check v_n^u\|)=\beta_n\,o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}})+o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}}),\]
while projection onto the strong stable direction gives
\[\beta_n(1+o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}}))+O(\alpha_n)
=\|\check v_n^s\|
=o(\tilde\chi^{3{m_n}}).\]
It follows that
\[\beta_n=o(\tilde\chi^{3{m_n}})
\quad\text{and}\quad
\alpha_n=o(\tilde\chi^{3{m_n}})o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}})=o(1).\]
Finally, returning to $\check w_n$, we obtain
\[\check w_n^c=\chi_p^n\check v_n^c
=\chi_p^n\big(O(\alpha_n)+\beta_n\,o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}})\big)=o(1).\]
Since $\check w_n^c\to\check w^c$, we conclude that $\check w^c=0$, as claimed. It remains to prove that at most one coordinate of $\check w^s$ can be nonzero.

First, recall that
\[\check w_n^s = A^{m_n} \check v_n^s
= \alpha_n A^{m_n} u_n^s + \beta_n A^{m_n} e_n^s.\]
Using the asymptotics of $\alpha_n=o(1)$, $\beta_n=o(\tilde\chi^{3{m_n}})$, and
$e_n^s = \xi_n e_0^s + o(\tilde\chi^{-3{m_n}})$, we obtain
\[\check w_n^s = \beta_n \xi_n A^{m_n} e_0^s + o(1).\]
Suppose that there exists $1 \le i_0 \le s$ such that the
$i_0$-th coordinate $\check w^s(i_0) \neq 0$. Then
\[0\neq\check w^s(i_0)= \lim_{n \to \infty} \check w_n^s(i_0)
= \lim_{n \to \infty}\beta_n \xi_n \lambda_{i_0}^{m_n} e_0^s(i_0),\]
where $\lambda_{i_0}$ denotes the $i_0$-th strong stable multiplier of $p$ given in Assumption~\ref{saddle}.
Since these multipliers have distinct moduli, such a nonzero and finite limit can occur for at most one index $i_0$.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
We argue by contradiction and assume that the statement of the theorem does not hold. Fix $Y_0\in\mathcal Z$. By Proposition~\ref{prop-subvar}, there exist an integer $n_0\geq0$, an open neighborhood $\mathcal Z_0$ of $Y_0$ in $\mathcal Z$, and a family $(\Gamma_Y)_{Y\in\mathcal Z_0}$ of $u$-graphs in $B_p$ such that $\Gamma_Y\subset f^{n_0}(Y)$ for all $Y\in\mathcal Z_0$, and such that
\[\Gamma_Y\cap W^s_{p,loc}=(b^c,b^s(Y)),\]
where the map $Y\mapsto b^s(Y)$ is not constant on $\mathcal Z_0$.

We may therefore choose a holomorphic disc $(Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb{D}}$ contained in $\mathcal Z_0$ and centered at $Y_0$, such that the map $t\mapsto b^s(t)$ is nonconstant. In particular, near any noncritical point of $b^s$, the germs of the polydiscs $\Gamma_t$ near $W^s_{p,loc}$ are pairwise disjoint. Possibly after restricting to a smaller holomorphic disc and taking an iterate, we may assume that the polydiscs $\Gamma_t$ are pairwise disjoint.


On the other hand, by Assumption~\ref{blender}, for every $n\geq0$ the graph transform $f^n(\Gamma_0)$ intersects the local stable manifold $W^s_{x_n,loc}$ of some point $x_n\in\Lambda\cap\mathcal U_+$ at a unique point, which we denote by $y_n$. By our contradiction assumption, all these intersections persist along the family, so that for each $n$ the intersection
\[f^n(\Gamma_t)\cap W^s_{x_n,loc}\]
is given by a holomorphic map $t\mapsto y_n(t)$ with $y_n(0)=y_n$. Moreover, there are subsequences such that $(x_{m_n})$ converges to some $x_\infty\in\Lambda\cap\mathcal U_+$ and $(y_{m_n})$ converges to
\[y_\infty\in W^u_{p,loc}\cap W^s_{x_\infty,loc}.\]
Since the graphs $\Gamma_t$ are pairwise disjoint, these maps are injective. Therefore, differentiating at $t=0$ yields a nonzero tangent vector
\[w_n \in T_{y_{m_n}}W^s_{x_{m_n},loc}.\]
Up to a subsequence, we have that $w_n/\|w_n\|$ converges to $w_\infty\in T_{y_\infty}W^s_{x_\infty,loc}.$
Since $x_\infty\in\Lambda\cap\mathcal U_+,$ $w_\infty$ is the image of some vector in $C_\eta^{ss}$ by the differential of the inverse branche $G_+\colon f(\mathcal U_+)\to\mathcal U_+.$ Hence, Assumption~\ref{grille} implies that $w_\infty$ does not belong to
\[T_{y_\infty} W^u_{p(f),loc} \oplus\mathcal E^{s,i}_{y_\infty}\]
for any $1 \le i \le s$, where $\mathcal E^{s,i}_{y_\infty}$ denotes the dynamical
direction at $y_\infty$ associated with the eigenvalue $\lambda_i$.

We now apply Lemma~\ref{le-grille} to the sequence of points
\[\hat x_n := f^{-m_n}(y_{m_n})\in \Gamma_0\]
and tangent vectors
\[v_n := D_{y_{m_n}}f^{-{m_n}}\left(\frac{w_n}{\|w_n\|}\right) \in T_{\hat x_n}V,\]
where
\[V:=\bigcup_{t\in\mathbb{D}}\Gamma_t.\]
Lemma~\ref{le-grille} therefore forces
\[w_\infty \in T_{y_\infty} W^u_{p(f),loc} \oplus\mathcal E^{s,i}_{y_\infty}\]
for some $1 \le i \le s$, contradicting the above consequence of Assumption~\ref{grille}.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Let $(Y',f')\in\mathcal Y_{\rm reg}$ satisfy~\eqref{eq-pitch}.
We fix an arbitrarily small neighborhood $\mathcal Y_0$ of $(Y',f')$
in $\mathcal Y$ on which \eqref{eq-pitch} and the condition
$f\in\Omega_u$ hold. As explained in~\eqref{eq-inter-non-vide}, it
suffices to prove that
\[
\mathcal Y_0\cap\textup{supp}(\mu_{\mathcal Y})\neq\varnothing.
\]


As in Section~\ref{sec-main-blender}, after possibly shrinking
$\mathcal Y_0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:local-normalization} allows us to
choose
\[
 (Y_0,f_0)\in\mathcal Y_0\cap\mathcal Y^\circ
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 f_0\in\tilde\Omega\subset\Omega_u
\]
such that simultaneous conjugacy identifies $\mathcal Y_0$ with a
complex submanifold of
\[
 \mathcal X_D^u\times\tilde\Omega
\]
whose projection
\[
 \pi_{\tilde\Omega}:\mathcal Y_0\to\tilde\Omega
\]
is a surjective submersion. Recall that
\[
 N:=\dim\tilde\Omega=\dim\mathscr M_d^k,
\]
so the fibers of $\pi_{\tilde\Omega}$ have dimension $\dim\mathcal Y-N$.

We freely shrink $\mathcal Y_0$ and $\tilde\Omega$ in what follows.

We also use all the reductions introduced in
Section~\ref{sec-standard}. In particular, the periodic points
$r_1(f),\ldots,r_N(f)$ are defined on $\tilde\Omega$ and the multiplier
map
\[
f\mapsto
\bigl(\chi_{r_1(f)},\ldots,\chi_{r_N(f)}\bigr)
\]
is a local biholomorphism onto its image.

Roughly speaking, the strategy is the following.
\begin{itemize}
\item Using Assumption~\ref{init}, choose a map $f_0\in\tilde\Omega$
such that $W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$ intersects a preimage of
$W^s_{r_0(f_0),loc}$ and
\[
\overline{\langle\chi_{p(f_0)},\chi_{r_0(f_0)}\rangle}=\mathbb{C}^*.
\]

\item This stable/unstable relation defines a hypersurface
$A_1\subset\tilde\Omega$.

\item Using the homoclinic intersection from
Assumption~\ref{homoclinic}, we successively impose new
stable/unstable relations, defining a decreasing sequence of analytic
subsets
\[
A_1\supset A_2\supset\cdots\supset A_N
\]
of $\tilde\Omega$. Theorem~\ref{th-point} ensures that this process can
be continued until $A_N$ reduces to a point.

\item Taking inverse images by the submersion $\pi_{\tilde\Omega},$ these relations lift to corresponding relations in $\mathcal Y_0.$ Once the dynamical parameter is fixed,
Theorem~\ref{th-subvar}, together with~\eqref{eq-pitch}, allows us to
successively impose new relations coming from variations of $Y$ until
we obtain a zero-dimensional intersection.

\item Finally, using the density of periodic points in $\Lambda(f)$,
the inclination lemma, and the persistence of proper intersections, we
replace all these relations by relations satisfying
\ref{it:cond21} and~\ref{it:cond22}.
\end{itemize}

We now give the details.

\bigskip

\noindent\emph{\textbf{Initialization.}}
Using Assumption~\ref{init}, we fix $f_0\in\tilde\Omega$, $m_0\geq0$
and $\tilde r_0(f_0)\in W^s_{\Lambda(f_0),loc}$ such that
\[
\overline{\langle\chi_{p(f_0)},\chi_{r_0(f_0)}\rangle}=\mathbb{C}^*,
\qquad
\tilde r_0(f_0)\in W^u_{p(f_0),loc},
\]
and
\[
f_0^{m_0}(\tilde r_0(f_0))
\in W^s_{r_0(f_0),loc}.
\]
By Assumption~\ref{free}, this relation is not persistent. Hence,
possibly after shrinking $\tilde\Omega$,
\[
A_1:=
\left\{
f\in\tilde\Omega\ ;\
f^{m_0}(W^u_{p(f),loc})\cap W^s_{r_0(f),loc}
\neq\varnothing
\right\}
\]
defines a hypersurface of $\tilde\Omega$ containing $f_0$.

On the other hand, Assumption~\ref{homoclinic} provides a local
submanifold contained in the global unstable manifold $W^u_{p(f)}$
and transverse to $W^s_{p(f),loc}$. Using the inclination lemma and
possibly replacing it by an iterate, we obtain a holomorphic family
$(\Gamma(f))_{f\in\tilde\Omega}$ of $u$-graphs contained in
$W^u_{p(f)}$. The iterates of these graphs will be used to produce the
successive stable/unstable relations.

The only technical difficulty is that $A_1$ need not be irreducible
at $f_0$. A non-persistent relation may therefore decrease the
dimension of only one local component and fail to give the proper
intersection needed below.

\bigskip

\noindent\emph{\textbf{Move to a smooth point.}}
To overcome this difficulty, we proceed as in
\textbf{Step~2} of the proof of~\cite[Theorem~C]{gtv}.
The condition
\[
\overline{\langle\chi_{p(f)},\chi_{r_0(f)}\rangle}=\mathbb{C}^*
\]
is very generic in the real analytic sense. We may therefore replace
$f_0$ by a smooth point $f_1$ of $A_1$ satisfying the same condition,
and choose a neighborhood $\tilde\Omega_1$ of $f_1$ such that
$A_1\cap\tilde\Omega_1$ is smooth, connected and closed in
$\tilde\Omega_1$.

We now argue inductively. Assume that, for some $1\leq i<N$, we have
constructed a smooth connected analytic submanifold
$A_i\subset\tilde\Omega_i$ of codimension $i$, containing a point
$f_i$ such that
\[
\overline{\langle\chi_{p(f_i)},\chi_{r_0(f_i)}\rangle}=\mathbb{C}^*.
\]
If no new stable/unstable relation defines a hypersurface of $A_i$
near $f_i$, Theorem~\ref{th-point} implies that $A_i$ is reduced to a
point. Since $i<N=\dim\tilde\Omega$, this is impossible.

Hence there exist $m_i\geq0$ and $x_i\in\Lambda$ such that
\[
A_{i+1}:=
\left\{
f\in A_i\cap\tilde\Omega_i\ ;\
f^{m_i}(\Gamma(f))\cap W^s_{x_i(f),loc}
\neq\varnothing
\right\}
\]
defines locally a hypersurface of $A_i$. As above, we may move to a
smooth point $f_{i+1}$ of a suitable component of $A_{i+1}$ satisfying
the dense subgroup condition and choose a neighborhood
$\tilde\Omega_{i+1}$ such that $A_{i+1}$ is smooth, connected and
closed there.

Iterating this procedure, we obtain
\[
A_1\supset A_2\supset\cdots\supset A_N,
\qquad
\text{codim}_{\tilde\Omega}A_i=i,
\]
and, after the last reduction,
\[
A_N=\{f_N\}.
\]

\bigskip

\noindent\emph{\textbf{Variations coming from subvarieties.}}
We now use the fact that $\pi_{\tilde\Omega}\colon\mathcal Y_0\to\tilde\Omega$ is a submersion and, for $1\leq i\leq N$, set
\[
\mathcal A_i:=\pi_{\tilde\Omega}^{-1}(A_i)\cap\mathcal Y_0.
\]
After shrinking around the final parameter, we may assume that
$\mathcal A_N$ is a connected open subset of the fiber
\[
\pi_{\tilde\Omega}^{-1}(f_N).
\]
In particular,
\[
\dim\mathcal A_N=\dim\mathcal Y-N.
\]

If $\mathcal A_N$ is not reduced to a point, condition~\eqref{eq-pitch}
and the inclination lemma put us in the setting of
Theorem~\ref{th-subvar}. Hence we can impose a new relation between an
iterate of the varying subvariety $Y$ and the local stable manifold of
a point of $\Lambda(f_N)$, defining a hypersurface of $\mathcal A_N$.

Repeating the argument, we obtain a decreasing sequence
\[
\mathcal A_N\supset\mathcal A_{N+1}\supset\cdots
\supset\mathcal A_{N'},
\qquad
N':=\dim\mathcal Y,
\]
where, for every $N<i\leq N'$, the set $\mathcal A_i$ is locally of
the form
\[
\left\{
(Y,f_N)\in\mathcal A_{i-1}\ ;\
f_N^{m_{i-1}}(U_Y)\cap W^s_{x_{i-1},loc}
\neq\varnothing
\right\}
\]
for some local family $(U_Y)$, some $m_{i-1}\geq0$ and
$x_{i-1}\in\Lambda(f_N)$. Theorem~\ref{th-subvar} ensures that the
procedure can be continued as long as the current family has positive
dimension. Therefore
\[
\mathcal A_{N'}=\{(Y_*,f_N)\}
\]
is reduced to a single point.

\bigskip

\noindent\emph{\textbf{Genuine Misiurewicz relations.}}
The construction above gives $N'=\dim\mathcal Y$ independent
stable/unstable relations. We now replace them by relations involving
periodic points in $\Lambda$ and iterates of $Y$, as required in
\ref{it:cond21} and~\ref{it:cond22}.

Indeed, consider the corresponding intersection in
\[
\mathcal Y_0\times(\mathbb{P}^k)^{N'}.
\]
For the first $N$ coordinates, the local $u$-graphs involved are
respectively contained in iterates of
\[
W^u_{p(f),loc},\ \Gamma(f),\ldots,\Gamma(f),
\]
whereas for the remaining coordinates they are contained in iterates
of the varying subvariety $Y$. Let $Z$ denote the analytic set obtained
by putting these $N'$ local $u$-graphs together, and let
\[
\mathcal W^s_{x,loc}:=
\left\{
(Y,f,z_1,\ldots,z_{N'})\ ;\
z_i\in W^s_{x_i(f),loc},\ 1\leq i\leq N'
\right\}.
\]
By construction,
\[
\dim\bigl(Z\cap\mathcal W^s_{x,loc}\bigr)=0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\dim Z=(u+1)N',
\qquad
\dim\mathcal W^s_{x,loc}=(s+1)N',
\]
whereas
\[
\dim\bigl(\mathcal Y_0\times(\mathbb{P}^k)^{N'}\bigr)
=(k+1)N'.
\]
Since $k=s+u+1$, the intersection is proper.

Periodic points are dense in $\Lambda(f)$. Hence, by persistence of
proper intersections, we may replace each $x_i$ by a periodic point
$x_i'$ arbitrarily close to it. Furthermore, by the inclination lemma
and~\eqref{eq-pitch}, sufficiently large iterates of suitable local
pieces of $Y$ can be chosen arbitrarily close to all the $u$-graphs
appearing in the first $N$ relations. After shrinking the corresponding
local pieces, we therefore obtain periodic points
\[
x_1'(f),\ldots,x_{N'}'(f)\in\Lambda(f)
\]
and local families satisfying conditions~\ref{it:cond21}
and~\ref{it:cond22} with
\[
m=N'=\dim\mathcal Y.
\]

In particular, this proves that the maximal integer $m$ introduced in
Section~\ref{sec-main-blender} is equal to $\dim\mathcal Y$.

By Lemma~\ref{le-cond2}, condition~\ref{it:cond2} of
Proposition~\ref{prop-positivevolume} follows. On the other hand,
Assumption~\ref{misu} and Lemma~\ref{le-cond1} give
condition~\ref{it:cond1}. Proposition~\ref{prop-positivevolume}
therefore applies and yields
\[
\mathcal Y_0\cap\textup{supp}(\mu_{\mathcal Y})\neq\varnothing.
\]

Since the original neighborhood $\mathcal Y_0$ was arbitrarily small
around $(Y',f')$, and $\textup{supp}(\mu_{\mathcal Y})$ is closed, we conclude
that
\[
(Y',f')\in\textup{supp}(\mu_{\mathcal Y}).
\]

label: th-existence
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-existence}
For each codimension $1\leq u\leq k-1,$ there exist $a,\alpha,\epsilon,\beta,\tilde w(a)\in\mathbb{C},$ $\tau,\gamma\in\mathbb{C}^s,$ $\sigma\in\mathbb{C}^{u-1}$ and a small perturbation $f\in\mathrm{Poly}_d^k$ of the map $f_0:\mathbb{C}^k\to\mathbb{C}^k$ defined, for $(z,x,y,w)\in\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}^s\times\mathbb{C}^{u-1}\times\mathbb{C}$ by
\[f_0(z,x,y,w)=\left(\alpha z+\epsilon w+\beta zw+\tau\cdot x(w-\tilde w(a)),\gamma x,\sigma\left(y+\frac{w-\tilde w(a)}{6}\right),a(w^2-1)\right)\]
such that $f$ admits a neighborhood $\Omega_u$ in $\mathrm{End}_d^k$ (or $\mathrm{Poly}_d^k$) which satisfies all the assumptions described in Section~\ref{sec-ass}.

label: le-blender
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-blender}
There exist constants $\eta>100$ and $\delta>100$ such that, if $|a|>\delta$, then for every $(\alpha,\beta,\epsilon)\in\hat M$, the map ${\mathcal F}_{\lambda}$, with $\lambda:=(a,\alpha,\beta,\epsilon)$, satisfies the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item On each of the sets $\mathbb{D}_R\times V_-(a)$ and $\mathbb{D}_R\times V_+(a)$, the map $\mathcal F^2_\lambda$ is injective, expanding, and contracts the cone field $C_\eta$. Moreover,
\[
\overline{\mathbb{D}_R\times (U_+(a)\cup U_-(a))}\subset \overline{\mathbb{D}_R\times \mathbb{D}_2}
\subset
\mathcal F^2_\lambda(\mathbb{D}_R\times V_\pm(a)).
\]
In particular, the set
\[
\Lambda(\lambda):=\bigcap_{n\geq0}\mathcal F^{-2n}_\lambda\bigl(\mathbb{D}_R\times (V_-(a)\cup V_+(a))\bigr)
\]
is a hyperbolic repelling invariant set for $\mathcal F^2_\lambda$.
\item For every $i\in\{1,2,3,4\}$, any vertical graph in $\mathbb{D}\times V_i(a)$ tangent to the cone $C_\eta$ intersects $\Lambda(\lambda)$.
\end{itemize}
Moreover, both conclusions are stable under small $C^1$-perturbations of ${\mathcal F}_\lambda$.

\quad\text{and}\quad
M:=D_\infty\times \hat M,

label: rk-S
title: \bf Remark
body_md:
\label{rk-S}
In Section~\ref{sec-chasse} below, we need the same local construction directly in higher degrees. But all the results of this subsection also hold for
\[
\mathcal F_{a,S}(z,w)=\bigl((\alpha+\beta wS(w))z+\epsilon w,
 \tilde w(a)+a(w^2-\tilde w(a)^2)S(w)\bigr),
\]
where $S$ is a fixed polynomial of degree $D$ sufficiently close to $1$ on $\overline{\mathbb{D}_3}$, provided $|a|$ is sufficiently large.
Indeed, the second coordinates has $D+2$ inverse branches when $|a|$ is large, $D$ corresponding to the roots of $S$ and $2$ others, $g_{\pm,a}$ close to $w=\pm1.$
They satisfy $g_{\pm,a}(w)=\pm1+O(1/a)$ and $g_{\pm,a}'=O(1/a)$ on fixed large discs. Set
\[
\alpha_S=\alpha+\frac\beta2\bigl(S(1)-S(-1)\bigr),\qquad
\beta_S=\frac\beta2\bigl(S(1)+S(-1)\bigr).
\]
The limiting affine maps are exactly those above with
$(\alpha,\beta)$ replaced by $(\alpha_S,\beta_S)$, and both the
covering argument and the multiplier-transversality argument apply
in the same way, provided $\alpha_S$ and $\beta_S$ satisfy \eqref{def-M}. Thus $S$ may be fixed close to $1$ on $\overline\mathbb{D}_3$ first and $|a|$ then taken
large.

body_md:
\label{le-ass1et2}
Possibly by increasing the constant $\delta>0$ then, for the choice of parameters as above, the map $f_0$ satisfies Assumptions~\ref{verti} and \ref{hyperbolic} on these sets. In particular,
\[\Lambda(f_0):=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_0^{-2n}(\mathcal V)\]

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Each point is straightforward, and we leave precise details to the reader.

The injectivity of $f_0$ on these sets follows from that of $q_a$ on $U_\pm(a)$, since $f_0$ acts affinely with
full rank on each hyperplane of the pencil, except on
$\{w=-\alpha/\beta\}$. However, $|\alpha/\beta|>20>2$.

The cone field conditions follow from a direct computation of the
differential of $f_0$. The only delicate point concerns the
expansion of the stable cone field: with our choice
$|\gamma_1|<\cdots<|\gamma_s|<2|\gamma_1|$, we need that each component of
$\tau$ satisfies $|\tau_i|<(10\eta s)^{-1}$, which is ensured by
$|\tau_i|<\delta^{-1}$ if $\delta$ is chosen large enough.

The horizontal-like behavior of $f_0$ and $f_0^2$ on $\mathcal U_\pm$ and $\mathcal V$ respectively come from
\[U_\pm^u\Subset\mathbb{B}_2^u\Subset G(U_\pm^u),\quad G^2(V^u_\pm)=\mathbb{B}_2^u,\]
and the fact that the $w$-coordinates on $U_\pm^u$ is almost equal to $\pm1.$

The locally maximal set
\[\Lambda(f_0)=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} f_0^{-2n}(\mathcal V)\]
is contained in the invariant plane $\{x=0\}$. On this plane,
$f_0$ is conjugate, via the projection $(z,y,w)\mapsto(z,w)$,
to the map $\mathcal F_\lambda$ studied in
Section~\ref{sec-dim2}. Since $\mathcal F_\lambda$ is expanding
on the corresponding set by Lemma~\ref{le-blender}, and since the
additional factor $\sigma(y+w-\tilde w(a))$ is also expanding,
it follows that $\Lambda(f_0)$ is a repelling hyperbolic set for
$f^2_{0|\{x=0\}}$.

Moreover, on this plane, the fibration by lines
$\{(y,w)=\mathrm{cst}\}$ is invariant. For $(y,w)\in V^u_\pm$,
the differential of $f_0^2$ along these lines is essentially
$\alpha^2-\beta^2$, which is much smaller than the other expansion
rates (of order $|4a^2|$ and $|\sigma_i|^2$). Hence, this
direction defines a central unstable direction for
$\Lambda(f_0)$.

On the other hand, since the plane $\{x=0\}$ is uniformly
attracting, it follows that $\Lambda(f_0)$ is hyperbolic of
index $(s,u+1)$ and the bunching conditions in Assumption~\ref{hyperbolic} are satisfied with $\tilde\chi:=2|a|^{1/4}.$

Finally, a direct computation of $f^2_0|_{\{x=0\}}$ gives that the first coordinate of the fixed point $r_0(f_0)$ for this map is smaller than
\[|\epsilon(\beta+\alpha-1)|<3|\epsilon|<3/10.\]

title: Démonstration
body_md: The only point which does not directly comes from the choice of the parameters is that $W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$ is a $u$-graph above $\mathbb{D}$ and not a larger disc. Each $u$-graph in $\mathbb{D}\times \mathbb{B}^s\times V_+^u$ (resp. $\mathbb{D}\times \mathbb{B}^s\times V_-^u$)  tangent to $C^{uu}_{\eta}$ intersects the stable set of $\Lambda(f_0)$

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The key ingredient is that, as we have seen, the first factor of $f_0^4$ is arbitrarily close to $\phi_{j,\hat\lambda}$ on $\mathbb{D}_R\times\mathbb{B}^s\times V^u_j,$ which implies the inclusion \eqref{eq-cover2}.

Recall that $\rho>0$ is the Lebesgue number of the cover $\overline{\mathbb{D}_{2-r}}\subset \bigcup_{j=1}^4H_j$ and that $\eta>4\rho^{-1}.$ Observe that $\rho$ is also the Lebesgue number of the cover
\[\overline{\mathbb{D}_{2-r}\times\mathbb{B}^s_{1/2}}\subset \bigcup_{j=1}^4H_j\times\mathbb{B}^s.\]
 Hence, the vertical projection of $u$-graph $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{D}_{2-r}\times\mathbb{B}^s_{1/2}\times\mathbb{B}^u_2$ tangent to $C^{uu}_\eta$ must have diameter smaller than $\rho$ and thus, is compactly contained in on of the $H_j\times\mathbb{B}^s.$


Now, let $j_0\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ and let $\Gamma_0\subset H_{j_0}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times V^u_{j_0}$ be a $u$-graph tangent to $C^{uu}_\eta.$ Its image by $f_0^4$ is a $u$-graph in $\mathbb{D}_{2-r}\times\mathbb{B}^s_{1/2}\times\mathbb{B}^u_2$ and by what we have just said, there exists $j_1\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that its vertical projection is compactly contained in $H_{j_1}\times\mathbb{B}^s.$  Thus, $f_0^4(\Gamma_0)$ contains a $u$-graph $\Gamma_1\subset H_{j_1}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times V^u_{j_1}$ tangent to $C^{uu}_\eta.$ By induction, we obtain a sequence of vertical graph $\Gamma_n\subset f_0^{4n}(\Gamma_0)$ in some $H_{j_n}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times V^u_{j_n}$ and thus $\Gamma_0$ intersects 
\[\bigcap_{n\geq0} f_0^{-4n}\left(\mathbb{D}_R\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^4V^u_j\right)\right).\]
By definition of the sets $V^u_j$ and by \cite[Paper~I, Corollary~2.6]{jonsson-phd}, this intersection is exactly the stable set of $\Lambda(f_0)$.
Moreover, all these arguments are robust under small $C^1$ perturbations.
head: environment

label: le-decalage
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
We need a more precise description of the coordinate hyperplanes in the
linearizing coordinates of $W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$.

A first remark is that $W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$ is contained in the plane
$\{x=0\}$. Moreover, the affine subspace
\[\{x=0,\ w=\tilde w(a)\}\]
is invariant, and the restriction of $f_0$ to it is given by
\[(z,y)\mapsto\big(z(\alpha+\beta\tilde w(a))+\epsilon\tilde w(a),\sigma y\big).\]
It follows that, for $1\le i\le u-1$, the curve corresponding in a
linearization chart to the axis associated to the multiplier $\sigma_i$ is precisely the affine
line
\[
p(f_0)+\mathbb{C}\cdot e_i^u.
\]
The last unstable direction, corresponding to the multiplier
$2a\tilde w(a)$, is less explicit. However, by our choice of parameters,
this multiplier dominates a power of the other unstable multipliers.
Hence, if $r>0$ is fixed, the cone field
\[
C_r^w:=\left\{(v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1},v_k)\in\mathbb{C}^k\ ;\
r\max_{1\le j\le k-1}|v_j|<|v_k|\right\}
\]
is contracted by $f_0^{-1}$ provided $\delta$ is large enough.
Therefore, the strong unstable manifold $W^{uu}_{p(f_0),loc}$ is a curve
arbitrarily close to the affine line
\[
p(f_0)+\mathbb{C}\cdot e_u^u.
\]
On the other hand, the hyperbolic set $\Lambda(f_0)$ is also contained in
the plane $\{x=0\}$, and each of its local stable manifolds is transverse
to that plane, intersecting it in a unique point. Thus, for $f_0$, every
intersection point between $W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$ and
$W^s_{\Lambda(f_0),loc}$ actually belongs to $\Lambda(f_0)$, which is a
highly nongeneric situation.

To understand where these points lie, observe that the dynamics of
$f_0^2$ in the $(y_i,w)$-coordinates is given by
\[
H_i\colon (y_i,w)\mapsto\left(
\sigma_i\Big(\sigma_i(y_i+\frac{w-\tilde w(a)}{6})
+\frac{q_a(w)-\tilde w(a)}{6}\Big),\,q_a^2(w)\right).
\]
If $w\in V_+(a)$, then Lemma~\ref{le-U} gives
\[
|w-\tilde w(a)-2|<6|a|^{-1}
\quad\text{and}\quad
|q_a(w)-\tilde w(a)|<6|a|^{-1},
\]
and similarly, with the obvious sign changes, if $w\in V_-(a)$.
Using moreover
\[
8|a|^{3/4}<|\sigma_1|<\cdots<|\sigma_{u-1}|<|a|^{4/5},
\]
we obtain
\[
\left(D(1/3,|a|/2)\cup D(0,|a|/2)\right)\times \mathbb{D}_2
\subset
H_i\big(D(-1/3,a/\sigma_i^2)\times V_+(a)\big)
\cap
H_i\big(D(0,a/\sigma_i^2)\times V_-(a)\big).
\]
In particular, if $(z,x,y,w)\in\Lambda(f_0)\cap\mathcal U_+$, then
\[
w\in V_+(a)\subset D(1,3|a|^{-1})
\quad\text{and}\quad
y_i\in D(-1/3,|a/\sigma_i^2|),
\]
where $|a/\sigma_i^2|<|a|^{-1/2}$.

Combining the two previous discussions, we conclude that no point of
$W^s_{\Lambda(f_0),loc}\cap\mathcal U_+$ can lie on one of the coordinate
hyperplanes of $W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$. This is exactly Assumption~\ref{decalage}.
head: environment

label: le-grille-2
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Fix $1\le i\le s$. The proof follows the same scheme as that of
Lemma~\ref{le-decalage} and relies on the following two claims.

\begin{itemize}
\item[\textbf{(1)}] Let $t\in W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$ and
$v\in\mathcal E^{s,i}_{f_0,t}$ for some $1\le i\le s$. Then
\[
v=v^ce^c+v_ie_i^s,
\qquad
\frac{|v^c|}{|v_i|}<\frac{6|\tau_1|}{|a|^{1/4}}.
\]
\item[\textbf{(2)}] Let
$G_+\colon f_0(\mathcal U_+)\to\mathcal U_+$ be the inverse branch
of $f_0$. If $t\in f_0(\mathcal U_+)$ and $v\in C_\eta^{ss}$, then,
setting $v':=D_tG_+(v)$, its components satisfy
\[
|v'^c|\geq\frac{|\tau_1|}{2}\left|\sum_{j=1}^s v_j'^{s}\right|-\frac{1}{|a|^{1/2}}\sum_{j=1}^s|v_j'^s|.
\]
In particular, if the only non-zero stable component is $v_i'^s$, then
\[
|v'^c|\geq\frac{|\tau_1|}{4}|v_i'^s|.
\]
\end{itemize}

Since $T_tW^u_{p(f_0),loc}\subset\{x=0\}$, these two estimates imply
the desired conclusion.

\bigskip
\noindent\textbf{Proof of (1).} By Proposition~\ref{prop-dynaslope} and
Remark~\ref{rk-dynaslope}, there exists a unique holomorphic
section of the projectivized tangent bundle over
$W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$, invariant under the dynamics and equal to
$e^s_i$ at $p(f_0)$.

Parametrizing $W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$ by the projection onto the
$(y,w)$-coordinates (possibly after shrinking the domain), and
choosing an affine chart in which the coordinate corresponding
to $e^s_i$ is identically equal to $1$, this yields a unique
holomorphic map from $W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$ to
$\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}^{s-1}\times\mathbb{C}^{u-1}\times\mathbb{C}$, equivariant under
the differential of $f_0$, of the form
\[(y,w)\mapsto\begin{array}{rl}
\big(A^c(y,w),A^s_1(y,w), \ldots,A^s_{i-1}(y,w), &\\
A^s_{i+1}(y,w),\ldots, & A^s_s(y,w),
A^u_1(y,w),\ldots,A^u_u(y,w)\big).
\end{array}\]

Since the $y_i$-component of $y$ only interacts with itself in
$f_0$, and since the differential of $f_0$ is independent of $y$,
the uniqueness of the section implies that it does not depend on
$y$. Moreover, as the differential of $f_0$ preserves the
subspace $E^{c,i}$ spanned by $e^c$ and $e^s_i$, it follows again
by uniqueness that all the above components vanish except for
$A^c(y,w)$.

We are thus left with studying this last component, which does
not depend on $y.$                                       

The action of the differential on $E^{c,i}$ at $(y,w)$ is
\[\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha+w\beta & \tau_i(w-\tilde w(a))\\
0 & \gamma_i
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi(\hat w) & \tau_i\hat w\\
0 & \gamma_i
\end{pmatrix},\]
where we set $\hat w:=w-\tilde w(a)$. Hence, setting
$A(\hat w):=A^c(y,w)$ and
\[\hat q_a(\hat w):=q_a(\hat w+\tilde w(a))-\tilde w(a)
= a\hat w(\hat w+2\tilde w(a)),\]
the invariance of the (projectivized) section implies that
\[\gamma_i A(\hat q_a(\hat w))
=
\phi(\hat w)A(\hat w)+\tau_i\hat w.\]

Using the inverse branch
\[g\colon \mathbb{D}_3\to \hat U_-(a)\subset D(0,3|a|^{-1}),\]
of $\hat q_a$, sending $\mathbb{D}_3$ into a neighborhood of $0$, we obtain
\[A(\hat w) =
\gamma_i^{-1}\big(
\phi(g(\hat w))A(g(\hat w))+\tau_i g(\hat w)
\big),\]
which allows us to define $A$ on $\mathbb{D}_3$ by iteration.


On the other hand, since $A(0)=0$, there exists a holomorphic
function $B$ such that
\[
A(\hat w)=\hat w\,B(\hat w).
\]
Since $g(0)=0$ and $|g(\hat w)|<3|a|^{-1}$ on $\mathbb{D}_3$,
Schwarz's lemma gives
\[
\left|\frac{g(\hat w)}{\hat w}\right|\leq |a|^{-1}.
\]
The sup-norm $\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb{D}_2}$ of $B$ on $\mathbb{D}_2$
then satisfies
\[
\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb{D}_2}
\leq
\frac{2\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb{D}_2}+|\tau_i|}{|a\gamma_i|},
\]
where the factor $2$ comes from $|\phi(\hat w)|<2$.
Thus, using $|\gamma_i|^{-1}<|a|^{3/4}$, we have,
for $|a|$ sufficiently large,
\[
\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb{D}_2}
\leq \frac{|\tau_i|}{|a\gamma_i|-2}
\leq \frac{2|\tau_i|}{|a|^{1/4}}.
\]
Since $g(\mathbb{D}_3)\subset\mathbb{D}_2$, the same bound holds
for $\|B\|_{\infty,\mathbb{D}_3}$.
Hence, for $|\hat w|<3$, we obtain
\[
|A(\hat w)|
\leq \frac{2|\tau_i|}{|a|^{1/4}}\,|\hat w|
< \frac{6|\tau_i|}{|a|^{1/4}},
\]
which proves that the central component is negligible compared
to the stable one when $|a|$ is large. This establishes
\textbf{(1)}.


\bigskip
\noindent\textbf{Proof of (2).} This follows directly from the computation of the differential
of $G_+$ and from the cone contraction property. More precisely,
let $v\in\mathbb{C}^k$, $t\in f_0(\mathcal U_+)$, and set
$v':=D_tG_+(v)$. Writing $w$ for the last coordinate of $t$, and
denoting by $g_+\colon \mathbb{D}_3\to U_+(a)$ the inverse branch of
$q_a$, the components of $v'$ satisfy
\[
v'^c=\psi(t)\left(
v^c-\tau_1\big(g_+(w)-\tilde w(a)\big)
\sum_{j=1}^s\gamma_j^{-1}v^s_j
+\phi(t)v^u_u
\right),
\qquad
v'^s_j=\gamma_j^{-1}v^s_j,
\]
where $\phi(t)=O(|a|^{-1})$ uniformly, and $\psi(t)=(\alpha+g_+(w)\beta)^{-1}$ has modulus
bounded between $1/2$ and $2$.

Since $g_+(w)-\tilde w(a)\simeq 2$ on $U_+(a)$, and since
$v\in C^{ss}_\eta$ implies that the sum of the stable components
dominates both $v^c$ and $v^u_u$, the desired estimate follows.
We leave the details to the reader.
head: environment

label: le-init
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The proof is a reduction to Lemma~\ref{le-init-dim2}. More precisely,
if, after shrinking $V_0$, one of the required properties still failed,
then the same failure would persist on a suitable open subset of the
parameter set $M$ appearing in Lemma~\ref{le-init-dim2}, contradicting
that lemma.

We first state two simple facts about $f_0$. The local unstable
manifold of $p(f_0)$ corresponds to the one associated to
$\mathcal P(\lambda)$, where $\lambda=(a,\alpha,\beta,\epsilon)$, for the
map
\[
\mathcal F_\lambda(z,w)=(\alpha z+\epsilon w+\beta zw,q_a(w))
\]
studied in Section~\ref{sec-dim2}, with the additional stable coordinates
$x$ are fixed to $0$, while the unstable coordinates $y$ are free.
Namely,
\[
W^u_{p(f_0),loc}
=
\{(z,x,y,w)\in\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}^s\times\mathbb{C}^{u-1}\times\mathbb{C}\ ;\
(z,w)\in W^u_{\mathcal P(\lambda),loc},\ x=0\}.
\]
Moreover, as already observed, $\Lambda(f_0)$ is contained in the plane
$\{x=0\}$, and every intersection between
$W^u_{p(f_0),loc}$ and $W^s_{\Lambda(f_0),loc}$ actually belongs to
$\Lambda(f_0)$.

The same facts hold for the maps $f_{\tilde\lambda}\in V_0$
obtained from $f_0$ by replacing
$\lambda=(a,\alpha,\beta,\epsilon)$ with
$\tilde\lambda=(\tilde a,\tilde\alpha,\tilde\beta,\tilde\epsilon)$. That is
\[
f_{\tilde\lambda}(z,x,y,w)
=
\left(\tilde\alpha z+\tilde\epsilon w+\tilde\beta zw
+\tau\cdot x(w-\tilde w(\tilde a)),
\gamma x,
\sigma\left(y+\frac{w-\tilde w(\tilde a)}{6}\right),
q_{\tilde a}(w)\right).
\]
Let $M_0$ be a connected open subset of the set $M$ of
Lemma~\ref{le-init-dim2} such that $f_{\tilde\lambda}\in V_0$ for all
$\tilde\lambda\in M_0$, and write
\[
\tilde M_0:=\{f_{\tilde\lambda}\ ;\ \tilde\lambda\in M_0\}\subset V_0.
\]

For $f\in V_0$, let $G_\pm\colon f^2(\mathcal V_\pm)\to\mathcal V_\pm$
denote the corresponding inverse branches. Then each word
$\omega\in\Sigma=\{-1,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ defines a stable manifold of
$\Lambda(f)$ by
\[
W^s_\omega(f):=
\bigcap_{n\geq0}
G_{\omega_0}\circ\cdots\circ G_{\omega_n}
(\mathbb{D}_R\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}^u_{3/2}).
\]
The set $\mathbb{D}_R\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}^u_{3/2}$ could in fact be replaced by
any of its $s$-graphs, and $W^s_\omega(f)$ coincides with the local
stable manifolds constructed in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop-hyp-graphs}.
Observe that different points of $\Lambda(f)$ may belong to the same
stable manifold.

By Proposition~\ref{prop-hyp-graphs}, the $s$-graph $W^s_\omega(f)$
depend holomorphically on $f\in V_0$ in
$\mathbb{D}_R\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}^u_{3/2}$. The same is true for
$W^u_{p(f),loc}$, viewed as a $u$-graph. Hence, by
Proposition~\ref{prop-relation}, the set
\[
\tilde X_\omega:=\{f\in V_0\ ;\
W^s_\omega(f)\cap W^u_{p(f),loc}\neq\varnothing\}
\]
is either equal to $V_0$ or is a (possibly empty) hypersurface of
$V_0$. The first case is impossible since, for
$\tilde\lambda\in M_0$ the description above gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq-xomega}
\{\tilde\lambda\in M_0\ ;\
W^u_{p(f_{\tilde\lambda}),loc}\cap W^s_\omega(f_{\tilde\lambda})
\neq\varnothing\}
=
M_0\cap X_\omega,
\end{equation}
where $X_\omega$ is the set introduced in Lemma~\ref{le-init-dim2}.
Thus, if $\tilde X_\omega=V_0$, then $M_0\cap X_\omega=M_0$, contradicting
the last point of Lemma~\ref{le-init-dim2}. Therefore each
$\tilde X_\omega$ is a proper analytic subset of $V_0$, which implies Assumption~\ref{free}.

It remains to prove Assumption~\ref{init}, possibly after shrinking
$V_0$. The argument is very close to that of~\cite[Lemma~4.12]{gtv}.

The identity~\eqref{eq-xomega} is a key ingredient, identifying
$\tilde M_0\cap\tilde X_\omega$ with $M_0\cap X_\omega$ via $f_{\tilde\lambda}\mapsto\tilde\lambda.$
Now let $\chi_{p(f)}$ and $\chi_{r_0(f)}$ denote the central
multipliers of the fixed point $p(f)$ and of the $2$-periodic point
$r_0(f)\in\Lambda(f)$, respectively. For $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\xi\in\mathbb{S}^1$,
set
\[
\tilde Y_{\xi,t}:=
\left\{f\in V_0\ ;\ \chi_{r_0(f)}=\xi\chi_{p(f)}^t\right\}.
\]

Let $\Sigma_0\subset\Sigma$ be the set of words eventually equal to $-1$.
A point $x\in W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ is eventually sent to
$W^s_{r_0(f),loc}$ if and only if $x\in W^s_\omega(f)$ for some
$\omega\in\Sigma_0$. Since $\Sigma_0$ is dense in $\Sigma$, and since
the blender property gives
\[
V_0=\bigcup_{\omega\in\Sigma}\tilde X_\omega,
\]
we obtain
\[
V_0\subset
\overline{\bigcup_{\omega\in\Sigma_0}\tilde X_\omega}.
\]
This already gives the first two points of
Assumption~\ref{init}. For the third one, it is enough to show that,
possibly after shrinking $V_0$, every regular point of a hypersurface
$\tilde Y_{\xi,t}$ is crossed by some $\tilde X_\omega$ in a proper way.
A small perturbation of $\omega$ inside $\Sigma_0$ then gives the desired
statement.

We first claim that there exists a neighborhood $\tilde V_0$ of
$\tilde M_0$ such that every irreducible component of some
$\tilde X_\omega$ meeting $\tilde V_0$ also meets $\tilde M_0$.
Otherwise, one could find a sequence $(\omega_n)$, which can be assumed to converge to some $\omega_\infty$ by compactness, and irreducible components
$\tilde Z_{\omega_n}\subset\tilde X_{\omega_n}$, approaching
$\tilde M_0$ without intersecting it. By persistence of proper intersections,
$\tilde X_{\omega_\infty}$ cannot intersect $\tilde M_0$ properly, hence
$\tilde M_0\subset \tilde X_{\omega_\infty}$. Using
\eqref{eq-xomega}, this would imply that $M_0\subset X_{\omega_\infty}$,
again contradicting Lemma~\ref{le-init-dim2}.

Now fix $(\xi,t)\in\mathbb{S}^1\times\mathbb{R}$ and let
$f\in\tilde V_0\cap\tilde Y_{\xi,t}$ be a regular point of
$\tilde Y_{\xi,t}$. By Lemma~\ref{le-blender-selle},
$W^s_{\Lambda(f),loc}$ intersects every $u$-graph in
$\mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times V_+^u$ and in
$\mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times V_-^u$. Since $W^u_{p(f),loc}$ is a $u$-graph in
$\mathbb{D}\times\mathbb{B}^s\times\mathbb{B}^u_{3/2}$, it contains $u$-graphs in both
regions. Therefore there exist at least two different words
$\omega_1,\omega_2\in\Sigma$ such that
\[
f\in \tilde X_{\omega_1}\cap \tilde X_{\omega_2}.
\]

Assume that both intersections
$\tilde X_{\omega_i}\cap\tilde Y_{\xi,t}$ are non-proper at $f$.
Then there exist irreducible components
$\tilde Z_{\omega_i}\subset\tilde X_{\omega_i}$ containing $f$ and
contained in $\tilde Y_{\xi,t}$. Since $f$ is a smooth point of
$\tilde Y_{\xi,t}$, we must have $\tilde Z_{\omega_1}=\tilde Z_{\omega_2}\subset \tilde Y_{\xi,t}.$ By the choice of $\tilde V_0$, this common component meets $\tilde M_0$,
hence, by \eqref{eq-xomega}, the corresponding components in $M_0$
coincide as well. This is impossible by Lemma~\ref{le-init-dim2} since $\omega_1\neq\omega_2$.
Therefore at least one of the two intersections is proper at $f$, which
gives the last point of Assumption~\ref{init}.

This concludes the proof after replacing $V_0$ by $\tilde V_0$.
