label: le-misu
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-misu}
There exists a regular polynomial endomorphism $f_1\in V_0$ such that
Assumptions~\ref{misu} and~\ref{homoclinic} hold in a neighborhood of
$f_1$ in $\operatorname{End}_d^k$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Fix $a$ and all the parameters chosen above. For $c\in\mathbb{C}^*$ sufficiently
small, set
\[
q_c(w):=q_a(w)+cw^d.
\]
The fixed point $\tilde w(a)$ has a holomorphic continuation
$\tilde w_c$ satisfying
\[
q_c(\tilde w_c)=\tilde w_c.
\]
Consider the regular polynomial endomorphism
\[
f_c(z,x,y,w)
=
\left(
\begin{array}{c}
\alpha z+\epsilon w+\beta zw
+\tau\cdot x(w-\tilde w_c)+cz^d\\[0.2em]
(\gamma_i x_i+cx_i^d)_{1\leq i\leq s}\\[0.2em]
\left(\sigma_j\left(y_j+\dfrac{w-\tilde w_c}{6}\right)
+cy_j^d\right)_{1\leq j\leq u-1}\\[0.2em]
q_c(w)
\end{array}
\right).
\]

The plane $\{x=0\}$ is invariant under $f_c$ and contains
$\Lambda(f_c)$ together with all its unstable manifolds. Identifying it
with $\mathbb{C}^{u+1}$, the restriction of $f_c$ takes the form
\[
g(z,y,w)
=
\bigl(g_0(z,w),g_1(y_1,w),\ldots,g_{u-1}(y_{u-1},w),g_u(w)\bigr)
\]
and preserves the sequence of fibrations
\[
\mathbb{C}^{u+1}\to\mathbb{C}^u\to\cdots\to\mathbb{C}.
\]
Applying successively~\cite[Corollary~1.2]{dupont-t-int}, all repelling
periodic points of $g$ belong to the support of its equilibrium measure
$\mu_g$. In particular,
\[
[W^u_{\hat t,loc}]\wedge\mu_g\neq0
\qquad
\text{for every }\hat t\in\hat\Lambda(f_c).
\]
Moreover,
\[
(G_{f_c})|_{\{x=0\}}=G_g,
\qquad
\mu_g=({dd^c} G_g)^{\wedge(u+1)}.
\]
Thus, writing $T_{f_c}:={dd^c} G_{f_c}$,
\[
[W^u_{\hat t,loc}]\wedge T_{f_c}^{\wedge(u+1)}
=
[W^u_{\hat t,loc}]\wedge\mu_g\neq0.
\]
Hence Assumption~\ref{misu} holds in a neighborhood of $f_c$.

For Assumption~\ref{homoclinic}, we now set
\begin{equation}\label{eq-fcA}
f_{c,A}
:=
f_c+A(w-\tilde w_c)^2(1,\mathbf 1_s,0,0),
\qquad
\mathbf 1_s:=(1,\ldots,1),
\end{equation}
where $A\neq0$ will be chosen arbitrarily small. Since this perturbation
vanishes to first order on $\{w=\tilde w_c\}$, the fixed point $p$ and
its multipliers do not depend on $A$. In particular, the bunching conditions in Assumption~\ref{homoclinic}
remain satisfied, and the $z$-axis and the $x_i$-axes remain the coordinate
axes in the linearizing chart of $W^s_{p,loc}$ since the dynamics on it is simply a product dynamics.

Let $g_{c,+}$ and $g_{c,-}$ be the continuations of the inverse branches
$g_+$ and $g_-$ of $q_a$. We set
\[
m_2:=g_{c,+}(\tilde w_c),
\qquad
m_1:=g_{c,-}(m_2).
\]
Hence
\[
q_c(m_1)=m_2,
\qquad
q_c(m_2)=\tilde w_c,
\]
with $m_1,\tilde w_c\in U_-$ and $m_2\in U_+$. By
Lemma~\ref{le-U}, after decreasing $|c|$ if necessary,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-m1m2}
|m_1-\tilde w_c|\leq\frac6{|a|},
\qquad
|m_2-\tilde w_c|\geq2-\frac6{|a|}.
\end{equation}
A direct estimate on $q_c'$ also gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq-gc}
|g_{c,-}(w)-\tilde w_c|
\leq\frac2{|a|}|w-\tilde w_c|
\qquad\text{on }U_-.
\end{equation}

The problem is independent of $y$ so we simply ignore these coordinates in what follows.

The $y$-coordinates play no role in the argument and will be omitted
from now on. Since the $z$-, $x$- and $w$-coordinates of $f_{c,A}$ do
not depend on $y$, the corresponding coordinates of
$W^u_{p,loc}$ depend only on $w$. We denote them by $z_A(w)$ and
$x_A(w)$, and set
\[
\tilde q_A:=\bigl(z_A(m_1),x_A(m_1),m_1\bigr)\in W^u_{p(f_{c,A}),loc}.
\]
Since $q_c^2(m_1)=\tilde w_c$, we write
\[
q_A:=f_{c,A}^2(\tilde q_A)
=
\bigl(z_A^{(2)},x_A^{(2)},\tilde w_c\bigr)\in W^s_{p(f_{c,A}),loc}\cap W^u_{p(f_{c,A})}.
\]

We show that all the stable coordinates of $q_A$ are nonzero. The
$x$-coordinates are simpler, so we only detail the $z$-coordinate.
For $c$ small, the $x$-maps are $1/2$-Lipschitz and the $z$-map is
$2$-Lipschitz on the polydiscs under consideration. We also use
$\|\tau\|_1<1$, which follows from our previous choice of $\delta$.

The invariance equation for the $x$-components and~\eqref{eq-gc}
give
\begin{equation}\label{eq-xA}
\|x_A(w)\|_\infty
\leq
\frac{5|A|}{|a|^2}|w-\tilde w_c|^2.
\end{equation}
Indeed, if
\[
M_A^x:=
\sup_{w\neq\tilde w_c}
\frac{\|x_A(w)\|_\infty}
{|A||w-\tilde w_c|^2},
\]
then
\[
M_A^x
\leq
\frac2{|a|^2}M_A^x+\frac4{|a|^2}.
\]

Set
\[
u_A(w):=z_A(w)-z_0(w)
\]
and
\[
M_A^z:=
\sup_{w\neq\tilde w_c}
\frac{|u_A(w)|}
{|A||w-\tilde w_c|^2}.
\]
Using the invariance equation, \eqref{eq-gc}, \eqref{eq-xA} and
$|w-\tilde w_c|\leq6|a|^{-1}$ on $U_-$, we obtain
\[
M_A^z
\leq
\frac8{|a|^2}M_A^z
+\frac4{|a|^2}
+\frac{240}{|a|^6}.
\]
Since $|a|>100$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-zA}
M_A^z\leq\frac5{|a|^2}.
\end{equation}

Let $z_A^{(1)},z_A^{(2)}$ and $x_A^{(1)},x_A^{(2)}$ denote the
coordinates after the first and second iterates of $\tilde q_A$.
Equations~\eqref{eq-m1m2}, \eqref{eq-xA} and \eqref{eq-zA} give,
with deliberately coarse constants,
\[
|z_A^{(1)}-z_0^{(1)}|
\leq\frac{40}{|a|^2}|A|,
\qquad
\|x_A^{(1)}\|_\infty
\leq\frac{40}{|a|^2}|A|.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-zA-return}
\left|
z_A^{(2)}-z_0^{(2)}
-A(m_2-\tilde w_c)^2
\right|
\leq
\frac{300}{|a|^2}|A|.
\end{equation}

Let $z_p$ be the $z$-coordinate of $p$. If
$z_0^{(2)}\neq z_p$, then $z_A^{(2)}\neq z_p$ for $A$ sufficiently
small by continuity. If $z_0^{(2)}=z_p$, then
\eqref{eq-m1m2} and~\eqref{eq-zA-return} give
\[
|z_A^{(2)}-z_p|
\geq
|A|
\left[
\left(2-\frac6{|a|}\right)^2
-\frac{300}{|a|^2}
\right]>0.
\]
Thus
\[
z_A^{(2)}\neq z_p.
\]

For every $1\leq i\leq s$, the same computation, without the coupling
term involving $\tau$, gives
\[
|x_{i,A}^{(2)}|
\geq
|A|
\left[
\left(2-\frac6{|a|}\right)^2
-\frac{20}{|a|^2}
\right]>0.
\]


Finally, the orbit segment from $\tilde q_A$ to $q_A$ stays in the
domains where the map is locally biholomorphic, and the cone conditions
give the transversality of
\[
f_{c,A}^2(W^u_{p,loc})
\quad\text{and}\quad
W^s_{p,loc}
\]
at $q_A$. Therefore $q_A$ is the homoclinic intersection required in
Assumption~\ref{homoclinic}.

Since $A$ can be chosen arbitrarily small and Assumption~\ref{misu} is
open, both Assumptions~\ref{misu} and~\ref{homoclinic} hold in a
neighborhood of $f_1:=f_{c,A}$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Let $f_1$ be given by Lemma~\ref{le-misu}. Taking a sufficiently
small neighborhood $\Omega_u$ of $f_1$ in $\operatorname{End}_d^k$ (or in
$\operatorname{Poly}_d^k$), contained in $V_0$, Assumptions~\ref{misu} and
\ref{homoclinic} hold throughout $\Omega_u$.

All the remaining assumptions also hold on $\Omega_u$:
Assumptions~\ref{verti}, \ref{hyperbolic} and~\ref{repelling} by
Lemma~\ref{le-ass1et2}, Assumption~\ref{saddle} by
Lemma~\ref{le-ass-saddle}, Assumption~\ref{blender} by
Lemma~\ref{le-blender-selle}, Assumptions~\ref{free} and~\ref{init} by
Lemma~\ref{le-init}, Assumption~\ref{decalage} by
Lemma~\ref{le-decalage}, and Assumption~\ref{grille} by
Lemma~\ref{le-grille-2}. This completes the proof.
head: environment

label: th-chasse-d2
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-chasse-d2}
Assume that $d=2$. There exist arbitrarily large values of $a$ and arbitrarily small $A,B\in\mathbb{C}$ such that the rational self-map of $\mathbb{P}^2$
\[
f_{\lambda}[z:w:t]
=
\bigl[
\alpha zt+\epsilon wt+\beta zw:
a(w^2-t^2)+Az\ell_a(w,t):
t^2+Bw\ell_a(w,t)
\bigr],
\]
with $\lambda=(a,A,B),$ has the following property. There exists $(Z,f)\in\mathcal Z$, with
$f\in\mathrm{End}_2^2$ arbitrarily close to $f_{\lambda}$ in
$\mathrm{Rat}_{2}^2$, such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item\label{it-chasse-1}
$f$ satisfies all the conditions of Section~\ref{sec-ass} for $k=2$,

\item\label{it-chasse-2}
there exists $n\geq0$ such that $f^n(Z)$ intersects
$W^s_{p(f),\mathrm{loc}}$ transversely, where $p(f)$ is given by
Assumption~\ref{saddle}.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: \bf Remark
body_md:
Although this reduction of \ref{it-chasse-2} may look elementary, our proof is quite specific to
the present setting. So far, we do not know how to extend it to higher dimensions (in
particular to subvarieties of higher codimension), nor to the polynomial locus
$\mathrm{Poly}_d^2$, where the strategy breaks down.
head: environment

label: le-homof0
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-homof0}
For $|a|$ large enough, $p(f_a)$ admits a transverse homoclinic satisfying Assumption~\ref{homoclinic} with $r=1$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Let $g_-$ be the inverse branch
of $q_a$ fixing $c_a$. Since $g_-(w)=c_a+O(|a|^{-1})$ on $\mathbb{D}_2$
and $|\rho_a|=|\alpha+\beta c_a|<1$, the local unstable manifold at $p(f_a)$ is given by a graph
\[
 \{(\varphi_a(w),w)\,:\,w\in\mathbb{D}_2\}\subset W^u_p,\ \text{ with } \varphi_a(w)=z_a+O(|a|^{-1}).
\]
As $q_a(-c_a)=c_a$, the point $x_a=f_a(\varphi_a(-c_a),-c_a)$
belongs to $W^u_{p(f_a)}\cap W^s_{p(f_a)}$. This intersection is transverse
because $q_a'(-c_a)\neq0$. Moreover, the Jacobian of $f_a$ at $(\varphi_a(-c_a),-c_a)$ is $(\alpha-\beta c_a)q_a'(-c_a)\neq0$.
Finally, using
$z_a=\epsilon c_a/(1-\rho_a)$ and $c_a=-1+O(|a|^{-1})$,
we obtain
\[
 \pi_z(x_a)-z_a
 =(\rho_a-2\beta c_a)\varphi_a(-c_a)-\epsilon c_a-z_a
 =\frac{2\epsilon c_a(\alpha-1)}{1-\rho_a}
   +O(|a|^{-1}).
\]
Since $\epsilon(1-\alpha)\neq0$, we have $x_a\neq p(f_a)$
for $|a|$ sufficiently large.
head: environment

label: rk-homoclinic
title: \bf Remark
body_md:
\label{rk-homoclinic}\normalfont
Observe that in our setting Assumption~\ref{homoclinic} is a little bit artificial. Indeed, the saddle point $p(f_a)$ has a single stable multiplier. Therefore, the assumptions on the multipliers in Proposition~\ref{prop-zariski-dense-unstable} are automatically satisfied with $r=1$, by Assumption~\ref{saddle}. Moreover, in dimension $2$, the Zariski density of $W^u_{p(f)}$ can in fact be established by a much simpler argument.
head: environment

label: le-stable
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-stable}
For $\lambda=(a,A,B)$ sufficiently close
to $\lambda_a$, the map $f_\lambda$ has a saddle fixed point
$p(f_\lambda)$ satisfying
\[
 W^s_{p(f_\lambda)}=L_a\setminus\{I\}.
\]
Moreover, $f_\lambda$ preserves the pencil of lines through $I$
when $A=0$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The line $L_a$ is invariant, and the restriction of $f_\lambda$ to
$L_a\setminus\{I\}$ is the affine map
\[
 z\mapsto \rho_a z+\epsilon c_a.
\]
Since $0<|\rho_a|<1$, this map has a unique attracting fixed point.
For $\lambda$ sufficiently close to $\lambda_a$, its transverse
multiplier remains of modulus greater than one, giving the first
assertion.

If $A=0$, the last two homogeneous coordinates of $f_\lambda$
depend only on $(w,t)$. Hence $f_\lambda$ induces a rational map
on the base of the pencil of lines through $I$.
head: environment

label: le-fixed
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-fixed}
The line $L_\infty$ is totally invariant and $I$ is the only indeterminacy point. Blowing up $I$
in the source resolves $F$ as a morphism
\[
 \pi:X=\mathrm{Bl}_I\mathbb{P}^2\to\mathbb{P}^2,
 \qquad
 \hat F:X\to\mathbb{P}^2.
\]
The morphism $\hat F$ is finite and maps the exceptional divisor
isomorphically onto $L_\infty$. In particular, $F$ contracts no curve. Its topological degree
is $3$, and, for every irreducible curve $C\subset\mathbb{P}^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-degree-curve}
 e_C\deg F(C)=2\deg C-\mathrm{mult}_I(C),
 \qquad e_C=\deg(F_{|C}).
\end{equation}
The restriction to $L_\infty\setminus\{I\}$ extends to the homography
\begin{equation}\label{eq-infinity-d2}
 [H:U]\mapsto[(a+\beta)H-a\beta U:H].
\end{equation}
Its fixed points $q=[\beta:1:0]$ and $s=[a:1:0]$ are respectively
saddle and attracting for $F$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Since $B=0$, the last homogeneous coordinate of $F$ is $T^2$.
Thus there is no indeterminacy in $\mathbb{C}^2$, and $L_\infty$ is totally
invariant. On $T=0$, the first two coordinates are
\[
 U\bigl((a+\beta)H-a\beta U\bigr)
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad UH.
\]
As $a\beta\neq0$, their only common zero on $L_\infty$ is $I$.

In the chart $H=1$ centered at $I=[1:0:0]$, a first-order expansion
of \eqref{eq-family} in the coordinates \eqref{eq-HUT} gives
\[
 F[1:U:T]
 =
 \left[
 (a+\beta)U+\rho_a T+O\bigl(\|(U,T)\|^2\bigr):
 U:T^2
 \right].
\]
On the blowup, writing $U=\sigma u$ and $T=\sigma v$ and cancelling
the common factor $\sigma$, we obtain
\[
 \left[
 (a+\beta)u+\rho_a v+O(\sigma):
 u:\sigma v^2
 \right].
\]
Consequently, the exceptional divisor $E=\pi^{-1}(I)$ is mapped by
\[
 [u:v]\mapsto[(a+\beta)u+\rho_a v:u:0].
\]
Since $\rho_a\neq0$, this is a bijection onto $L_\infty.$ Thus no
indeterminacy remains after this single blowup of the source.

Now, let \(\mathcal L\) denote the class of a line in \(\mathbb{P}^2\), and set $\mathcal H=\pi^*\mathcal L.$ Since the homogeneous coordinates of \(F\) have degree \(2\), their pullbacks define sections of the class \(2\mathcal H\). The preceding computation shows that these sections have a common exceptional factor \(\tau\), vanishing to order one along \(E=\{\tau=0\}\). After cancelling this common factor, the resulting class is \(2\mathcal H-E\). Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq-resolution-class}
\hat F^*\mathcal L=2\mathcal H-E.
\end{equation}



On the other hand, let $C\subset\mathbb{P}^2$ be an irreducible curve, and write
$D=\deg C$ and $m=\mathrm{mult}_I(C)$.
The total transform formula
\[
 \pi^*C=\hat C+mE
\]
gives $\hat C=D\mathcal H-mE$.
Using
\[
 \mathcal H^2=1,\qquad \mathcal H\cdot E=0,\qquad E^2=-1,
\]
we obtain
\[
 \hat F^*\mathcal L\cdot\hat C
 =(2\mathcal H-E)\cdot(D\mathcal H-mE)
 =2D-m\geq D>0,
\]
since $m\leq D.$ By the projection formula (see e.g. \cite[\S1.3]{DF01}),
\[
 e_C\deg F(C)
 =\mathcal L\cdot\hat F_*\hat C
 =\hat F^*\mathcal L\cdot\hat C
 =2\deg C-\mathrm{mult}_I(C).
\]
Thus, $\hat F$ contracts no curve different from $E$ and we have already seen that $E$ is sent on $L_\infty.$ Therefore, $\hat F$ is finite and the same holds for $F.$

Moreover, by \cite[Corollary~3.4]{DF01}, the topological degree is
\begin{equation}\label{eq-topological-degree}
(\hat F^*\mathcal L)^2
 =(2\mathcal H-E)^2=3.
\end{equation}



Finally, cancelling the factor $U$ in the restriction to $T=0$
gives~\eqref{eq-infinity-d2}. The tangent multipliers at $q$
and $s$ are $a/\beta$ and $\beta/a$, respectively, while both
transverse multipliers are zero. Since $|a|>|\beta|$, the points
$q$ and $s$ are respectively saddle and attracting for $F$.
head: environment

title: \bf Remark
body_md:
The total invariance of $L_\infty$ does not by itself imply that the blow-up
of the map at an indeterminacy point contained in $L_\infty$ is equal to
$L_\infty$. This is already illustrated by the case $A=B=0$.
head: environment

label: rk-contract
title: \bf Remark
body_md:
\label{rk-contract}
Since the set of degree-$d$ rational maps that do not contract any curve is Zariski open, Lemma~\ref{le-fixed} implies that a generic map $f_\lambda$ in our family does not contract any curve.
head: environment

label: le-delta
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
We have $F^n(C)=L_a$ and $F^{m-1}(C)=L_a\neq \tilde L_\lambda$, so $C$ is not
a component of $\Delta_m$. Let $\xi=L_a\cap \tilde L_\lambda=[0:0:1]$ and
$N=m-n-1$. The affine action on $L_a$ is an automorphism. Choose
$y\in L_a\cap\mathbb{C}^2$ with $F^N(y)=\xi$. The finite proper map
$F^n:C\cap\mathbb{C}^2\to L_a\cap\mathbb{C}^2$ is onto, so $y$ has an affine
preimage $x\in C$. Then $F^{m-1}(x)=\xi\in \tilde L_\lambda$, as required.
head: environment

label: cor-fixed
title: \bf Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-fixed}
For any $n\geq1,$ the set of $n$-periodic points of $F$ is finite.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Let $C$ be an irreducible curve of $n$-periodic points. Set $C_j=F^j(C)$ and $D_j=\deg Y_j$, for $0\leq j\leq n$.
Since $F^n_{C}$ is the identity, we have that $e_{C_j}$ is equal to $1.$ Hence, by~\eqref{eq-degree-curve},
\[
 D_{j+1}=2D_j-\mathrm{mult}_I(C_j)\geq D_j.
\]
By periodicity, we must have equality, hence $\mathrm{mult}_I(C)=\deg C$. Therefore, $C$ has to be a line through $I.$ However, $\tilde L_\lambda$ intersects any such line and contains no periodic points.
head: environment

label: prop-rigidity
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-rigidity}
Let $Z\subset\mathbb{P}^2$ be an irreducible curve. Suppose that for every
$n\geq0$ and every irreducible component $D$ of $\Delta_n$, the curves
$Z$ and $D$ have no intersection in $\mathbb{C}^2$. Then $Z=L_\infty$.
Equivalently, the same conclusion holds if all strict forward images by $F^n$
of $Z$ avoid $L_a\cap\mathbb{C}^2$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
As $Z$ has no intersection in $\mathbb{C}^2$ with the components of $\Delta_n,$ $n\geq0,$ it cannot be one of these components.

Now, assume $Z\neq L_\infty$. Let $\nu\colon C\to Z$ be its normalization,
$\Sigma=\nu^{-1}(Z\cap L_\infty)$, and write
$(h_m,u_m)=F^m\circ\nu$ on $C\setminus\Sigma$, in the affine
coordinates $(H/T,U/T)$. By~\eqref{eq-third-value},
\[
 u_m:C\setminus\Sigma\to
      \mathbb{P}^1\setminus\{0,r-c,\infty\}.
\]
If one $u_m$ is constant then $F^m(Z\cap\mathbb{C}^2)$ is an entire horizontal line, which is impossible since in this case it meets $\tilde L$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$.
The finiteness of the set of holomorphic maps from an algebraic curve to  $\mathbb{P}^1\setminus\{0,r-c,\infty\}$ implies that $\{u_m\ ;\ m\geq0\}$ is
finite. Since $u_{m+1}=u_mh_m$, the pairs $(h_m,u_m)$ also form a
finite family. Hence $F^{m+p}\circ\nu=F^m\circ\nu$ for some
$m\geq0$, $p\geq1$. The curve $C=F^m(Z)$ is consequently fixed
pointwise by $F^p$ and thus is a curve of $p$-periodic curve. This is impossible by Corollary~\ref{cor-fixed} and gives the desired contradiction.
head: environment

label: prop-DMM
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-DMM}
Assume that $\mathbf{(C_2)}$ fails for some $(Z,f_{\lambda'})\in\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F}$, with $\lambda'=(a,A',0)\in V_*$ and $A'\neq0$. After possibly shrinking $V_*$, there exists an integer $k\geq0$ such that, for every $(Z,f_\lambda)\in\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F}$ with $\lambda\in V_*$, the reduced strict image $f_\lambda^k(Z)$
\begin{itemize}
    \item is irreducible,
    \item is invariant under $f_\lambda$,
    \item contains $s(f_\lambda)$ and
    $W^u_{q(f_\lambda),loc}$,
    \item is independent of $Z$, i.e.,
    $f_\lambda^k(Z)=f_\lambda^k(Y)$ whenever
    $(Y,f_\lambda)\in\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F}$.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
We first show that every member of the fiber over $F=f_{\lambda_*}$ is supported on $L_\infty$. Suppose that such a member $Z$ has a component different
from $L_\infty$. By Proposition~\ref{prop-rigidity} and Lemma~\ref{le-delta}, $Z$ has a nonempty proper intersection with some $\Delta_m$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$.
Indeed, if $Z$ shares a component with some $\Delta_n$, we choose $m$ larger than all the corresponding indices and apply Lemma~\ref{le-delta}. Otherwise, Proposition~\ref{prop-rigidity} applies directly.

This intersection persists for nearby pairs $(Y,f_\lambda)$, and its image under $f_\lambda^m$ lies in $L_a\setminus\{I\}$. By~\eqref{eq-proper-int}, we must therefore have $L_a\subset f_\lambda^m(Y)$ on a nonempty open subset of $\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F}$. For this fixed $m$, the containment condition is Zariski closed over $\mathcal V_0$. By irreducibility, it holds throughout the family over $\mathcal V_0$, contradicting the hypothesis.

Thus the fiber over $\lambda_*$ consists only of $L_\infty$. The restriction of $F$ to $L_\infty$ extends to a homography for which $q(F)$ is repelling and $s(F)$ is attracting. Hence $W^u_{q(F),loc}\subset L_\infty$ contains points in the basin of $s(F)$, while $W^s_{q(F),loc}$ intersects $L_\infty$ properly. 


Thus, possibly by reducing $V_*,$ we can assume that for all $(Z,f_\lambda)\in\mathcal Z$ with $f_\lambda\in V_*$, every irreducible component $Z'$ of $Z$ satisfies
\begin{itemize}
\item $Z'\sim L_\infty,$
\item $Z'\cap W^s_{q(f_\lambda),loc}$ is proper,
\item $Z'$ intersects the basin of attraction of $s(f_\lambda).$
\end{itemize}
From this, there are two possibilities for each pair $(Z', f_\lambda)$. The first is that there exists an integer $k \geq 0$ such that $f_\lambda^k(Z')$ contains $W^u_{q(f_\lambda),loc}$. Since its image contains the same germ and $f_\lambda^k(Z')$ is irreducible, it is $f_\lambda$-invariant. In this case, since $Z'$ intersects the basin of $s(f_\lambda)$, the iterate $f_\lambda^k(Z')$ must contain this point. Observe that if the same property holds for $f_\lambda^l(Y')$ for an irreducible component $Y'$ of $Y$ with $(Y,f_\lambda)\in\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F}$, then necessarily $f_\lambda^l(Y') = f_\lambda^k(Z')$, since both contain $W^u_{q(f_\lambda), loc}$.                                                              

Therefore, if this case applies to all $(Z, f_\lambda) \in \mathcal{Z}_{\mathcal F}$ over $V_*$ and every irreducible component $Z' \subset Z$, a density argument implies that we may choose the integer $k \geq 0$ uniformly, and thus the conclusion of the lemma follows.


Otherwise, there exists a pair $(Z', \lambda)$ such that $f_\lambda^N(Z')$ does not contain $W^u_{q(f_\lambda), loc}$ for any $N \geq 0$. A graph transform argument  then implies that if $C$ is a curve intersecting $W^u_{q(f_\lambda), loc}$ properly at a point $x\neq q(f_\lambda)$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq-inter}
\#\left( \bigcup_{N \geq 0} f_\lambda^N(Z') \cap C \right) = +\infty.
\end{equation}
Since the sequence $(x_n)_{n\geq1}$ defined above converges to $q(f_{\lambda_*})$, we may choose $n\geq1$ such that $x_n\neq q(f_{\lambda_*})$ belongs to $W^u_{q(f_{\lambda_*}),loc}$. Let $D_n(\lambda)$ be the continuation of the local branch of $\Delta_n$ through $x_n$. After shrinking $V_1$, this branch intersects $W^u_{q(f_\lambda),loc}$ properly, and the restriction of $f_\lambda^n$ to it is nonconstant. Applying \eqref{eq-inter} with $C=D_n(\lambda)$ gives infinitely many intersection points. Only finitely many of them are mapped to $I$ by $f_\lambda^n$, so there exist $N\geq0$ and
\[
x\in f_\lambda^N(Z')\cap f_\lambda^{-n}(L_a)
\]
such that $f_\lambda^n(x)\neq I$. In other words, $x$ is a proper intersection point between $f_\lambda^N(Z')$ and $f_\lambda^{-n}(W^s_{p(f_\lambda)})$.
head: environment

label: prop-delta_n
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-delta_n}
Assume that, for every \((Z',f_{\lambda'})\in\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F}\) with \(\lambda'=(a,A',0)\in V_*\), condition $\mathbf{(C_2)}$ holds. Then, the same is true for all \((Z,f_\lambda)\in\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F}\) when \(\lambda=(a,A,0)\) and \(A\neq0\) is arbitrarily small.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
For each fixed $m\geq0$, the condition $L_a\subset f_\lambda^m(Z)$ is Zariski closed over $\mathcal V_0$. Moreover, if it holds for some $m$, then it holds for every $m'\geq m$. Therefore, it holds for a fixed $m\geq0$ for every

$$
(Z',f_{\lambda'})\in\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F},
\qquad \lambda'=(a,A',0)\in V_*.
$$

By Zariski closedness, the same condition then holds on every irreducible component of $\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F}$ over $\mathcal A:=\{f_\lambda:\lambda=(a,A,0),\ A\in\mathbb C\}$ that dominates $\mathcal A$. The remaining components are vertical, hence lie over finitely many parameters $A$. We may therefore choose $A\neq0$, arbitrarily close to $0$, outside this finite exceptional set. For such $A$, every point of the fiber lies on a component dominating $\mathcal A$, and the conclusion follows.
head: environment

label: le-pinceau
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-pinceau}
Assume that $g_B$ has degree $2$ and
\[
B\neq \frac{2a}{c}.
\]
Then $L_a$ is not totally invariant. If $Z\subset\mathbb{P}^2$ is an algebraic
curve such that, for every $n\geq0$, the strict preimage
$f_{(a,0,B)}^{-n}(L_a)$ has no proper intersection with $Z$ outside $I$, then
$Z$ is a union of lines through $I$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The line $L_a$ is totally invariant if and only if the fixed point
$[c:1]$ is totally invariant under $g_B$. Using $a(c^2-1)=c$, the equation
for its preimages factorizes as
\[
a(w^2-t^2)-c\bigl(t^2+Bw(w-ct)\bigr)
=(w-ct)\bigl((a-cB)w+ac\,t\bigr).
\]
When $g_B$ has degree $2$, the second factor defines the same point as
$w-ct$ if and only if $B=2a/c$. Thus, under our assumptions, the backward
orbit of $[c:1]$ is infinite, and the successive strict preimages of $L_a$
contain infinitely many distinct lines of the pencil.

Let $D:=\deg Z$, and choose affine coordinates centered at $I$,
with the line at infinity of this chart chosen not to be a component of
$Z$. Write
\[
h=h_0+\cdots+h_D
\]
for an equation of $Z$, with $h_j$ homogeneous of degree $j$. For infinitely many lines $L$ of the pencil, we have $Z\cap L=\{I\}$. Hence, the
restriction of $h$ to each such line vanishes at $I$ with multiplicity $D$.
Therefore, if $[u:v]$ is the direction of $L$,
\[
h_j(u,v)=0,\qquad j=0,\ldots,D-1.
\]
Since this holds for infinitely many directions, $h_j=0$ for every $j<D$.
Thus $h=h_D$ is homogeneous, and $Z$ is a union of lines through $I$.
head: environment

label: th-inter
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-inter}
Let $a$ and $V_a$ be as above. Let
$\mathcal Z \subset \mathcal X_D^{1} \times \mathrm{Rat}_{2}^2$
be an algebraic subvariety that surjects onto $\mathrm{Rat}_{2}^2$, and assume
that we are in the case covered by Proposition~\ref{prop-DMM}.
Then there exist $Z \subset \mathbb{P}^2$ and $\lambda\in V_a\cap P_a$
with $(Z,f_\lambda)\in\mathcal Z$ such that, for some $n\geq0$,
$Z$ and $f_\lambda^{-n}(W^s_{p(f_\lambda)})$ intersect properly.

label: rk-inter
title: \bf Remark
body_md:
\label{rk-inter}
Actually, this gives a contradiction with our assumptions, i.e., \eqref{eq-proper-int} and the one of Proposition~\ref{prop-DMM}. To be more precise, an intersection as in Theorem~\ref{th-inter} is persistent. Therefore, it also holds for some $(Z',f_{\lambda'})\in\mathcal Z$ with $\lambda'\in\mathcal V_0\cap V_a$. If \eqref{eq-proper-int} is verified then this implies that $f_{\lambda'}^n(Z')$ contains $L_a$ in a persistent way. This contradicts the assumption of Proposition~\ref{prop-DMM} that we also used.  At the end, the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{th-inter} is that either \eqref{eq-proper-int} does not hold or Proposition~\ref{prop-delta_n} is satisfied.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
In order to apply Proposition~\ref{prop-DMM}, consider
\[
\mathcal Z_{P_a}
:=
\{(Z,\lambda)\in\mathcal X_D^1\times P_a\,;\,
  (Z,f_\lambda)\in\mathcal Z\},
\]
from which we remove the irreducible components that do not surject onto
$P_a$.

Choose one irreducible component $\mathcal T$ coming from the dominating
family to which Proposition~\ref{prop-DMM} applies. We denote by
$\mathcal T_{V_a}$ and $\mathcal T_{V_*}$ its restrictions over
$V_a\cap P_a$ and $V_*\cap P_a$, respectively.

By Proposition~\ref{prop-DMM}, there exists $k\geq0$ such that, for $\lambda\in V_*\cap P_a$, the reduced strict image $f_\lambda^k(Z)$ is irreducible, invariant, contains $s(f_\lambda)$ and $W^u_{q(f_\lambda),loc}$, and depends only on $\lambda$. In particular, it equals $L_\infty$ when $B=0$ and $A\neq0$.

We restrict to a dense Zariski open subset of $\mathcal T$ where these images have constant degree, and denote again by $\mathcal Z_{P_a}$ the closure of their family in the corresponding Chow variety. We may thus assume that $k=0$ generically, while allowing the special fibers to have several components or multiplicities. The monodromy argument below will exploit the fact that this image family is generically single-valued.

We also need to control its fibers over $B=0$. Near $\lambda_*=(a,A_*,0)$, the same blow-up of $I$ resolves all nearby maps in our family, as in Lemma~\ref{le-fixed}. When taking limits, strict transforms may acquire additional components on the exceptional divisor. At $B=0$, these components map into $L_\infty$, which is invariant. Thus any additional components arising in limits of the iterated images remain supported on $L_\infty$.

On the other hand, Proposition~\ref{prop-DMM} gives $f_\lambda^k(Z)=L_\infty$ for $\lambda=(a,A,0)$ near $\lambda_*$. Every limiting image cycle over these parameters is therefore supported on $L_\infty$. By algebraicity, the same holds for generic $A$ along the line $B=0$.

In this situation, the projection
\[
\pi:\mathcal Z_{P_a}\to P_a,
\qquad
(Z,\lambda)\mapsto\lambda,
\]
is then generically one-to-one.


Let $E_0$ be the set of bad values of $B$ given by Lemma~\ref{le-pinceau} (and above), i.e.,
\[
E_0:=\left\{-\frac1{1-c},-\frac1{1+c},\frac{2a}{c}\right\}.
\]
For $B\notin E_0$, the map $g_B$ has degree $2$ and $L_a$ is not totally invariant. If a cycle $Z$ in the fiber of $\pi$ over $\lambda=(a,0,B)$ had a proper intersection outside $I$ with a strict preimage of $L_a$, this intersection would persist for nearby generic parameters. By invariance of the generic image curves, this would give an intersection with $L_a\setminus\{I\}$, a contradiction. Lemma~\ref{le-pinceau} therefore shows that every cycle in this fiber is supported on lines of the pencil through $I$.

Moreover, the invariance at a generic parameter gives at $\lambda$
\[
 f_\lambda(Z\setminus\{I\})\subset Z.
\]
Since no point outside $I$ is mapped to $I$, even a contracted line is mapped to a point outside $I$, which belongs to a line of the support. 
Thus the component directions form a finite forward-invariant set for $g_B$, and are preperiodic. There are only countably many such directions, hence only countably many possible cycles of the prescribed degree. Hence, the fiber of $\pi$ are finite above such $\lambda=(a,0,B).$

Consequently, since $\pi$ is generically one-to-one, there exists a neighborhood $M\subset P_a$ of
\[
 \{(a,0,B):B\notin E_0\}
\]
on which $\pi$ is an isomorphism over $M$. We may therefore write its fibers as $(Z_\lambda,\lambda)$, with $Z_\lambda$ depending holomorphically on $\lambda\in M$.


By the preceding control of the limiting cycles along
$B=0$, we have $Z_{\lambda_a}=L_\infty.$ Since infinity is superattracting for $g_0$, it is still contained in an attracting domain for $g_B$ when
$B$ is small. Thus, all component directions of $Z_{(a,0,B)}$ lie in this disk. They form a nonempty finite
forward-invariant set, so they contain a periodic point.
The only such point in the disk is the fixed point
continued from infinity. Its line is therefore a
component of $Z_{(a,0,B)}$.

It remains to show that this is incompatible with
monodromy. Parametrize the lines of the pencil different
from $\{w=0\}$ by
\[
 D_\tau:=\{t=\tau w\},
\]
so that $L_\infty=D_0$.
The fixed directions satisfy
\[
 (1-c\tau)\bigl(B-a\tau+(1-ac)\tau^2\bigr)=0.
\]
The first factor corresponds to $L_a$. Since
$1-ac=-a/c$, the other two fixed directions satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq-fixed-lines-B}
 \tau^2+c\tau-\frac ca B=0.
\end{equation}
At $B=0$, they correspond to $L_\infty$ and $D_{-c}$.
They merge at
\[
 B_*=-\frac{ac}{4},
\]
which lies outside $E_0$ for $|a|$ sufficiently large.
A loop based at $0$, avoiding $E_0\cup\{B_*\}$ and winding
once around $B_*$, exchanges these two directions.

The condition
\[
 D_\tau\subset Z_{(a,0,B)}
\]
is algebraic and closed on the curve
\eqref{eq-fixed-lines-B}, over the good parameters.
It holds along the local branch through $(B,\tau)=(0,0)$,
and hence remains valid after continuation along the loop.
Since the family $Z_{(a,0,B)}$ is single-valued, we obtain
\[
 D_{-c}\subset Z_{\lambda_a}=L_\infty,
\]
a contradiction.

label: prop-trans
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-trans}
Let  $\lambda$ be in $V_a\cap\mathcal V_0$ and let $U$ be a small neighborhood of $f_\lambda$ in $\mathrm{Rat}_d^2$ such that Lemma~\ref{le-homof0} still holds on $U.$ If for some $(Z,g)\in\mathcal Z$, with $g\in U,$ we have that for some $n\geq0$
\[
 Z\cap g^{-n}(W^s_{p(g),loc})
\]
is proper, then there exist $(Z',f)\in\mathcal Z$ arbitrarily close to $(Z,g)$,
with $f\in\mathrm{End}_d^2$, and $N\geq n$ such that
$f^N(Z')$ intersects $W^s_{p(f),loc}$ transversely.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
There are two difficulties: the forward image could contain the
stable manifold, or their intersection could be proper but not
transverse. We use Fakhruddin's
\cite[Theorem~1.2]{fakhruddin-generic} to exclude the first
possibility and the local argument of Bedford-Lyubich-Smillie
\cite[Lemma~6.4]{BedfordLyubichSmillie2} to rule out the second.

Choose $(Z',f)\in\mathcal Z$ sufficiently close to $(Z,g)$, with
$f\in\mathrm{End}_d^2$ very general. Persistence of proper
intersections and continuity of the local
stable manifold give a proper intersection of $Z'$ with
$f^{-n}(W^s_{p(f),loc})$. By Fakhruddin's theorem, $f$ has no
invariant algebraic curves. Consequently, the curve
$C:=f^n(Z')$ cannot contain $W^s_{p(f),loc}$ and thus $C$
and $W^s_{p(f),loc}$ intersect properly.

Near $p(f)$, the distinct local stable plaques of $E(f)$ form
a perfect family of pairwise disjoint holomorphic disks.
By continuity and persistence of proper intersections, nearby
plaques still meet $C$. Since $C$ has only finitely many singular
points, one of these plaques meets its regular locus. If the
intersection is tangent, \cite[Lemma~6.4]{BedfordLyubichSmillie2}
gives a transverse intersection with a nearby distinct plaque.
By openness of transversality and density of periodic points
in $E(f)$, we may choose such a plaque based at a periodic point
$q$ homoclinically related to $p(f)$. The inclination lemma then
gives a transverse intersection of $f^N(Z')$ with
$W^s_{p(f),loc}$ for some $N\geq n$.

label: prop-DFR
title: \bf Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-DFR}
For every parameter $\lambda=(a,A,0)\in V_a$ to which
Proposition~\ref{prop-delta_n} applies, there exist arbitrarily small
$\delta,\theta\in\mathbb{C}^*$ and a pair $(Z,f)\in\mathcal Z$, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq-DFR}
f\colon(z,w)\mapsto
\bigl(\alpha z+\epsilon w+\beta zw+\delta z^2,\,
q_a(w)+Az(w-c_a)+\theta\bigr),
\end{equation}
such that $f^n(Z)$ intersects $W^s_{p(f),\mathrm{loc}}$ properly
for some $n\geq0$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
By assumption, when $\lambda=(a,A,0)$ with $A\neq0$ small enough, for every pair
$(Z_\lambda,f_\lambda)\in\mathcal Z_{\mathcal F}$, there exists
$m\geq0$ such that $L_a\subset f_\lambda^m(Z_\lambda)$.
In particular, since $W^u_{p(f_\lambda),\mathrm{loc}}$ is Zariski
dense by Lemma~\ref{le-homof0}, $f_\lambda^m(Z_\lambda)$ intersects
this local manifold properly. Therefore, for sufficiently small
$\delta,\theta\in\mathbb{C}^*$ and $f$ as in the statement, there exists
$(Z,f)\in\mathcal Z$ such that $f^m(Z)$ intersects
$W^u_{p(f),\mathrm{loc}}$ properly near $p(f)$.

There are now two possibilities. If this intersection always
consists only of $p(f)$, then $f^m(Z)$ intersects
$W^s_{p(f),\mathrm{loc}}$, and this intersection must be proper
by Lemma~\ref{le-WsZar}.

Otherwise, the intersection does not always consist only of
$p(f)$. After possibly passing to a ramified cover of the
parameter space, we can follow it holomorphically, denoting it by $h(f)$. We then consider a
linearization $\psi_f\colon\mathbb{C}\to W^u_{p(f)}$ of the dynamics,
depending holomorphically on $f$, such that $\psi_f(0)=p(f)$
and $\psi_f(1)$ is the homoclinic intersection given by
Lemma~\ref{le-homof0}. For sufficiently small
$\delta,\theta\in\mathbb{C}^*$, the point $h(f)$ lies in the image of
a neighborhood of $0$ on which $\psi_f$ is invertible.
We therefore let $\tilde h(f)$ be the unique point near $0$
such that $\psi_f(\tilde h(f))=h(f)$. If $\rho(f)$ denotes the
unstable multiplier of $p(f)$, then
\[
f^n(h(f))=\psi_f\bigl(\rho(f)^n\tilde h(f)\bigr).
\]

On the other hand, the family
$\{f\mapsto\rho(f)^n\tilde h(f)\}_{n\geq0}$ is not normal.
Hence there exist arbitrarily small $\delta,\theta\in\mathbb{C}^*$
such that, for the corresponding map $f$ and some $n\geq0$,
$\rho(f)^n\tilde h(f)$ equals either $1$ or $\rho(f)^{-1}$.
Therefore, $f^{m+n}(Z)$ or $f^{m+n+1}(Z)$ intersects
$W^s_{p(f),\mathrm{loc}}$, and this intersection must be proper,
as above.
head: environment

label: le-WsZar
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-WsZar}
Fix $\lambda=(a,A,0)$, with $A\neq0$, as in
Proposition~\ref{prop-DFR}. For all sufficiently small
$\delta,\theta\in\mathbb{C}^*$, the map $f$ defined by
\eqref{eq-DFR} has a Zariski-dense local stable manifold
$W^s_{p(f),\mathrm{loc}}$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Write $c=c_a$. For $\delta\neq0$ sufficiently small, we have
$a\delta-\beta A\neq0$, so $f$ extends to an endomorphism of
$\mathbb{P}^2$ of degree $2$.

Suppose that $W^s_{p(f),\mathrm{loc}}$ is not Zariski dense,
and let $Y$ be its irreducible algebraic closure. Then $Y$ is
$f$-invariant. It intersects $L_\infty$ in a totally invariant set for its normalisation. Thus, this set has at most $2$ points. As it also possesses a non-critical attracting fixed point, there is only one exceptional point, thus $Y\cap L_\infty$ consists of a single point $\xi,$ which must be fixed.




In the coordinate $u=w/z$, the restriction to $L_\infty$ is
\[
f_\infty(u)=\frac{u(A+au)}{\delta+\beta u}.
\]
Its three fixed points, $\infty,$ $(\delta-A)/(a-\beta)$ and $0.$ The first $2$ are perturbations of the points $s$ and $q$ in Lemma~\ref{le-fixed} respectively, thus they are (non-critical) attracting and repelling. For $0$, which corresponds to the indeterminacy point before perturbation, the multiplier is $A/\delta\neq0.$

By \cite[Theorem~2.1]{DFR}, there are local coordinates
$(x,y)$ centered at $\xi$, with $L_\infty=\{y=0\}$, in which
\[
f(x,y)=\bigl(xU(x,y),\,y^2V(x,y)\bigr),
\qquad U(0,0)V(0,0)\neq0.
\]
Here $\{x=0\}$ is the smooth invariant curve transverse to
$L_\infty$ constructed by Dujardin-Favre-Ruggiero.
The unique branch of $Y$ at $\xi$ must coincide with this curve.
Indeed, the induced map on its normalization has local degree
$2$, so orbits on the branch converge super-exponentially to
$\xi$. On the other hand, $U(0,0)\neq0$ implies
$|x_n|\geq\kappa^n|x_0|$ for some $\kappa>0$.
Thus $x_0=0$, and the branch coincides with the smooth
transverse curve $\{x=0\}$. Hence $Y$ is smooth and transverse to
$L_\infty$ at its unique point at infinity. By Bézout,
$\deg Y=1$.

It remains to exclude a line containing
$W^s_{p(f),\mathrm{loc}}$. Its direction is the stable
eigendirection at $p(f)$, which converges to the horizontal
direction as $(\delta,\theta)\to(0,0)$. Thus, for sufficiently
small parameters, this line cannot correspond to the fixed points $\infty$ and $(\delta-A)/(a-\beta)$ since $A\neq0.$ The remaining case corresponds to horizontal lines $\{w=cst\}$ which cannot be invariant by the choice of \eqref{eq-DFR}, as soon as $\theta\neq0.$

title: Démonstration
body_md:
As explained above, Theorem~\ref{th-inter} gives the following
dichotomy. Either, for some $\lambda\in V_a\cap\mathcal V_0$,
an iterate $f_\lambda^n(Z)$ intersects $L_a\setminus\{I\}$
properly, or, by Proposition~\ref{prop-delta_n}, we have $L_a\subset f_\lambda^n(Z)$ for every $\lambda=(a,A,0)\in V_a$ with $A\neq0$.

In either case, fix $\lambda_0=(a,A,0)$ with $a^{-1}$ and
$A\neq0$ sufficiently small. By Theorem~\ref{th-chasse-julia}, there is a neighborhood
$\Omega$ of $f_{\lambda_0}$ in $\mathrm{Rat}_2^2$ such that
every map in $\Omega\cap\mathrm{End}_2^2$ satisfies all the
assumptions of Section~\ref{sec-ass}.

In the second case, Proposition~\ref{prop-DFR} provides a pair
$(Z,f)\in\mathcal Z$, with $f\in\Omega\cap\mathrm{End}_2^2$,
such that some iterate $f^N(Z)$ intersects
$W^s_{p(f),\mathrm{loc}}$ properly. By
Proposition~\ref{prop-trans}, a further perturbation within
$\Omega$ makes this intersection transverse.

In the first case, the locus of such proper intersections
is nonempty and Zariski open, so we may choose the corresponding
map $f_{\lambda'}$ to be very close to $f_\lambda$ and thus in $\Omega$. Proposition~\ref{prop-trans}
again gives the required transverse intersection after
perturbation into $\Omega\cap\mathrm{End}_2^2$.

label: th-chasse-d3
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-chasse-d3}
Let $d\geq3$ and fix $\eta\neq0$ sufficiently small. The conclusion
of Theorem~\ref{th-chasse-d2} holds with $\mathrm{End}_d^2$ and
$\mathrm{Rat}_d^2$ in place of $\mathrm{End}_2^2$ and
$\mathrm{Rat}_2^2$, for the family \eqref{eq-higher-family}.

label: le-rplus
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-rplus}
Let $f\in\mathrm{End}_d^2$ satisfy Assumptions~\ref{verti}
and~\ref{hyperbolic} with $s=0$ and $u=1$. With the notation
of these assumptions, $f$ has a unique fixed point $r_+(f)$
in $\mathcal U_+$. Moreover, if $r_+(f)\in J_2(f)$ and
$r_+(f)\in\mathbb{D}_R\times U_+$, then
\[
 \Lambda(f)\subset J_2(f).
\]
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
By Assumption~\ref{verti}, $f_{|\mathcal U_+}$ is a horizontal-like map of degree $1$ and index $(0,2)$.
Its inverse branch $G_+$ is defined near $\overline{\mathcal U_+}$ and satisfies
\[
 G_+(\overline{\mathcal U_+})\Subset\mathcal U_+.
\]
It therefore has a unique fixed point $r_+(f)$, which is also the unique fixed point of $f$ in $\mathcal U_+$.

By Assumption~\ref{hyperbolic}, the two maps $f^2_{|\mathcal V_\pm}$ have inverse branches $g_\pm$ on
the common domain $\mathcal D=\mathbb{D}_R\times\mathbb{D}_{3/2}$,
with images relatively compact in $\mathcal D$.
These branches define the limit set $\Lambda(f)$.
If $r_+(f)\in J_2(f)\cap(\mathbb{D}_R\times U_+)$, then
$r_+(f)\in\mathcal D$, and all iterated compositions of
$g_+$ and $g_-$ applied to $r_+(f)$ belong to $J_2(f)$
by total invariance. Every point of $\Lambda(f)$ is a limit
of such points, so closedness gives $\Lambda(f)\subset J_2(f)$.

label: th-dtd-entropy
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-dtd-entropy}
Let $f$ be in $\mathrm{End}_d^2$. If $\nu$ is an invariant ergodic
measure on $\mathbb{P}^2$ of entropy larger than $\log d$, then
$\textup{supp}(\nu)\subset J_2(f)$.
In particular, if $f^N$ admits $M>d^N$ inverse branches on a
bidisk $D$, with pairwise disjoint images relatively compact
in $D$, then the associated limit set $K$ is contained in $J_2(f)$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The first point is simply the criterion of de Th\'elin and Dinh.
For the second, let $g_1,\ldots,g_M$ be inverse branches of $f^N$
on $D$, with pairwise disjoint images satisfying
$\overline{g_i(D)}\subset D$.
They automatically contract the Kobayashi metric of $D$, and
\[
 K=\bigcap_{n\geq1}\ \bigcup_{(i_1,\ldots,i_n)\in\{1,\ldots,M\}^n}
 \overline{g_{i_1}\circ\cdots\circ g_{i_n}(D)}.
\]
This set is invariant under $f^N$ and supports a Bernoulli measure
of entropy $\log M>N\log d$. Thus,
$K\subset J_2(f^N)=J_2(f)$.

label: th-chasse-julia
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{th-chasse-julia}
Fix $d\geq2$ and $S$ as above, and let $A\neq0$ be sufficiently
small. For $|a|$ sufficiently large, every $f\in\mathrm{End}_d^2$
sufficiently close to $F_{a,A}$ satisfies
\[
 \Lambda(f)\subset J_2(f).
\]
head: environment

title: \bf Remark
body_md:
The neighborhood may depend on $a,A,S$. In particular, this makes
no assertion about arbitrary perturbations of the map with $A=0$.
For $d\geq3$, we keep $\eta\neq0$ fixed throughout the proof.
Together with the local construction, the theorem supplies the
remaining small Julia condition in Section~\ref{sec-ass} for $k=2$.
head: environment

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The proof has three main steps. First, we find a suitable rescaling under which the inverse dynamics converges to a correspondence.
Then, we construct sufficiently many inverse branches to apply Theorem~\ref{th-dtd-entropy} in a neighborhood of $F_{a,A}$.
Finally, we verify that the fixed point $r_+(f)$ lies in the required region.

\medskip

\noindent\emph{\textbf{The limiting correspondence.}}
The preimage of the invariant line
$L_a=\{w=c_a\}$ consists of $L_a$,
$\widetilde L_\lambda=\{Az+a(w+c_a)=0\}$, where
$\lambda=(a,A,0)$, and the additional lines $\{w=r\}$ with
$S(r)=0$ when $d\geq3$.

For $A\neq0$, the intersection of $L_a$ and
$\widetilde L_\lambda$ is $(-2ac_a/A,c_a)$, a critical point
of $F_{a,A}$ which escapes to infinity as $A\to0$.
Moreover, for small $A$ and large $|a|$, the
corresponding domains $\mathcal U_-$ and $\mathcal U_+$ in
Assumption~\ref{verti} lie in tubular neighborhoods of radius
$O(|a|^{-1})$ around $L_a$ and $\widetilde L_\lambda$,
respectively.

To keep this geometry for $A\neq0$ and $a$ finite, we rescale
coordinates and parameters
\[
 \tau=1/a,\qquad v=Az/a,\qquad \varepsilon_\tau=A\epsilon/a.
\]
Viewed as a function of $\tau$, the fixed point $c_a$ extends holomorphically to $\tau=0$,
with value $-1$. In these coordinates, the two lines become $\{w=c_a\}$ and
$\{w=-c_a-v\}$, meeting at $(-2c_a,c_a)$.
As $\tau\to0$, they converge respectively to $\{w=-1\}$ and
$\{w=1-v\}$, whose intersection is $(v,w)=(2,-1)$.
This explains the special role of $v=2$ in what follows.

The inverse equations for the conjugated map are
\begin{equation}\label{eq-rescaling-inverse}
 \begin{cases}
 (\alpha+\beta wS(w))v+\varepsilon_\tau w-v'=0,\\
 \tau c_a+(w-c_a)S(w)(w+c_a+v)-\tau w'=0.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
At $(\tau,\varepsilon_\tau)=(0,0)$, the second equation becomes
\[
 (w+1)S(w)(w-1+v)=0.
\]
We keep the roots coming from $w=-1$ and $w=1-v$, whereas
those corresponding to $S=0$ will not be needed in what follows.
The retained inverse dynamics is then described by
\[
 \Gamma=\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal L)+\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal P),\qquad
 \mathcal L(v)=\chi_-v,\quad
 \mathcal P(v)=v\bigl[\alpha+\beta(1-v)S(1-v)\bigr],
\]
where $\chi_-:=\alpha-\beta S(-1)$. This multiplier plays a
special role below, as does
$\chi_+:=\mathcal P'(0)=\alpha+\beta S(1)$.
By our choice of parameters, $0<|\chi_-|<1<|\chi_+|$.
The fact that $\mathcal L$ is contracting is not an obstacle,
since we only need sufficiently many contracting inverse branches
of long iterates.

Since $\deg\mathcal P=d$, the correspondence has degrees
\begin{equation}\label{eq-julia-correspondence-degrees}
 d_0(\Gamma)=2,\qquad d_1(\Gamma)=d+1=:M>d.
\end{equation}

By the equidistribution theorem of Dinh--Sibony~\cite{DS-MT},
in the form \cite[Fact~4.3]{BS-correspondences}, there is a
probability measure $\nu$, charging no polar set, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-julia-equidistribution}
 \Gamma^*\nu=M\nu,\qquad
 M^{-n}(\Gamma^n)^*\delta_x\longrightarrow\nu
\end{equation}
outside a polar exceptional set of targets $x$. Since
$\mathcal L^*\nu+\mathcal P^*\nu=M\nu$, positivity gives
\[
 \mathcal P^{-1}(\textup{supp}\nu)\subset\textup{supp}\nu.
\]
This closed set has more than two points, so it contains
$J(\mathcal P)$. In particular, $0\in\textup{supp}\nu$, since $0$ is a
repelling fixed point of $\mathcal P$, with multiplier $\chi_+$.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-julia-distinguished-symbol}
 M^{-n}\mathcal P^*(\Gamma^{n-1})^*\delta_x
 \longrightarrow\nu^{\mathcal P}:=M^{-1}\mathcal P^*\nu.
\end{equation}
This measure gives positive mass to every neighborhood of $0$ and
counts itineraries whose first forward symbol is $\mathcal P$.

Let $\iota$ be the local inverse of $\mathcal P$ fixing $0$.
It gives a degenerate inverse branch in dimension $2$.
Indeed, choose a small bidisk $\mathcal N$ about $(0,1)$ such that
\[
 H_0(v',w')=(\iota(v'),1-\iota(v')),\qquad
 H_0(\mathcal N)\Subset\mathcal N,
\]
and a disk $V$ about $0$ whose lifted graph
$\{(v,1-v):v\in\overline V\}$ lies in $\mathcal N$.
This map has a unique fixed point $r_+:=(0,1)$, which will be useful
to connect the Julia set $J_2(f)$ to $\Lambda(f)$ after small
perturbations using Lemma~\ref{le-rplus}. Observe that, in these coordinates, the set
$\Lambda(F_{a,A})$ from Assumption~\ref{hyperbolic} degenerates
to the two points $\{(0,1),(0,-1)\}$, but the fact that $(0,1)$
also corresponds to $r_+$ cannot be used directly. What will be
useful is the persistence of inverse branches, i.e., for small
$\tau\neq0$ and $\varepsilon_\tau=A\epsilon\tau$, there is a
small perturbation of $H_0$ corresponding to an inverse branch
of the conjugated map $F_{a,A}$.

In order to construct more inverse branches and lift them to
dimension $2$, we consider regular inverse itineraries of the
correspondence avoiding the finite set
\[
 E=\{2,\infty\}\cup\mathrm{CV}(\mathcal P)
                  \cup\{1-r:S(r)=0\},
\]
where $\mathrm{CV}(\mathcal P)$ is the set of critical values
of $\mathcal P$. Observe that the source Jacobian determinants in
\eqref{eq-rescaling-inverse}, on the two retained sheets, are
\begin{equation}\label{eq-julia-lifting-jacobians}
 \chi_-(v-2)S(-1),\qquad
 (2-v)S(1-v)\mathcal P'(v).
\end{equation}
Regular inverse itineraries avoiding $E$ can therefore be lifted
to dimension $2$.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{\textbf{Returning inverse branches.}}
We now follow the inverse-branch construction in
\cite{BS-correspondences}.
In our case, we avoid a larger finite set $E$. The arguments
remain the same, but we recall them for convenience. Fix a disk $V_0\Subset V$ about $0$, choose
\[
 0<\xi<\frac1{10}\min\{1,\nu^{\mathcal P}(V_0)\},
\]
and put $e=\#E$. Take $l$ sufficiently large that
\[
 \frac{2e}{M-2}\left(\frac2M\right)^l<\xi.
\]
Choose bounded simply connected planar domains
\[
 W_0\Subset W\Subset U\Subset
 \mathbb{C}\setminus\bigcup_{j=0}^l\Gamma^j(E),
 \qquad \nu(W_0)>1-\xi.
\]
To obtain them, cut along parallel rays of zero $\nu$-mass from the
finitely many excluded points to infinity, and exhaust the simply
connected complement by conformal disks. Such a direction exists,
since $\nu$ has no atoms.

We consider inverse itineraries on $U$ which, at every stage, are regular and have images avoiding $E$.
We call them \emph{admissible} and denote their number at depth
$k$ by $G_k$. Then, by the choice of $U$,
\[
 G_l=M^l,\qquad G_{k+1}\geq MG_k-e2^{k+1}\quad(k\geq l).
\]
Indeed, each admissible itinerary has $M$ regular extensions,
since its initial image is simply connected and avoids
$\mathrm{CV}(\mathcal P)$, before excluding source images
meeting $E$. For each of the $2^{k+1}$ labelled words, distinct
inverse branches have disjoint source images, so at most $e$
extensions are excluded. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq-julia-branch-count}
 G_n\geq\left[1-\frac{2e}{M-2}\left(\frac2M\right)^l\right]M^n
 >(1-\xi)M^n\qquad(n\geq l).
\end{equation}
For the same reason, the sum of the spherical areas of the initial
images over all admissible itineraries on $U$ is at most $2^n$,
normalizing the area of $\mathbb{P}^1$ to one. Discarding at most $\xi M^n$
branches makes each remaining area at most $\xi^{-1}(2/M)^n$.
The area--diameter estimate \cite[Appendix]{briendduval2} then gives,
for large $n$,
\[
 \operatorname{diam}v_0(W)
 \leq C_{\xi,U,W}\left(\frac2M\right)^{n/2}.
\]
Apply~\eqref{eq-julia-equidistribution} and
\eqref{eq-julia-distinguished-symbol} at a point of $W_0$ outside
the polar exceptional set. The two discards have total relative
size less than $2\xi$. For large $n$, the remaining itineraries
therefore include $N_n\geq c_0M^n$ returns, with $c_0>0$ independent
of $n$, of the form
\[
 v_n(x)=x,\quad v_{i+1}=R_i(v_i),\quad
 R_i\in\{\mathcal L,\mathcal P\},\qquad v_0(W)\Subset W.
\]
These returns also include one with $R_0=\mathcal P$ and
$v_0(W)\Subset V$. Indeed, $\nu^{\mathcal P}\leq\nu$, so
\[
 \nu^{\mathcal P}(V_0\cap W_0)
 >\nu^{\mathcal P}(V_0)-\xi>9\xi.
\]
The shrinking diameters, together with $W_0\Subset W$ and
$V_0\Subset V$, give the stated compact inclusions.

Since $M=d+1>d$, fix $n$ and these finitely many itineraries so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq-julia-entropy-threshold}
 N_n>d^n.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\emph{\textbf{Lifting and perturbing.}}
At the limiting parameter $(\tau,\varepsilon_\tau)=(0,0)$,
lift an itinerary by setting $w_i=-1$ when $R_i=\mathcal L$
and $w_i=1-v_i$ when $R_i=\mathcal P$, for $0\leq i<n$.
Choose $\rho_1$ sufficiently large and put $D=W\times\mathbb{D}_{\rho_1}$.
The selected returns then give $N_n$ lifted maps $g_{j,0}$ with
$g_{j,0}(\overline D)\Subset D$, including a map $g_{0,0}$
satisfying $g_{0,0}(\overline D)\Subset\mathcal N$.
Composing this map with iterates of $H_0$ gives inverse
itineraries converging to $(0,1)$.

Two distinct branches cannot give
the same sequence of lifted points $(v_i,w_i)_{0\leq i\leq n}$.
Indeed, different symbols give different lifted points at the
corresponding step, since the two lines meet only at $v=2\in E$.
On the other hand, distinct branches with the same symbolic
itinerary have disjoint source images.

By~\eqref{eq-julia-lifting-jacobians}, these finitely many
itineraries and the local branch $H_0$ persist for small
$(\tau,\varepsilon_\tau)$. By compactness over $\overline D$,
distinct branches still give distinct sequences of lifted points
after continuation. For $\tau\neq0$, equality of two initial
points would force equality of their forward orbits, so the
continued return branches have pairwise disjoint images.

Taking $\varepsilon_\tau=A\epsilon\tau$, we obtain these branches
for $F_{a,A}$ when $A\neq0$ is small and $|a|$ is large, and then
for all $f\in\mathrm{End}_d^2$ sufficiently close to $F_{a,A}$.
We denote the continued branches by $g_{j,f}$ and $H_f$,
using the same rescaled coordinates.

By~\eqref{eq-julia-entropy-threshold} and
Theorem~\ref{th-dtd-entropy}, the return limit set satisfies
$K_f\subset J_2(f)$. The connecting inverse branch $g_{0,f}$ gives
\[
 \varnothing\neq g_{0,f}(K_f)\subset\mathcal N\cap J_2(f).
\]
The iterates of $H_f$ converge to its unique fixed point,
which we identify below with $r_+(f)$. Backward invariance
and closedness therefore give $r_+(f)\in J_2(f)$.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{\textbf{Identification of the positive fixed point.}}
It remains to check the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{le-rplus} for $r_+(f)$. Write $(z_+,w_+)$ for the original
coordinates of the fixed point just constructed for $F_{a,A}$.
Since $w_+$ is close to $1$ and $\chi_+\neq1$, its fixed-point
equations give
\[
 z_+=\frac{\epsilon w_+}{1-\alpha-\beta w_+S(w_+)},\qquad
 S(w_+)\bigl(w_++c_a+A\tau z_+\bigr)=\tau,
\]
where the second identity follows by dividing by $w_+-c_a\neq0$.
Since $S(1)\neq0$, these equations yield, uniformly for bounded
small $A$,
\[
 w_+=1+O(\tau),\qquad
 z_+=\frac{\epsilon}{1-\chi_+}+O(\tau).
\]
By uniqueness in the local construction, this is the positive
fixed point $r_+(F_{a,A})$. Thus its continuation $r_+(f)$
belongs to $J_2(f)$ for nearby $f$.

Moreover, by our choice of parameters,
$|\epsilon|<1/10$ and $|1-\chi_+|>1/2$, so $|z_+|<1/4$
for large $|a|$. Since this point belongs to $\mathcal U_+$,
it lies in $\mathbb{D}_R\times U_+$, and the same holds after a
sufficiently small perturbation. Lemma~\ref{le-rplus} now gives
$\Lambda(f)\subset J_2(f)$.
All inverse itineraries were chosen for fixed $S$ before taking
$|a|$ large. No uniformity across the degree drop $\eta=0$ is used.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Choose an irreducible component of $\mathcal Z$ whose incidence map dominates $\mathbb{P}^k\times M$, and still denote it by
$\mathcal Z$. Suppose that the conclusion does not hold.

Take a general relative linear section
$\mathcal T\subset\mathcal Z$ such that the map
\[
 \rho\colon\mathcal I:=\{(Y,x,f):(Y,f)\in\mathcal T,\ x\in Y\}
 \longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^k\times M,\qquad
 (Y,x,f)\longmapsto(x,f),
\]
is generically finite and dominant. More precisely, if $q=\dim\mathcal Z-\dim M$, we take a general linear section of codimension $q-(k-u)$ in the Chow factor. There exists  a dense Zariski open subset $U\subset\mathbb{P}^k\times M$ on which $\rho$ is a finite covering, and such that $x$ is a regular point of $Y$ for all $(Y,x,f)\in\mathcal I,$ with $(x,f)\in U.$

Choose a very general $f_0\in\Omega_u$ such that
$U_{f_0}:=\{x\in\mathbb{P}^k\,:\,(x,f_0)\in U\}$ is nonempty, $D_{p(f_0)}f_0$ only has simple eigenvalues and $p(f_0)$ is not
postcritical. In particular, the backward orbit of $p(f_0)$ is Zariski dense and thus, intersects $U_{f_0}.$

We may therefore choose $m\geq0$ and $(Y_0,x_0,f_0)$ over $U$ such that
\[
 f_0^m(x_0)=p(f_0).
\]
Since $D_{x_0}f_0^m$ is invertible and $Y_0$ is smooth at $x_0,$ we have that
\[
 T_0:=D_{x_0}f_0^m(T_{x_0}Y_0)
\]
is a subspace of dimension $u$ of the tangent space of $p(f_0).$ Moreover, we can follow $x_0$ as a preimage $x_f$ of $p(f)$ by $f^m$ for $f$ in a small neighborhood $V\subset\Omega_u$ of $f_0.$ As $\rho$ is a covering over $(x_0,f_0)\in U$, there exists also $Y_f$ depending holomorphically on $f\in V$ such that $x_f\in Y_f$ and $Y_{f_0}=Y_0.$ This defines a subspace $T_f:=D_{x_f}f^m(T_{x_f}Y_f)$ of dimension $u$ at $p(f).$

If, for some $f\in V$, $T_f$ is complementary to $T_{p(f)}W^s_{p(f),loc}$, we are done. In fact, a monodromy
argument shows that this can always be achieved, possibly after changing the preimage $x_f$ and the sheet $Y_f$ of the
covering $\rho$. More precisely, even if $T_0$ is not transverse to $T_{p(f_0)}W^s_{p(f_0),loc}$, we can extend a basis of $T_0$
to a basis of the full tangent space by adding eigenvectors of $D_{p(f_0)}f_0$. Let $E_0$ denote the $(s+1)$-dimensional
subspace spanned by these eigenvectors.

In the proof of \cite[Theorem~1.7]{t-gorbovickis}, the authors show that any two distinct eigendirections $v_1(f_0)$ and
$v_2(f_0)$ at a fixed point $p(f_0)\in\mathbb{C}^k$ with simple eigenvalues can be exchanged by continuation along a loop
in $M$ based at $f_0$, while the fixed point returns to itself. This holds for both $M=\mathrm{End}_d^k$ and $M=\mathrm{Poly}_d^k$.

Combining such loops, we obtain a loop $\gamma=(f_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ along which the continuations $p_t$ and $E_t$ satisfy
\[
 p_1=p(f_0),\qquad E_1=T_{p(f_0)}W^s_{p(f_0),loc}.
\]
Near $t=0$, this loop lifts to a path $(Y_t,x_t,f_t)$ with $Y_t=Y_{f_t}$, $x_t=x_{f_t}$ and $f_t^m(x_t)=p_t$.
The lift extends as long as $(x_t,f_t)\in U$ and $D_{x_t}f_t^m$ is invertible.

Recording also the continued eigendirections gives a finite algebraic covering of a suitable Zariski open subset of $M$. On the component containing our initial data, the condition
\[
 D_xf^m(T_xY)\oplus E=T_p\mathbb{P}^k
\]
is Zariski open and nonempty, since it holds initially. Its complement therefore projects to a proper algebraic subvariety of $M$. After slightly perturbing $f_0$ within $V$
and deforming $\gamma$ without changing its monodromy, we may avoid this subset and the loci where the lift ceases to be defined.

The lifted path is then defined for all $t\in[0,1]$ and preserves the above complementarity. At its endpoint, $x_1\in(Y_1)_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $f_0^m(x_1)=p(f_0)$, and
\[
 D_{x_1}f_0^m(T_{x_1}Y_1)
 \oplus T_{p(f_0)}W^s_{p(f_0),loc}
 =T_{p(f_0)}\mathbb{P}^k,
\]
as required.

The Zariski closure of the set of special pairs in $\mathcal X_D^u\times M$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. Each of its irreducible components is defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and contains a Zariski dense set of special pairs defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Let $(Y,f)$ be a special pair, and let $Z\supseteq Y$, $m\geq1$
and $g\colon Z\to Z$ be as in the definition, with
$g^*\mathcal A\simeq\mathcal A^{\otimes q}$ for some ample line
bundle $\mathcal A$ on $Z$ and some $q\geq2$.
By \cite[Corollary~2.2]{Fakhruddin}, there exist an embedding
$i\colon Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^N$ and an endomorphism $G$ of
$\mathbb{P}^N$ of degree at least $2$ such that $G\circ i=i\circ g$.

Hence $(Y,f)$ is special if and only if there exist such data
$(Z,g,i,G)$ and integers $m\geq1$, $a>b\geq0$ with
\[
Y\subseteq Z,\quad f^m(Z)=Z,\quad G\circ i=i\circ g,\quad
g\circ f^m=f^m\circ g\ \text{on } Z,\quad g^a(Y)=g^b(Y).
\]

We record $g$ and $i$ by their graphs, which are points of
Chow varieties of $\mathbb{P}^k\times\mathbb{P}^k$ and
$\mathbb{P}^k\times\mathbb{P}^N$, respectively, and $G$ by its coefficients.
Fix $m,a,b,N$, the degree of $G$, the dimension and degree
of $Z$, and the degrees of these graphs.
Observe that all the conditions are algebraic in these parameters, with rational coefficients but some, as $G$ being an endomorphism, are open. Therefore, the tuples $(Y,f,Z,g,i,G)$ satisfying the above conditions form a merely constructible set $\mathcal S$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Hence the points of $\mathcal S$ defined over
$\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ are Zariski dense in $\mathcal S$, and
they project to special pairs defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

As these discrete data vary, the projections of the countably
many sets $\mathcal S$ cover all special pairs. Therefore
the Zariski closure of the set of special pairs coincides
with that of the set of special pairs defined over
$\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.
Moreover, since these parameter sets and projections
are defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, the special pairs defined over
$\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ are invariant under the Galois action.
Their Zariski closure is therefore defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Its irreducible components are therefore defined over
$\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, and the preceding density statement shows
that each contains a Zariski dense set of special pairs
defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

label: le-arithmetic-transverse
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{le-arithmetic-transverse}
Let $\mathcal Z\subset\mathcal X_D^u\times M$ be an
irreducible algebraic family defined over a number field,
invariant under conjugacy and dominant over $M$.
Assume that its general member is irreducible and that some
$(Y,f)\in\mathcal Z$, with $f\in\Omega_u$, satisfies
\eqref{eq-pitch}. Then the special pairs are not Zariski
dense in $\mathcal Z$.

If $M=\mathrm{Poly}_d^k$, there also exist an integer $N\geq1$
and a dense Zariski open subset $\mathcal Z^\circ\subset\mathcal Z$,
defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and invariant under
conjugacy, such that, for every
$(Y,f)\in\mathcal Z^\circ(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, there is a proper
subvariety $W_{Y,f}\subsetneq Y$ of degree at most $N$ with
\[
 \mathrm{Preper}(f)\cap Y\subseteq W_{Y,f}.
\]

title: Démonstration
body_md:
The transverse intersection persists on a nonempty open subset
of $\mathcal Z$. Let $\mathcal S\subset M$ be the algebraic
family given by Lemma~\ref{good-family-end} or
Lemma~\ref{good-family-poly}, according to $M$.
Since $\mathcal Z$ is invariant under conjugacy, we can choose
an irreducible component
\[
 \mathcal Y\subset
 \mathcal Z\cap(\mathcal X_D^u\times\mathcal S)
\]
whose conjugacy translates are Zariski dense in $\mathcal Z$.
This family is dynamically full and maximally varying:
the projection of $\mathcal S$ to the moduli space is finite,
and the stabilizers of maps are finite.

The conjugacy translates of $\mathcal Y$ cover a dense
Zariski open subset of $\mathcal Z$. After conjugating
$\mathcal Y$ by an element of $G(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, we may
therefore assume that it meets the transverse open subset.


After restricting to the open set of maps used in
Proposition~\ref{prop-special}, Theorem~\ref{th-main-blender} and that proposition
give a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subset\mathcal Y$
contained in $\textup{supp}(\mu_{\mathcal Y})$ and containing no
special pair. If special pairs were Zariski dense, choose a
generic sequence of such pairs defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$,
and let $F_j$ be their Galois orbits over a number field of
definition of the family. Theorem~\ref{tm:small-distrib} gives
\[
 \frac{1}{\#F_j}\sum_{t\in F_j}\delta_t
 \longrightarrow
 \frac{\mu_{\mathcal Y}}{\mu_{\mathcal Y}(\mathcal Y)}.
\]
Every measure on the left gives zero mass to $\Omega$,
whereas the limit has positive mass there. This is a
contradiction.

Now suppose that $M=\mathrm{Poly}_d^k$.
Theorem~\ref{th-blender-poly} gives a nonempty open subset
$\Omega\subset\textup{supp}(\mu_{\mathcal Y}^{\mathrm{pol}})$.
The general member of $\mathcal Y$ is not contained in
$H_\infty$, since the transverse intersection given by \eqref{eq-pitch} lies in $\mathbb{A}^k$.
The function $G_{\mathcal Y}$ is continuous and nonnegative,
and
\[
 \mu_{\mathcal Y}^{\mathrm{pol}}
 =(dd^cG_{\mathcal Y})^{\wedge\dim\mathcal Y}.
\]
The function $G_{\mathcal Y}$ cannot vanish identically on
$\Omega$, since the measure
would then vanish there as well. Consequently,
\[
 \int_{\mathcal Y(\mathbb{C})}G_{\mathcal Y}\,
             \mu_{\mathcal Y}^{\mathrm{pol}}>0.
\]
Theorem~\ref{prop-empty-interior} now gives a dense Zariski
open subset $\mathcal Y^\circ$ and a uniform degree bound
for a proper subvariety containing the preperiodic
points of each algebraic pair in $\mathcal Y^\circ$.

The Zariski interior of the union of the conjugacy translates of $\mathcal Y^\circ$ gives the desired invariant open subset
$\mathcal Z^\circ$.

body_md:
Theorem~\ref{th-sparsity} is a direct consequence of Lemma~\ref{le-arithmetic-transverse}, applied to each irreducible component $\mathcal Z$ of $\mathcal X_D^u\times M$, possibly after decomposing $\mathcal Z$ into finitely many components of smaller degree, as explained in Section~\ref{sec-chow}.

For Theorem~\ref{th-special-hypersurface}, let $\mathcal Z_D^u$ be the Zariski closure of the special
pairs in $\mathcal X_D^u\times M$ and we do not yet assume that
it is proper. Since $\mathcal X_D^u$ is projective, the incidence map
\[
 \rho\colon
 \mathcal I_D^u:=
 \{(Y,x,f):(Y,f)\in\mathcal Z_D^u,\ x\in Y\}
 \longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^k\times M,\qquad
 (Y,x,f)\longmapsto(x,f),
\]
has a closed image $\mathcal H_D^u$ whose fiber over $f\in M$ is
\[
 \mathcal H_D^u(f):=\bigcup_{\substack{Y\in\mathcal X_D^u\\
                         (Y,f)\in\mathcal Z_D^u}}Y.
\]
Suppose that this image is all of $\mathbb{P}^k\times M$, and
choose an irreducible component of $\mathcal Z_D^u$ whose
incidence is dominant.

Passing to families of irreducible components of its members
if necessary, we obtain an irreducible family $\mathcal Z$
with generically irreducible members, dominant incidence
and a Zariski dense set of special pairs. This family is
defined over a number field and invariant under conjugacy.

By Theorem~\ref{th-mono-gorbo}, some pair in $\mathcal Z$
satisfies \eqref{eq-pitch}. This contradicts
Lemma~\ref{le-arithmetic-transverse}.
Thus $\mathcal H_D^u$ is a proper closed subset of
$\mathbb{P}^k\times M$, and $\mathcal H_D^u(f)$ is a proper subvariety of
$\mathbb{P}^k$, possibly empty, for general $f\in M$. Put
\[
 \mathcal H_D:=\bigcup_{u=1}^{k-1}\mathcal H_D^u.
\]
By the preceding argument, its fiber $\mathcal H_D(f)$ is a
proper algebraic subvariety of $\mathbb{P}^k$ for general $f\in M$.

Since $\mathcal H_D$ is algebraic, it is contained in a hypersurface of $\mathbb{P}^k\times M$ which is dominant over $M$ and thus, we can replace $\mathcal H_D$ by this hypersurface. Therefore, there exists a dense Zariski open subset
$\mathcal U_D\subset M$, such that the fiber $\mathcal H_D(f)$ is a hypersurface of constant degree $B.$ This defines a morphism
\[\mathcal U_D\to\mathcal X_B^{k-1}.\]
By construction, every $f$-special subvariety of degree
at most $D$ and dimension between $1$ and $k-1$ is contained
in $\mathcal H_D(f)$.
This proves Theorem~\ref{th-special-hypersurface}.

title: Démonstration
body_md:
Throughout, $M=\mathrm{Poly}_d^k$. We first work over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and argue by induction on the dimension, for all degree bounds at once. A density argument then
extends the result to $\mathbb{C}$. For now, we only seek a counting bound outside a proper closed subset of $\mathbb{P}^k\times M$. We will replace this exceptional set by
a family of hypersurfaces at the end. All the sets constructed below are defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

In dimension zero $u=0$, the degree bounds directly the number of points. Fix $u\geq1$ and $D\geq1$.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{\textbf{Reduction to smaller subvarieties.}}
We first find a proper closed subset $\mathcal E\subset\mathbb{P}^k\times M$ and an integer $N\geq1$ such that, for every pair $(Y,f)$ defined over
$\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, with $Y$ irreducible of dimension $u$ and degree at most $D$, either $Y\subset\mathcal E(f)$, or
\begin{equation}\label{eq-main-degree-reduction}
 \mathrm{Preper}(f)\cap Y\subseteq W_{Y,f} 
\end{equation}
for some proper subvariety $W_{Y,f}\subsetneq Y$ of degree at most $N$. Here, for a subvariety of mixed dimension, we add the degrees of its irreducible components.

Reduced irreducible cycles form open subsets of the $\mathcal X_e^u$, since their complements are finite unions of images of the proper maps~\eqref{eq-chow}. For $1\leq e\leq D$, we consider the irreducible components $\mathcal Z$ of the corresponding loci of pairs. They are defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and invariant under conjugacy, since the conjugacy group is connected.

If the incidence map of $\mathcal Z$ is not dominant over $\mathbb{P}^k\times M$, we put the closure of its image in $\mathcal E$. Otherwise, the argument of Theorem~\ref{th-mono-gorbo} gives a pair in $\mathcal Z$ satisfying~\eqref{eq-pitch}. Lemma~\ref{le-arithmetic-transverse}, applied to $\overline{\mathcal Z}$, then gives \eqref{eq-main-degree-reduction}, with a uniform degree bound, on a dense invariant Zariski open subset $\mathcal Z^\circ\subset\mathcal Z$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. We remove this open subset and repeat the argument on the components of $\mathcal Z\setminus\mathcal Z^\circ$.

The dimension drops at each step, so the process ends. The finitely many proper closed sets collected along the way give $\mathcal E$, and we choose $N\geq1$ at least as large as all the resulting degree bounds.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{\textbf{Counting the points.}}
Enlarge $\mathcal E$ by adding $H_\infty\times M$ and the exceptional sets already obtained in dimensions $1,\ldots,u-1$ for the degree bound $N$. Their union $\mathcal H$ is still proper.

Let $(Y,f)$ be a pair defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, with $Y$ irreducible of dimension $u$ and degree at most $D$. If $Y\subset\mathcal H(f)$, there is nothing to count.
Otherwise, its preperiodic points outside $\mathcal H(f)$ are affine, hence lie in $W_{Y,f}$. This subvariety has at most $N$ components, each of dimension less than $u$ and degree at most $N$. The bounds already obtained in smaller dimensions therefore bound the number of these points. Summing over the at most $D$ components of an arbitrary cycle gives the desired bound in dimension $u$.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{\textbf{Conclusion over $\overline\mathbb{Q}$.}}
For the given $D$, take the union of the exceptional sets obtained for $1\leq u\leq k-1$. As in the proof of Theorem~\ref{th-special-hypersurface}, over a dense Zariski open subset $\mathcal U_D\subset M$, its fibers lie in an algebraically varying hypersurface of constant degree. Choose $B$ at least as large as this degree and all the counting bounds. Adding a suitable multiple of $H_\infty$ gives a morphism
\[
 \mathcal H_D\colon\mathcal U_D\longrightarrow
 \mathcal X_B^{k-1},
\]
defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, satisfying the conclusion for pairs defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{\textbf{Passing to $\mathbb{C}$ by density.}}
Finally, suppose that the bound fails for some complex pair $(Y_0,f_0)$ with $f_0\in\mathcal U_D$. Choose $B+1$ distinct preperiodic points $x_1,\ldots,x_{B+1}$ in $Y_0\setminus\mathcal H_D(f_0)$, and fix integers $n_i>m_i\geq0$ such that $f_0^{n_i}(x_i)=f_0^{m_i}(x_i)$.

The set $X$ of tuples $(Y,f,z_1,\ldots,z_{B+1})
 \in\mathcal X_D^u\times\mathcal U_D\times(\mathbb{P}^k)^{B+1}$ such that
\[z_i\in Y,\ \ f^{n_i}(z_i)=f^{m_i}(z_i)
 \text{ for every }i
